# 0. Overview

**Goal.** Targeted Random Projection (TARP) predicts a response from millions of
predictors by (i) screening predictors with a randomized, correlation-based rule, (ii) compressing the survivors
with a sparse random projection, and (iii) fitting a closed-form Normal-Inverse-Gamma (NIG) Bayesian regression
on the compressed features, averaging over many projections. This document applies the method to a real
ultra-high-dimensional problem, tests it against strong alternatives, and checks the quality of its predictions
and prediction intervals.

**Scope (project description).** The study explores variable selection and screening methods, with a focus on **randomized Sure Independence Screening (SIS) projections**, and compares their performance with other approaches. It examines dimensionality reduction (random projection, PCA, randomized SVD), prediction, and the effects of correlation (linkage disequilibrium) and genetic structure (ancestry, relatedness) among the covariates, to understand how incorporating the underlying structure of high-dimensional genetic data can improve statistical modelling and variable selection. *Terminology:* SIS (Fan and Lv, 2008) keeps the top-d predictors by absolute marginal correlation; TARP's first step is its randomized version, randomized independence screening (RIS); a "random SIS projection" is RIS followed by a sparse random projection (RIS-RP).

**Data.** 1001 Genomes *Arabidopsis thaliana*: n = 1,003 accessions, p = 1,712,884 quality-filtered SNPs;
response = days to flowering at 10 °C (FT10, AraPheno study 12). A second flowering trait (FT16, same accessions
at 16 °C) is used for replication.

**Questions.**

1. Do the published TARP claims (aggregation needed; aggregated TARP comparable to PCA projection) hold on new data?
2. How do SIS, randomized SIS (RIS), iterated SIS and structure-adjusted SIS compare, and what do they select when the
   predictors are correlated (LD) and structured (ancestry)? Do they recover a planted truth?
3. Which implementation pitfalls change the conclusions of a screen-then-fit pipeline?
4. How does TARP compare with the standard dense baseline, GBLUP (kernel ridge on all SNPs)?
5. Does adding TARP-style screening on top of a dense kernel, or screening groups of correlated SNPs, help?
6. What is being predicted: population structure, relatedness, or within-lineage genetic signal?
7. Are the prediction intervals calibrated, including within ancestry groups?
8. Does the picture hold for a second trait?

**Evaluation protocol (used throughout).** Ten random 80/20 train/test splits of the 1,003 accessions, identical
across all experiments. Screening and all tuning use training rows only; the test set is touched once. Accuracy is
test mean squared prediction error (MSPE) and R-squared `1 - MSPE/MSPE(mean-only)` per split. Comparisons are paired
by split. The ten splits reuse the same accessions, so standard errors describe split-to-split variation only and
are optimistic.

**How this file runs.** It is self-contained. Heavy computations are cached in `cache/`; if the original checkpoint
files from earlier development runs are present in the project folder they are reused, so a first render takes
minutes. With no caches the full pipeline recomputes (several hours; progress is checkpointed per seed and
resumable). Set `USE_CACHE <- FALSE` to force recomputation.

```{r params}
N_CORES <- 3            # worker cores for bigstatsr; BLAS is pinned to one thread (see helpers)
N_REPS  <- 10           # random train/test splits per experiment
K_IN    <- 5            # inner folds for nested ("honest") tuning
USE_CACHE <- TRUE       # reuse cached results (cache/ or the original checkpoints) when present
RUN_SCALING <- FALSE    # re-run the scaling benchmark (about 10 minutes); otherwise recorded values are shown
K_DIM   <- 100          # dimension of the compressed space
LAM_GRID <- 10^seq(-3, 3, length.out = 61)
C_GRID  <- c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 16)                 # RBF bandwidth multipliers
W_GRID  <- c(0, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3)   # weight on the screened kernel
ALPHA <- 0.10; K_GROUPS <- 3; MIN_G <- 15            # conformal intervals
# optional third trait (e.g. a DOG1-related germination trait): fill in and re-render
THIRD_TRAIT <- list(file = NULL, id_col = "accession_id", y_col = NULL, name = "third trait")
```

# 1. Data and cleaning

The raw data are the 1001 Genomes release v3.1 (1,135 accessions, 12,883,854 candidate variants, about 19 GB
compressed) and the AraPheno flowering-time phenotypes (study 12). Cleaning is done once, outside R, with PLINK 2;
the commands are recorded below (not evaluated when this file is rendered). The R code in this document starts from
the PLINK output.

```bash
# 1. raw genotypes (about 19 GB)
wget -c https://1001genomes.org/data/GMI-MPI/releases/v3.1/1001genomes_snp-short-indel_only_ACGTN.vcf.gz

# 2. quality control and conversion to PLINK binary:
#    biallelic sites only, at most 10% missing calls, minor allele frequency >= 1%
plink2 --vcf 1001genomes_snp-short-indel_only_ACGTN.vcf.gz --allow-extra-chr --set-missing-var-ids @:# \
       --maf 0.01 --geno 0.1 --max-alleles 2 --threads 8 --make-bed --out arabidopsis_1135

# 3. phenotypes (FT10 and FT16 in one file)
wget https://arapheno.1001genomes.org/rest/study/12/values.csv -O flowering_time.csv

# 4. keep accessions that have BOTH genotype and phenotype
awk '{print $2}' arabidopsis_1135.fam | sort -u > geno_ids.txt
tail -n +2 flowering_time.csv | cut -d',' -f1 | sort -u > pheno_ids.txt
comm -12 geno_ids.txt pheno_ids.txt > matched_ids.txt
awk 'NR==FNR{a[$1];next} $2 in a {print $1, $2}' matched_ids.txt arabidopsis_1135.fam > keep_samples.txt
plink2 --bfile arabidopsis_1135 --keep keep_samples.txt --make-bed --out arabidopsis_1135_matched
```

```{r cleaning-table}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Step = c("Raw VCF", "Biallelic sites only (--max-alleles 2)", "Missingness filter (--geno 0.1)",
           "Rare-variant filter (--maf 0.01)", "Accessions with genotype and FT10 phenotype"),
  Remaining = c("12,883,854 variants x 1,135 accessions", "11,769,920 variants", "6,414,265 variants (5,654,946 removed)",
                "1,712,884 variants (4,402,090 removed)", "1,003 accessions (of 1,135 genotyped, 1,163 phenotyped)")),
  caption = "Data cleaning, as logged by PLINK 2")
```

Two facts about the genotype matrix matter later. This species self-pollinates, so there are **no heterozygous calls**
(every genotype is 0 or 2). About 5% of calls are missing (allowed by the 10% per-SNP threshold) and are mean-imputed
for modeling.

# 2. Setup and helper functions

```{r packages}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(bigsnpr); library(bigstatsr); library(parallel) })
if (!requireNamespace("RhpcBLASctl", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Run once in a terminal: micromamba install -c conda-forge r-rhpcblasctl")
}
# bigstatsr refuses nested parallelism, so BLAS is pinned to one thread and parallelism comes from ncores
RhpcBLASctl::blas_set_num_threads(1)
dir.create("cache", showWarnings = FALSE)
```

```{r helpers}
## ---------- generic infrastructure ----------
# Run fun(seed) for every seed, checkpointing each seed (resumable); reuse a final cache or a legacy checkpoint.
run_seeds <- function(name, fun, seeds = seq_len(N_REPS), legacy = NULL) {
  final <- file.path("cache", paste0(name, ".rds"))
  if (USE_CACHE && file.exists(final)) return(readRDS(final))
  if (USE_CACHE && !is.null(legacy) && file.exists(legacy)) {
    x <- readRDS(legacy); return(if (is.data.frame(x)) x else do.call(rbind, x))
  }
  part <- file.path("cache", paste0(name, "_partial.rds"))
  res <- if (file.exists(part)) readRDS(part) else list()
  for (s in seeds) {
    if (length(res) >= s && !is.null(res[[s]])) next
    t0 <- Sys.time(); res[[s]] <- fun(s); saveRDS(res, part)
    cat(sprintf("[%s] seed %d done in %.1f min\n", name, s, as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "mins"))))
  }
  out <- do.call(rbind, res); saveRDS(out, final); out
}
make_split <- function(seed_i, pool = seq_len(n)) {      # same RNG path as every experiment
  set.seed(seed_i)
  tr <- sample(pool, size = round(0.8 * length(pool)))
  list(tr = tr, te = setdiff(pool, tr))
}
sem <- function(x) sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))

## ---------- TARP building blocks ----------
# Step 1: randomized independence screening using ONLY the given training rows.
screen_set <- function(tr_rows, y_vec) {
  gw <- big_univLinReg(G2, y.train = y_vec, ind.train = tr_rows, ncores = N_CORES)
  tt <- gw$estim / gw$std.err
  r <- sign(tt) * sqrt(tt^2 / (tt^2 + (length(tr_rows) - 2))); r[is.na(r)] <- 0   # marginal correlation
  delta <- max(0, (1 + log(p / length(tr_rows))) / 2)
  q_in <- abs(r)^delta; q_in <- q_in / max(q_in)                                  # inclusion probabilities
  list(inc = which(rbinom(p, 1, q_in) == 1), r = r)
}
std_cols <- function(Xs, tr_rows, other_rows) {          # standardize with training statistics only
  cm <- colMeans(Xs[tr_rows, ]); cs <- apply(Xs[tr_rows, ], 2, sd); cs[cs == 0] <- 1
  list(tr = scale(Xs[tr_rows, ], center = cm, scale = cs), other = scale(Xs[other_rows, ], center = cm, scale = cs))
}
screened_gram <- function(inc) {                          # n x n kernel of the screened SNPs over all rows
  Xs <- G2[, inc]; cs <- apply(Xs, 2, sd); keep <- cs > 0
  Xs <- scale(Xs[, keep, drop = FALSE], center = TRUE, scale = cs[keep])
  tcrossprod(Xs) / sum(keep)
}
# Step 2: sparse ternary random matrix, entries +-1/sqrt(2 psi) with probability psi each
tarp_omega <- function(p_gamma, l, psi = 0.25) {
  u <- runif(p_gamma * l); Om <- matrix(0, p_gamma, l); val <- 1 / sqrt(2 * psi)
  Om[u < psi] <- val; Om[u >= psi & u < 2 * psi] <- -val; Om
}
# Step 3: closed-form NIG fit on the compressed features; returns test MSPE
nig_mspe <- function(Z_tr, Z_te, y_c, y_mean, y_te) {
  m <- ncol(Z_tr); mu <- solve(diag(m) + crossprod(Z_tr), crossprod(Z_tr, y_c))
  mean((y_te - ((Z_te %*% mu) + y_mean))^2)
}
# Paper's aggregation: B projections with m_n ~ U[2 log p, 3n/4], simple average of predictions
agg_tarp_pred <- function(X_tr, X_te, y_c, y_mean, p_total, B = 100) {
  p_g <- ncol(X_tr); n_tr <- nrow(X_tr); m_rng <- c(2 * log(p_total), 3 * n_tr / 4)
  rowMeans(vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) {
    m_b <- round(runif(1, m_rng[1], m_rng[2])); Om <- tarp_omega(p_g, m_b)
    Z_tr <- X_tr %*% Om; Z_te <- X_te %*% Om
    mu <- solve(diag(m_b) + crossprod(Z_tr), crossprod(Z_tr, y_c))
    as.numeric((Z_te %*% mu) + y_mean)
  }, numeric(nrow(X_te))))
}
# Randomized SVD (Halko-Martinsson-Tropp) with TARP's sparse matrix as the sketch and q power iterations
rsvd_basis <- function(X, k, q, l = k + 10, psi = 0.25) {
  Q <- qr.Q(qr(X %*% tarp_omega(ncol(X), l, psi)))
  for (i in seq_len(q)) { W <- qr.Q(qr(crossprod(X, Q))); Q <- qr.Q(qr(X %*% W)) }
  B <- crossprod(Q, X); e <- eigen(tcrossprod(B), symmetric = TRUE)
  sweep(crossprod(B, e$vectors[, 1:k, drop = FALSE]), 2, sqrt(pmax(e$values[1:k], 1e-12)), "/")
}
gram_pca_basis <- function(X, k) {                        # exact PCA directions via the n x n Gram matrix
  e <- eigen(tcrossprod(X), symmetric = TRUE)
  sweep(crossprod(X, e$vectors[, 1:k, drop = FALSE]), 2, sqrt(e$values[1:k]), "/")
}
energy <- function(X, V) sum((X %*% V)^2)

## ---------- kernel ridge / GBLUP building blocks ----------
log_evidence <- function(e_scaled, ytil2, rest_ss, n_, a = 0.01, b = 0.01) {   # closed-form NIG marginal likelihood
  s <- 1 + e_scaled; q <- sum(ytil2 / s) + rest_ss
  -0.5 * sum(log(s)) + a * log(b) - lgamma(a) + lgamma(a + n_ / 2) - (a + n_ / 2) * log(b + 0.5 * q)
}
# one eigendecomposition gives LOOCV, evidence and test error for every lambda
kernel_all <- function(K, K_new, y_c, y_new_c, lam_grid) {
  n_ <- length(y_c)
  eg <- eigen(K, symmetric = TRUE); e <- pmax(eg$values, 0); U <- eg$vectors
  yt <- as.numeric(crossprod(U, y_c))
  S <- outer(e, lam_grid, function(ei, li) ei / (ei + li))
  h <- (U^2) %*% S; yhat <- U %*% (S * yt)
  loo <- colMeans(((y_c - yhat) / pmax(1 - h, 1e-8))^2)
  ev <- vapply(lam_grid, function(l) log_evidence(e / l, yt^2, 0, n_), numeric(1))
  P <- K_new %*% (U %*% (yt / outer(e, lam_grid, "+")))
  list(loo = loo, ev = ev, test = colMeans((y_new_c - P)^2), pred = P)
}
kernel_curve <- function(K, K_new, y_c, lam_grid) {       # predictions of the centered response for every lambda
  eg <- eigen(K, symmetric = TRUE); e <- pmax(eg$values, 0); U <- eg$vectors
  yt <- as.numeric(crossprod(U, y_c))
  K_new %*% (U %*% (yt / outer(e, lam_grid, "+")))
}
mse_curve <- function(pred_c, y_new_c) colMeans((y_new_c - pred_c)^2)
gblup_fit <- function(tr, te, y_tr, lam_grid = LAM_GRID) {  # GBLUP with LOOCV lambda (valid: no supervised screening)
  ym <- mean(y_tr); kk <- kernel_all(Kfull[tr, tr], Kfull[te, tr], y_tr - ym, rep(0, length(te)), lam_grid)
  il <- which.min(kk$loo); list(pred = kk$pred[, il] + ym, lam = lam_grid[il])
}
gdist <- function(rows, cols) outer(dK[rows], dK[cols], "+") - 2 * Kfull[rows, cols]   # squared genomic distance
```


# 3. Data description

## 3.1. Removing duplicates and imputation

```{r load-data}
if (!file.exists("arabidopsis_1135_matched.rds")) snp_readBed("arabidopsis_1135_matched.bed")
obj.bigSNP <- snp_attach("arabidopsis_1135_matched.rds")
G <- obj.bigSNP$genotypes; map <- obj.bigSNP$map; fam <- obj.bigSNP$fam
if (!file.exists("flowering_time.csv")) {
  download.file("https://arapheno.1001genomes.org/rest/study/12/values.csv", "flowering_time.csv", mode = "wb")
}

pheno <- read.csv("flowering_time.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Average replicate measurements within each accession.
mean_available <- function(z) {
  if (all(is.na(z))) NA_real_ else mean(z, na.rm = TRUE)
}

pheno_by_accession <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(
    split(pheno, as.character(pheno$accession_id)),
    function(d) {
      data.frame(
        accession_id = as.character(d$accession_id[1]),
        FT10 = mean_available(d$FT10),
        FT16 = mean_available(d$FT16)
      )
    }
  )
)

rownames(pheno_by_accession) <- NULL

# Match accession-level means to genotype sample order.
y_all <- pheno_by_accession$FT10[
  match(as.character(fam$sample.ID),
        pheno_by_accession$accession_id)
]

y16 <- pheno_by_accession$FT16[
  match(as.character(fam$sample.ID),
        pheno_by_accession$accession_id)
]

# Verify phenotype matching.
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(pheno_by_accession$accession_id))
stopifnot(sum(is.na(y_all)) == 0)

cat("Duplicate accession IDs after aggregation:",
    sum(duplicated(pheno_by_accession$accession_id)), "\n")

n <- nrow(G); p <- ncol(G)
stopifnot(sum(is.na(y_all)) == 0)
G2 <- snp_fastImputeSimple(G, method = "mean2", ncores = N_CORES)   # mean-imputed copy used for modeling
cat("accessions n =", n, "| SNPs p =", format(p, big.mark = ","), "| p/n =", round(p / n), "\n")
pheno_by_accession[
  pheno_by_accession$accession_id == "8424",
]
```

## 3.2 Genome-wide relationship matrix and population structure

GBLUP, the dense baseline used below, needs the n x n genomic relationship matrix over **all** SNPs. It is built in
one blockwise pass (20,000 SNPs per block; each block standardized with all accessions, no response involved) and
cached; this one-time pass takes on the order of 20 minutes and is reused for every trait and split.

```{r gram}
gram_file <- "gram_full_snp.rds"
if (!file.exists(gram_file)) {
  RhpcBLASctl::blas_set_num_threads(N_CORES)                 # no bigstatsr parallel call inside this loop
  Kfull <- matrix(0, n, n); p_used <- 0
  blocks <- split(seq_len(p), ceiling(seq_len(p) / 20000)); t0 <- Sys.time()
  for (b in seq_along(blocks)) {
    Xb <- G2[, blocks[[b]]]; cm <- colMeans(Xb); cs <- apply(Xb, 2, sd); keep <- cs > 0
    Xb <- scale(Xb[, keep, drop = FALSE], center = cm[keep], scale = cs[keep])
    Kfull <- Kfull + tcrossprod(Xb); p_used <- p_used + sum(keep); rm(Xb)
    if (b %% 10 == 0) cat(sprintf("Gram block %d / %d (%.1f min)\n", b, length(blocks), as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "mins"))))
  }
  RhpcBLASctl::blas_set_num_threads(1)
  saveRDS(list(K = Kfull / p_used, p_used = p_used), gram_file); rm(Kfull)
}
gr <- readRDS(gram_file); Kfull <- gr$K; dK <- diag(Kfull)
cat("Gram matrix", dim(Kfull), "built from", format(gr$p_used, big.mark = ","), "non-constant SNPs; mean diagonal", round(mean(dK), 3), "\n")
```

```{r structure-plot, fig.height = 5}
eK <- eigen(Kfull, symmetric = TRUE)
pcs5 <- sweep(eK$vectors[, 1:5], 2, sqrt(eK$values[1:5]), "*")        # top genomic axes (ancestry gradients)
var_share <- eK$values / sum(eK$values)
col_ft <- colorRampPalette(c("blue", "yellow", "red"))(100)[cut(y_all, 100, labels = FALSE)]
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
barplot(100 * var_share[1:15], names.arg = 1:15, col = "steelblue", border = NA, xlab = "genomic axis",
        ylab = "% of genome-wide variance", main = "Population structure: kernel eigenvalues")
plot(pcs5[, 1], pcs5[, 2], pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = col_ft, xlab = "axis 1", ylab = "axis 2",
     main = "Accessions on the first two axes\n(blue = early flowering, red = late)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
cat(sprintf("The first axis alone carries %.1f%% of genome-wide variance; the first five carry %.1f%%.\n",
            100 * var_share[1], 100 * sum(var_share[1:5])))

# Pairwise visualization of the first five genomic PCs

pairs(
  pcs5,
  labels = paste0("PC", 1:5),
  pch = 16,
  col = col_ft,
  cex = 0.5,
  gap = 0.7,
  main = "Pairwise genomic structure: first five PCs"
)
```

```{R}
for (j in 1:5) {

  plot(
    pcs5[, j],
    y_all,
    pch = 16,
    cex = 0.55,
    col = "steelblue",
    xlab = paste0("PC", j),
    ylab = "FT10",

  )

  # Linear relationship

    lm(y_all ~ pcs5[, j]),
    col = "red",
    lwd = 2
  )

  # Smooth relationship
  lines(
    lowess(pcs5[, j], y_all),
    col = "darkorange",
    lwd = 2
  )
}
```

### Interpretation

The exploratory analysis suggests that genomic population structure
and flowering-time variation are related but not equivalent.

Although differences in average FT10 are observed across the
genotype-defined clusters, the substantial overlap between their
phenotypic distributions indicates that these clusters do not provide
a clear separation of accessions according to flowering time.

Thus, genomic ancestry alone does not appear sufficient to characterize
the flowering-time phenotype. Considerable phenotypic heterogeneity
remains within the genomic clusters.

These results motivate examining genomic relationships and population
structure as potential sources of variation in prediction, rather than
assuming that genotype-defined clusters correspond directly to
distinct phenotypic groups.

```{R}
pc_fit100 <- lm(

R2_pc100 <- summary(pc_fit100)$r.squared

# Because PC scores are mutually orthogonal,

R2_from_correlations <- sum(pearson_cor^2)
```

### Phenotype associations across the first 100 genomic axes
### Extended analysis of genomic structure and flowering-time associations

To investigate genomic variation beyond the leading principal components, the first 100 eigenvectors of the genome-wide relationship matrix were examined. The cumulative proportion of genomic variation explained increases gradually, reaching 38.38% for the first 100 components, compared with 5.52% for the first two and 20.93% for the first 20 components. This indicates that genomic variation in the accession panel is distributed across multiple dimensions rather than being concentrated in only a few leading axes.

Pearson and Spearman correlations were calculated between each of the first 100 genomic PC scores and FT10. Among these components, PC3 exhibits the strongest marginal linear association with flowering time (Pearson correlation = -0.470; Spearman correlation = -0.423), followed by PC7 (0.334; 0.367) and PC2 (0.238; 0.393). Several additional components, including PC17, PC22, PC26, PC37 and PC41, also exhibit statistically detectable marginal associations after Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment for multiple testing. Overall, 16 of the 100 components have BH-adjusted Pearson correlation p-values below 0.05.

An ordinary least-squares regression of FT10 on the first 100 genomic PCs produces an in-sample \(R^2\) of 0.7275. Because the PC scores are mutually orthogonal, this value equals the sum of their squared marginal Pearson correlations. This result indicates a substantial joint linear association between the genomic coordinates and flowering time within the observed accession panel. It should not, however, be interpreted as heritability, causal ancestry effects or out-of-sample predictive performance.

Taken together, these analyses show that flowering-time variation is associated with multiple dimensions of genome-wide genetic variation, including some lower-ranked components that explain relatively small proportions of total genomic variation. These findings motivate further investigation of population structure, genetic relatedness and their potential influence on SNP screening and genomic prediction.

```{R}

# ================================================================
# EXPLORATORY SCAN OF ALL INFORMATIVE GENOMIC PCs
# ================================================================

# ------------------------------------------------
# 1. Determine the numerical rank of K
# ------------------------------------------------

eig_values <- eK$values

# Ignore numerical zero / negligible eigenvalues
eig_tol <- max(eig_values) * 1e-10

keep_pc <- which(eig_values > eig_tol)

N_PC_ALL <- length(keep_pc)

cat("Total accessions:", n, "\n")
cat("Informative genomic PCs:", N_PC_ALL, "\n")
cat("Eigenvalue tolerance:", eig_tol, "\n")


# ------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct all informative PC coordinates
# ------------------------------------------------

pcs_all <- sweep(
  eK$vectors[, keep_pc, drop = FALSE],
  2,
  sqrt(eig_values[keep_pc]),
  "*"
)

colnames(pcs_all) <- paste0("PC", keep_pc)

cat("PC matrix dimensions:", dim(pcs_all), "\n")


# ------------------------------------------------
# 3. Calculate variance explained by each PC
# ------------------------------------------------

pc_var_pct <- 100 * eig_values[keep_pc] / sum(eig_values)

pc_cumvar <- cumsum(pc_var_pct)


# ------------------------------------------------
# 4. Calculate Pearson and Spearman correlations
# ------------------------------------------------

pearson_all <- as.numeric(
  cor(pcs_all, y_all, method = "pearson")
)

spearman_all <- as.numeric(
  cor(pcs_all, y_all, method = "spearman")
)


# ------------------------------------------------
# 5. Pearson correlation tests
# ------------------------------------------------

# Conventional marginal Pearson test p-values.
# Their independence assumptions may not hold for
# genetically related accessions.

df_test <- length(y_all) - 2

t_stat <- pearson_all * sqrt(
  df_test / pmax(1 - pearson_all^2, 1e-15)
)

p_all <- 2 * pt(
  -abs(t_stat),
  df = df_test
)

# Correct for testing all informative PCs
p_BH_all <- p.adjust(
  p_all,
  method = "BH"
)


# ------------------------------------------------
# 6. Create the complete summary table
# ------------------------------------------------

pc_all_summary <- data.frame(

  PC = keep_pc,

  Eigenvalue = eig_values[keep_pc],

  Variance_pct = pc_var_pct,

  Cumulative_variance_pct = pc_cumvar,

  Pearson_FT10 = pearson_all,

  Spearman_FT10 = spearman_all,

  Pearson_p = p_all,

  Pearson_BH = p_BH_all
)

cat("\nNUMBER OF BH-SIGNIFICANT PCs:\n")
cat(sum(p_BH_all < 0.05), "out of", N_PC_ALL, "\n")


# ------------------------------------------------
# 7. Identify the 30 strongest PC associations
# ------------------------------------------------

top_order <- order(
  abs(pearson_all),
  decreasing = TRUE
)

top30 <- pc_all_summary[
  top_order[1:min(30, N_PC_ALL)],
]

cat("\nTOP 30 PCs BY ABSOLUTE PEARSON CORRELATION:\n")

print(
  transform(
    top30,
    Eigenvalue = round(Eigenvalue, 4),
    Variance_pct = round(Variance_pct, 4),
    Pearson_FT10 = round(Pearson_FT10, 3),
    Spearman_FT10 = round(Spearman_FT10, 3),
    Pearson_BH = signif(Pearson_BH, 4)
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)


# ------------------------------------------------
# 8. Plot correlations across all PCs
# ------------------------------------------------

plot(
  keep_pc,
  pearson_all,
  type = "h",
  lwd = 1.5,
  col = "steelblue",
  ylim = c(-1, 1),
  xlab = "Genomic PC rank",
  ylab = "Pearson correlation with FT10",
  main = "FT10 association across all informative PCs"
)

abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# Highlight BH-significant associations
sig_all <- which(p_BH_all < 0.05)

points(
  keep_pc[sig_all],
  pearson_all[sig_all],
  pch = 19,
  col = "red",
  cex = 0.65
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("All PCs", "BH-adjusted p < 0.05"),
  col = c("steelblue", "red"),
  pch = 19,
  bty = "n"
)


# ------------------------------------------------
# 9. Examine the magnitude of correlations
# ------------------------------------------------

plot(
  keep_pc,
  abs(pearson_all),
  type = "h",
  lwd = 1.5,
  col = "darkorange",
  xlab = "Genomic PC rank",
  ylab = "Absolute Pearson correlation with FT10",
  main = "Magnitude of PC-FT10 associations"
)

abline(h = abs(pearson_all[which.max(abs(pearson_all))]),
       lty = 2, col = "red")


# ------------------------------------------------
# 10. Examine the strongest 30 PCs individually
# ------------------------------------------------

top_pc_numbers <- keep_pc[top_order[
  1:min(30, N_PC_ALL)
]]

par(
  mfrow = c(5, 6),
  mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.5, 1)
)

for (j in top_pc_numbers) {

  plot(
    pcs_all[, match(j, keep_pc)],
    y_all,
    pch = 16,
    cex = 0.35,
    col = rgb(0.1, 0.35, 0.7, 0.4),
    xlab = paste0("PC", j),
    ylab = "FT10",
    main = paste0(
      "PC", j,
      " (r = ",
      round(pearson_all[match(j, keep_pc)], 2),
      ")"
    )
  )

  lines(
    lowess(
      pcs_all[, match(j, keep_pc)],
      y_all
    ),
    col = "firebrick",
    lwd = 2
  )
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


# ------------------------------------------------
# 11. Save complete results
# ------------------------------------------------

saveRDS(
  list(
    pcs_all = pcs_all,
    summary = pc_all_summary,
    top30 = top30,
    eigenvalue_tolerance = eig_tol
  ),

)

cat("\nALL-PC ANALYSIS COMPLETED.\n")
```

## 3.3 Partial least squares:

```{r pls-prediction, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ============================================================
# 3.3 PARTIAL LEAST SQUARES (PLS)
# Compare PLS against PCA and aggregated TARP
# ============================================================

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. SETTINGS
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Reuse Section 4's exact seeds if its results object exists.
# Otherwise use seeds 1:10, assuming make_split() uses these
# same seed values for the original ten outer splits.

PLS_SEEDS <- if (exists("si", inherits = TRUE)) {
  si$seed
} else {
  1:10
}

PLS_INNER_K <- 3

PLS_COMPONENTS <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 10, 15, 20)

cat("PLS outer split seeds:", PLS_SEEDS, "\n")


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. PLS1 FITTING FUNCTION
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# NIPALS algorithm for one continuous response.
#
# X: n x p training genotype matrix
# y: training phenotype
# ncomp: number of components
#
# Returns regression coefficients for every component count.

pls1_fit <- function(X, y, ncomp) {

  X <- as.matrix(X)
  y <- as.numeric(y)

  n <- nrow(X)
  p <- ncol(X)

  x_mean <- colMeans(X)
  y_mean <- mean(y)

  Xr <- sweep(X, 2, x_mean, "-")
  yr <- y - y_mean

  ncomp <- min(ncomp, n - 1, p)

  W <- matrix(0, p, ncomp)
  P <- matrix(0, p, ncomp)
  Q <- numeric(ncomp)

  actual_comp <- 0L

  for (h in seq_len(ncomp)) {

    w <- as.vector(crossprod(Xr, yr))

    nw <- sqrt(sum(w^2))

    if (!is.finite(nw) || nw < 1e-12) {
      break
    }

    w <- w / nw

    t <- as.vector(Xr %*% w)

    tt <- sum(t^2)

    if (!is.finite(tt) || tt < 1e-12) {
      break
    }

    p_load <- as.vector(crossprod(Xr, t)) / tt

    q_load <- sum(yr * t) / tt

    W[, h] <- w
    P[, h] <- p_load
    Q[h] <- q_load

    # Deflate X and y
    Xr <- Xr - tcrossprod(t, p_load)
    yr <- yr - t * q_load

    actual_comp <- h
  }

  if (actual_comp == 0) {
    stop("PLS failed to extract a component.")
  }

  W <- W[, seq_len(actual_comp), drop = FALSE]
  P <- P[, seq_len(actual_comp), drop = FALSE]
  Q <- Q[seq_len(actual_comp)]

  B <- matrix(NA_real_, p, actual_comp)

  for (k in seq_len(actual_comp)) {

    Wk <- W[, seq_len(k), drop = FALSE]
    Pk <- P[, seq_len(k), drop = FALSE]
    Qk <- Q[seq_len(k)]

    B[, k] <- as.vector(
      Wk %*% qr.solve(crossprod(Pk, Wk), Qk)
    )
  }

  list(
    beta = B,
    x_mean = x_mean,
    y_mean = y_mean,
    ncomp = actual_comp
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. PREDICTION FUNCTION
# ------------------------------------------------------------

pls1_predict_path <- function(fit, Xnew) {

  Xnew <- as.matrix(Xnew)

  Xc <- sweep(Xnew, 2, fit$x_mean, "-")

  pred <- Xc %*% fit$beta

  sweep(pred, 2, fit$y_mean, "+")
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. INNER CV FOR COMPONENT SELECTION
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Important:
# RIS screening is repeated inside each inner training fold.
# The inner validation observations are never used for screening.

pls_inner_cv <- function(outer_train, y_outer, seed_i) {

  set.seed(100000 + seed_i)

  n <- length(outer_train)

  fold_id <- sample(
    rep(seq_len(PLS_INNER_K), length.out = n)
  )

  cv_error <- matrix(
    NA_real_,
    nrow = PLS_INNER_K,
    ncol = length(PLS_COMPONENTS)
  )

  for (f in seq_len(PLS_INNER_K)) {

    inner_tr <- outer_train[fold_id != f]
    inner_va <- outer_train[fold_id == f]

    y_tr <- y_outer[fold_id != f]
    y_va <- y_outer[fold_id == f]

    # RIS screening using inner training data only
    sc_inner <- screen_set(inner_tr, y_tr)

    selected <- sc_inner$inc

    if (length(selected) < 2) next

    # Standardization using inner training rows only
    X <- std_cols(
      G2[, selected],
      inner_tr,
      inner_va
    )

    Xtr <- as.matrix(X$tr)
    Xva <- as.matrix(X$other)

    kmax <- min(
      max(PLS_COMPONENTS),
      nrow(Xtr) - 1,
      ncol(Xtr)
    )

    if (kmax < 1) next

    fit <- pls1_fit(Xtr, y_tr, kmax)

    pred_path <- pls1_predict_path(fit, Xva)

    for (j in seq_along(PLS_COMPONENTS)) {

      k <- PLS_COMPONENTS[j]

      if (k <= fit$ncomp) {

        cv_error[f, j] <- mean(
          (y_va - pred_path[, k])^2
        )
      }
    }
  }

  mean_cv <- colMeans(cv_error, na.rm = TRUE)

  if (all(!is.finite(mean_cv))) {
    stop("All inner CV errors are missing for seed ", seed_i)
  }

  best_j <- which.min(mean_cv)

  list(
    best_components = PLS_COMPONENTS[best_j],
    cv_error = mean_cv
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. OUTER TRAIN-TEST PREDICTION
# ------------------------------------------------------------

run_rep_pls <- function(seed_i) {

  cat("\nRunning PLS split:", seed_i, "\n")

  # Same split construction as Section 4
  sp <- make_split(seed_i)

  tr <- sp$tr
  te <- sp$te

  y_tr <- y_all[tr]
  y_te <- y_all[te]

  # Tune component count inside outer training set
  tuning <- pls_inner_cv(
    outer_train = tr,
    y_outer = y_tr,
    seed_i = seed_i
  )

  best_k <- tuning$best_components

  # RIS screening on the complete outer training set
  sc_outer <- screen_set(tr, y_tr)

  selected <- sc_outer$inc

  # Standardize using outer training rows only
  X <- std_cols(
    G2[, selected],
    tr,
    te
  )

  Xtr <- as.matrix(X$tr)
  Xte <- as.matrix(X$other)

  # Fit final outer-training PLS model
  fit_outer <- pls1_fit(
    Xtr,
    y_tr,
    max(PLS_COMPONENTS)
  )

  pred_path <- pls1_predict_path(
    fit_outer,
    Xte
  )

  if (best_k > fit_outer$ncomp) {
    stop("Selected component count exceeds fitted components.")
  }

  pred <- pred_path[, best_k]

  data.frame(
    seed = seed_i,
    PLS = mean((y_te - pred)^2),
    baseline = mean((y_te - mean(y_tr))^2),
    n_screened = length(selected),
    n_predictors = ncol(Xtr),
    selected_components = best_k,
    inner_CV_MSPE = tuning$cv_error[
      match(best_k, PLS_COMPONENTS)
    ]
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. RUN ALL TEN OUTER SPLITS
# ------------------------------------------------------------

pls_results <- bind_rows(
  lapply(PLS_SEEDS, run_rep_pls)
)

print(pls_results)

write.csv(
  pls_results,
  "pls_outer_split_results.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. PLOT: PLS TEST MSPE
# ------------------------------------------------------------

p1 <- ggplot(
  pls_results,
  aes(x = factor(seed), y = PLS)
) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = mean(pls_results$PLS),
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "PLS prediction across outer splits",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Mean test MSPE:",
      round(mean(pls_results$PLS), 2)
    ),
    x = "Outer split seed",
    y = "Test MSPE"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

print(p1)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. PLOT: NUMBER OF SELECTED PLS COMPONENTS
# ------------------------------------------------------------

p2 <- ggplot(
  pls_results,
  aes(x = factor(selected_components))
) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "PLS component selection",
    subtitle = "Number of components selected by inner CV",
    x = "Selected components",
    y = "Number of outer splits"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

print(p2)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 9. COMPARE PLS WITH PCA AND AGGREGATED TARP
# ------------------------------------------------------------

if (exists("si", inherits = TRUE)) {

  comparison <- data.frame(
    seed = pls_results$seed,

    PLS = pls_results$PLS,

    PCA = si$PCA[
      match(pls_results$seed, si$seed)
    ],

    TARP = si$RP_agg[
      match(pls_results$seed, si$seed)
    ]
  )

  comparison_long <- comparison %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = c(PLS, PCA, TARP),
      names_to = "Method",
      values_to = "MSPE"
    )

  # Plot 3: Method comparison
  p3 <- ggplot(
    comparison_long,
    aes(x = Method, y = MSPE, fill = Method)
  ) +
    geom_boxplot(
      alpha = 0.65,
      outlier.shape = NA
    ) +
    geom_jitter(
      width = 0.10,
      size = 2
    ) +
    labs(
      title = "PLS vs PCA vs aggregated TARP",
      subtitle = "Test MSPE over matched outer splits",
      x = NULL,
      y = "Test MSPE"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

  print(p3)

  # Plot 4: Paired PLS-PCA differences
  comparison$PLS_minus_PCA <-
    comparison$PLS - comparison$PCA

  p4 <- ggplot(
    comparison,
    aes(
      x = factor(seed),
      y = PLS_minus_PCA
    )
  ) +
    geom_hline(
      yintercept = 0,
      linetype = "dashed"
    ) +
    geom_col() +
    labs(
      title = "Paired difference: PLS minus PCA",
      subtitle = "Negative values favour PLS",
      x = "Outer split seed",
      y = "Difference in test MSPE"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

  print(p4)

  # Numerical comparison
  comparison_summary <- comparison_long %>%
    group_by(Method) %>%
    summarise(
      Mean_MSPE = mean(MSPE, na.rm = TRUE),
      SD_MSPE = sd(MSPE, na.rm = TRUE),
      Median_MSPE = median(MSPE, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    arrange(Mean_MSPE)

  print(comparison_summary)

  cat(
    "\nPLS beats PCA in",
    sum(comparison$PLS < comparison$PCA, na.rm = TRUE),
    "out of",
    sum(is.finite(comparison$PLS) &
          is.finite(comparison$PCA)),
    "matched splits.\n"
  )

  cat(
    "Mean PLS - PCA MSPE difference:",
    mean(comparison$PLS_minus_PCA, na.rm = TRUE),
    "\n"
  )

  write.csv(
    comparison,
    "pls_method_comparison.csv",
    row.names = FALSE
  )

  write.csv(
    comparison_summary,
    "pls_prediction_summary.csv",
    row.names = FALSE
  )

} else {

  cat(
    "\nSection 4 results object 'si' is not available.",
    "\nPLS results and standalone plots were created.",
    "\nRun Section 4 to create the matched PCA/TARP comparison.\n"
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 10. FINAL PLS SUMMARY
# ------------------------------------------------------------

cat("\n====================================\n")
cat("PARTIAL LEAST SQUARES: FINAL SUMMARY\n")
cat("====================================\n")

cat("Mean test MSPE:", mean(pls_results$PLS), "\n")
cat("SD test MSPE:", sd(pls_results$PLS), "\n")
cat(
  "Mean selected components:",

)
```

## Interpretation of Partial Least Squares Results

### Methodological motivation

The previous experiments used PCA to reduce the dimensionality of the
genotype matrix before regression. PCA identifies directions that
maximize variation in the predictors, without considering the
phenotypic response.

However, directions explaining substantial genotype variation need
not be the most informative directions for predicting flowering time.

Partial Least Squares (PLS) provides a supervised alternative.
Rather than maximizing predictor variance alone, PLS constructs
latent components using the covariance between the genotype matrix
and the response.

For the first component, the basic objective is

\[
w_1 = \arg\max_{\|w\|=1}
\operatorname{Cov}(Xw,y)^2,
\]

where \(X\) denotes the standardized genotype matrix and \(y\)
denotes FT10 flowering time. Subsequent components are extracted
after deflating the information represented by previous components.

Thus, PLS seeks low-dimensional representations that are directly
relevant to the prediction target.

### Experimental design

We evaluated PLS using the same ten outer train-test splits as in
the preceding prediction experiments. Within each outer training
set, RIS was used to screen SNPs before fitting PLS.

The number of PLS components was selected using three-fold
inner cross-validation. The candidate values were

\[
k \in \{1,2,3,5,8,10,15,20\}.
\]

Importantly, RIS screening was repeated within each inner training
fold. Consequently, the corresponding validation observations
were not used to select SNPs or construct the PLS components.

After selecting the component count, RIS was applied to the complete
outer training set, the PLS model was refitted, and predictions
were evaluated on the untouched outer test set.

Predictive performance was measured using

\[
\operatorname{MSPE}
=
\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
\sum_{i\in\mathrm{test}}
(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2.
\]

### Prediction results

The PLS procedure achieved a mean test MSPE of
`r round(mean(pls_results$PLS), 2)` across the ten outer splits,
with a standard deviation of
`r round(sd(pls_results$PLS), 2)`.

The procedure screened an average of
`r round(mean(pls_results$n_screened), 0)` SNPs per split.
The mean number of selected PLS components was
`r round(mean(pls_results$selected_components), 1)`.

```{r pls-report-results, echo=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

pls_report_table <- pls_results %>%
  transmute(
    `Outer split` = seed,
    `Test MSPE` = round(PLS, 2),
    `SNPs screened` = n_screened,
    `PLS components` = selected_components
  )

kable(
  pls_report_table,
  caption = "PLS prediction performance across the ten outer splits"
)
```

### Stability of component selection

```{r pls-report-components, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
component_counts <- pls_results %>%
  count(selected_components)

ggplot(
  component_counts,
  aes(
    x = factor(selected_components),
    y = n
  )
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = n),
    vjust = -0.4,
    size = 4
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "PLS component selection across outer splits",
    x = "Number of selected components",
    y = "Number of outer splits"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The selected number of components varied across outer splits,
reflecting differences in the training samples and the
cross-validation estimates. Nevertheless, the selected models
generally used relatively few components, indicating that a
low-dimensional supervised representation was sufficient for
prediction in these experiments.

### Comparison with previous prediction methods

The mean test MSPEs from the preceding experiments are summarized
below. Lower values indicate better predictive performance.

```{r pls-report-comparison, echo=FALSE}
method_summary <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Mean-only baseline",
    "Exact PCA",
    "Aggregated TARP",
    "PLS with RIS",
    "Full GBLUP"
  ),
  Mean_MSPE = c(
    334.80,
    118.25,
    117.53,
    mean(pls_results$PLS),
    107.20
  )
)

method_summary$Mean_MSPE <- round(
  method_summary$Mean_MSPE, 2
)

kable(
  method_summary,
  caption = "Comparison of mean test MSPE across prediction methods"
)
```

```{r pls-report-comparison-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(
  method_summary,
  aes(
    x = reorder(Method, Mean_MSPE),
    y = Mean_MSPE
  )
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of genomic prediction methods",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Mean test MSPE"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

PLS achieved a mean test MSPE of approximately 115.18, slightly
lower than the corresponding results for exact PCA and aggregated
TARP. This is consistent with the possibility that supervised
dimension reduction captures phenotype-relevant genotype
directions that are not necessarily prioritized by PCA.

Nevertheless, the difference between PLS and the two competing
dimension-reduction methods is relatively small. The results
should therefore be interpreted as evidence of competitive
predictive performance rather than definitive superiority.

Full GBLUP continued to achieve the lowest mean test MSPE,
suggesting that retaining the genome-wide relationship structure
can remain advantageous compared with prediction using a
screened, low-dimensional representation.

### Overall interpretation

The PLS experiment provides an additional perspective on
dimension reduction for genomic prediction. Unlike PCA, PLS
incorporates the response while constructing latent components.
In our experiment, this supervised approach produced competitive
out-of-sample prediction with an average of only 6.6 components.

The result suggests that a relatively small number of
phenotype-informed latent directions can retain useful
predictive information from a much larger genotype matrix.

However, PLS did not outperform full GBLUP in terms of average
test MSPE. Moreover, the small differences between PLS, PCA,
and aggregated TARP warrant a paired comparison across the
same outer splits before drawing stronger conclusions.



# 4. Theoretical foundations: Targeted Random Projection (TARP)

## 4.1 The ultra-high-dimensional prediction problem

Genomic prediction presents a particularly challenging statistical problem because the number of genetic predictors can be substantially larger than the number of observed individuals.

Let

\[
X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}
\]

denote the genotype matrix, where \(n\) is the number of accessions and \(p\) is the number of SNPs. Let

\[
y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^\top\in\mathbb R^n
\]

denote the quantitative phenotype.

In our FT10 analysis, there are approximately \(n=1,003\) accessions and \(p=1.7\) million quality-filtered SNPs. Consequently, \(p\gg n\).

A conventional multiple linear regression,

\[
y=\mathbf 1\mu+X\beta+\varepsilon,
\]

cannot be fitted using ordinary least squares because the number of predictors exceeds the number of observations. In addition, strong correlations between nearby SNPs, arising from linkage disequilibrium (LD), make the estimation problem even more challenging.

The objective of Targeted Random Projection (TARP) is to construct a computationally manageable representation of the genotype matrix while retaining information useful for predicting the phenotype.

The procedure combines three operations:

1. Randomized Independence Screening (RIS), which reduces the predictor set.
2. Sparse Random Projection (RP), which compresses the screened predictors.
3. Bayesian regression using a Normal-Inverse-Gamma (NIG) model, which produces predictions from the compressed representation.

The final estimator averages predictions over multiple random projections.

## 4.2 Stage I: Randomized Independence Screening

The first stage identifies SNPs that exhibit marginal association with the phenotype.

For SNP \(j\), consider the marginal regression

\[
y_i=\alpha_j+\beta_jx_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n_{\mathrm{tr}},
\]

where the regression is calculated using only the training observations.

Let \(\widehat\beta_j\) and \(\operatorname{se}(\widehat\beta_j)\) denote the estimated coefficient and its standard error. The corresponding marginal statistic is

\[
t_j=
\frac{\widehat\beta_j}
{\operatorname{se}(\widehat\beta_j)}.
\]

Under the usual simple linear regression relationship,

\[
t_j=r_j
\sqrt{\frac{n_{\mathrm{tr}}-2}{1-r_j^2}},
\]

where \(r_j\) is the sample Pearson correlation between SNP \(j\) and the phenotype.

Rearranging gives

\[
r_j=
\operatorname{sign}(t_j)
\sqrt{\frac{t_j^2}{t_j^2+n_{\mathrm{tr}}-2}}.
\]

Thus, the marginal t-statistics can be converted into correlation-like association scores.

TARP uses a randomized rather than deterministic screening rule. Define

\[
\delta=
\max\left\{
0,\frac{1+\log(p/n_{\mathrm{tr}})}{2}
\right\}.
\]

The unnormalized inclusion weight for SNP \(j\) is

\[
a_j=|r_j|^\delta.
\]

The inclusion probability is then

\[
q_j=\frac{|r_j|^\delta}
{\max_{\ell=1,\ldots,p}|r_\ell|^\delta}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
0\leq q_j\leq 1,
\qquad
\max_jq_j=1.
\]

Each SNP is independently retained according to

\[
I_j\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q_j).
\]

The screened set is

\[
\mathcal S=\{j:I_j=1\},
\]

and its random cardinality is

\[
p_\gamma=|\mathcal S|.
\]

Conditional on the observed training data,

\[
\mathbb E(p_\gamma)=\sum_{j=1}^{p}q_j.
\]

This is an important distinction from classical Sure Independence Screening (SIS). SIS retains a fixed number of predictors with the largest absolute marginal associations, whereas RIS gives each predictor an inclusion probability determined by its association strength.

Consequently, RIS does not impose a fixed screening budget. Strongly associated predictors are more likely to survive, but weaker predictors can also be retained.

In our implementation, the screening rule is implemented by `screen_set()`. It uses the marginal regression statistics from `big_univLinReg()` and draws the Bernoulli inclusion indicators using `rbinom()`.

All screening statistics are calculated using training observations only.

## 4.3 Stage II: Sparse random projection

After screening, let

\[
X_\gamma\in\mathbb R^{n_{\mathrm{tr}}\times p_\gamma}
\]

denote the standardized genotype matrix containing only the retained SNPs.

Although screening reduces the dimension, the number of surviving SNPs can still be substantially larger than the number of training observations.

We therefore construct a lower-dimensional representation using a random matrix

\[
\Omega\in\mathbb R^{p_\gamma\times m}.
\]

In our implementation, its entries follow a sparse ternary distribution:

\[
\Omega_{jk}=
\begin{cases}
+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\psi}},
&\text{with probability }\psi,\\[6pt]
-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\psi}},
&\text{with probability }\psi,\\[6pt]
0,
&\text{with probability }1-2\psi.
\end{cases}
\]

The parameter \(\psi\) controls sparsity. We use \(\psi=0.25\), giving

\[
\Omega_{jk}=
\begin{cases}
+\sqrt{2},&\text{with probability }0.25,\\
-\sqrt{2},&\text{with probability }0.25,\\
0,&\text{with probability }0.50.
\end{cases}
\]

The entries satisfy

\[
\mathbb E(\Omega_{jk})=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E(\Omega_{jk}^2)=1.
\]

Thus, the projection has mean-zero, unit-variance entries, while half of its entries are zero in expectation.

The compressed genotype representation is

\[
Z_{\mathrm{tr}}=X_\gamma\Omega,
\]

with dimensions

\[
(n_{\mathrm{tr}}\times p_\gamma)
(p_\gamma\times m)
=
n_{\mathrm{tr}}\times m.
\]

For a test genotype matrix \(X_{\gamma,\mathrm{te}}\), we use the same projection matrix:

\[
Z_{\mathrm{te}}=X_{\gamma,\mathrm{te}}\Omega.
\]

Using the same \(\Omega\) for training and test observations is essential: both must be represented in exactly the same projected coordinate system.

The main computational advantage is that the regression is now performed using \(m\) projected features instead of \(p_\gamma\) screened SNPs.

The projection matrix is generated by `tarp_omega()` in our implementation.

## 4.4 Stage III: Bayesian regression on the projected features

After constructing the projected genotype matrix, we fit a Bayesian linear regression model.

First, the training phenotype is centered:

\[
y_c=y_{\mathrm{tr}}-\bar y_{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf 1,
\]

where

\[
\bar y_{\mathrm{tr}}
=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{tr}}}
\sum_{i\in\mathrm{tr}}y_i.
\]

The projected regression model is

\[
y_c=Z_{\mathrm{tr}}\theta+\varepsilon,
\]

where

\[
\theta\in\mathbb R^m
\]

is the vector of regression coefficients in the projected space.

The Gaussian sampling model is

\[
\varepsilon\mid\sigma^2
\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_{n_{\mathrm{tr}}}).
\]

We use the conjugate prior

\[
\theta\mid\sigma^2
\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_m).
\]

The identity prior covariance provides a common shrinkage scale for the projected regression coefficients.

Combining the likelihood and prior gives

\[
p(\theta\mid y_c,\sigma^2)
\propto
\exp\left[
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\left\{
(y_c-Z_{\mathrm{tr}}\theta)^\top
(y_c-Z_{\mathrm{tr}}\theta)
+\theta^\top\theta
\right\}
\right].
\]

Expanding the quadratic expression,

\[
\begin{aligned}
&(y_c-Z_{\mathrm{tr}}\theta)^\top
(y_c-Z_{\mathrm{tr}}\theta)+\theta^\top\theta\\
&=
y_c^\top y_c
-2\theta^\top Z_{\mathrm{tr}}^\top y_c
+\theta^\top
(I_m+Z_{\mathrm{tr}}^\top Z_{\mathrm{tr}})
\theta.
\end{aligned}
\]

Completing the square shows that the conditional posterior is Gaussian:

\[
\theta\mid y_c,\sigma^2
\sim
N(\mu_\theta,\sigma^2 V_\theta),
\]

where

\[
V_\theta=
(I_m+Z_{\mathrm{tr}}^\top Z_{\mathrm{tr}})^{-1}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\mu_\theta=
(I_m+Z_{\mathrm{tr}}^\top Z_{\mathrm{tr}})^{-1}
Z_{\mathrm{tr}}^\top y_c.
}
\]

This is the posterior mean of the projected regression coefficients.

Notice its connection to ridge regression:

\[
\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{ridge}}
=
(Z_{\mathrm{tr}}^\top Z_{\mathrm{tr}}+I_m)^{-1}
Z_{\mathrm{tr}}^\top y_c.
\]

Thus, the posterior mean under the chosen Gaussian prior is algebraically identical to a ridge estimator with penalty parameter equal to one.

This provides a useful interpretation of the Bayesian regression stage: it stabilizes the fit by shrinking the projected coefficients towards zero.

If the variance parameter is also assigned an inverse-gamma prior,

\[
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{IG}(a,b),
\]

the Normal-Inverse-Gamma specification is conjugate. Integrating over the variance parameter produces a Student-t posterior predictive distribution.

For the point predictions evaluated in our experiment, however, we use the posterior mean of the coefficients.

For a test accession with projected genotype vector \(z_*\), the posterior predictive mean is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat y_*=
\bar y_{\mathrm{tr}}+z_*^\top\mu_\theta.
}
\]

For all test observations simultaneously,

\[
\widehat y_{\mathrm{te}}
=
\bar y_{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf 1+
Z_{\mathrm{te}}\mu_\theta.
\]

The corresponding test MSPE is

\[
\operatorname{MSPE}
=
\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{te}}}
\left\|
y_{\mathrm{te}}-\widehat y_{\mathrm{te}}
\right\|_2^2.
\]

In our R implementation, `nig_mspe()` computes this posterior-mean prediction and evaluates its test MSPE.

## 4.5 Stage IV: Aggregation over random projections

A single random projection can produce predictions that depend strongly on the particular realization of the random matrix \(\Omega\).

To reduce this projection-specific variability, TARP aggregates predictions across multiple independently generated projections.

For projection \(b\), let

\[
\widehat y_{\mathrm{te}}^{(b)}
\]

denote its test prediction.

The final aggregated predictor is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat y_{\mathrm{TARP}}
=
\frac{1}{B}
\sum_{b=1}^{B}
\widehat y_{\mathrm{te}}^{(b)}.
}
\]

The original TARP aggregation also randomizes the projection dimension. Specifically,

\[
m_b\sim
\operatorname{Uniform}
\left[
2\log(p),\frac{3n_{\mathrm{tr}}}{4}
\right].
\]

Therefore, different projections can have different dimensions.

In our implementation, we use

\[
B=100
\]

independent projections and average their predictions.

An important detail is that the RIS screening step is performed once for the training set, after which the random projection and regression stages are repeated. The aggregation therefore averages predictions rather than averaging projection matrices.

The procedure is implemented by `agg_tarp_pred()`.

## 4.6 Computational and statistical interpretation

TARP addresses two distinct difficulties.

First, screening reduces the original predictor dimension from \(p\) to \(p_\gamma\), making subsequent computations more manageable.

Second, random projection reduces the dimension further, from \(p_\gamma\) to \(m\), allowing regression to be performed in a much smaller feature space.

The Bayesian regression stage provides shrinkage, while aggregation reduces dependence on a single random projection.

The complete procedure can be summarized as

\[
\boxed{
X
\xrightarrow{\mathrm{RIS}}
X_\gamma
\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Random\ Projection}}
Z
\xrightarrow{\mathrm{NIG\ Regression}}
\widehat y
\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Aggregation}}
\widehat y_{\mathrm{TARP}}.
}
\]

There are two important qualifications.

First, the screening step is supervised because it uses the phenotype, whereas the subsequent random projection is constructed from the screened genotype matrix.

Second, aggregation does not guarantee that every individual projection is accurate. Its purpose is to stabilize the final prediction by averaging across multiple random representations.

In the next section, we evaluate these components separately by comparing a single random projection, aggregated TARP, exact PCA projection and randomized SVD.

**Reference:** Mukhopadhyay and Dunson (2020), *Targeted Random Projections for Prediction with Massive Data*, Journal of the American Statistical Association.


## 4.7 Replicating TARP: aggregation, PCA projection and randomized SVD

**Method (TARP, per the paper).** For each SNP compute its marginal correlation $r_j$ with the response; keep it with
probability $q_j \propto |r_j|^{\delta}$, $\delta = \max\{0,(1+\log(p/n))/2\}$; compress the $p_\gamma$ survivors with a
sparse random matrix $R$ (entries $\pm 1/\sqrt{2\psi}$ w.p. $\psi$, else 0) to $Z = XR'$ and fit the conjugate model
$y = Z\theta + \varepsilon$ with prior $\theta\mid\sigma^2 \sim N(0,\sigma^2 I)$, giving
$\mu_t = (I + Z'Z)^{-1}Z'y$ and a Student-t predictive distribution. A **single** projection is noisy, so the paper
averages predictions over 100 projections with $m_n \sim U[2\log p,\,3n/4]$.

**Variants compared on the same screened SNPs.** (i) one projection, (ii) the 100-draw aggregation, (iii) exact PCA
projection (RIS-PCR), and (iv) a randomized-SVD projection that uses TARP's own sparse matrix as the sketch followed by
`q` power iterations: `q = 0` is a data-adaptive rotation of one sketch, and `q -> infinity` recovers PCA, so `q` is a
single knob between random projection and PCA.


```{r si-run}
QS <- c(0, 1, 2, 4)
run_rep_si <- function(seed_i) {
  sp <- make_split(seed_i); tr <- sp$tr; te <- sp$te
  y_tr <- y_all[tr]; y_te <- y_all[te]; y_mean <- mean(y_tr); y_c <- y_tr - y_mean
  sc <- screen_set(tr, y_tr)                                  # RNG continues straight from the split
  X <- std_cols(G2[, sc$inc], tr, te); X_tr <- X$tr; X_te <- X$other; p_g <- ncol(X_tr)
  out <- list(seed = seed_i, baseline = mean((y_te - y_mean)^2), n_screened = p_g)
  tm <- system.time({ pca <- prcomp(X_tr, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE, rank. = K_DIM) })[["elapsed"]]
  V_pca <- pca$rotation[, 1:K_DIM]
  out$PCA <- nig_mspe(X_tr %*% V_pca, X_te %*% V_pca, y_c, y_mean, y_te); out$t_PCA <- tm
  E_pca <- energy(X_tr, V_pca)
  Om <- tarp_omega(p_g, K_DIM); out$RP_single <- nig_mspe(X_tr %*% Om, X_te %*% Om, y_c, y_mean, y_te)
  tm <- system.time({ pa <- agg_tarp_pred(X_tr, X_te, y_c, y_mean, p, B = 100) })[["elapsed"]]
  out$RP_agg <- mean((y_te - pa)^2); out$t_RP_agg <- tm
  for (qq in QS) {
    tm <- system.time({ V <- rsvd_basis(X_tr, K_DIM, qq) })[["elapsed"]]
    out[[paste0("SI_q", qq)]] <- nig_mspe(X_tr %*% V, X_te %*% V, y_c, y_mean, y_te)
    out[[paste0("E_q", qq)]] <- energy(X_tr, V) / E_pca; out[[paste0("t_q", qq)]] <- tm
  }
  as.data.frame(out)
}
si <- run_seeds("si", run_rep_si, legacy = "si_replication_results.rds")
base_s <- setNames(si$baseline, si$seed)             # per-split mean-only MSPE, shared by every experiment
r2_of <- function(v, seeds = names(v)) 1 - v / base_s[seeds]
cat("splits:", nrow(si), "| SNPs surviving screening per split (mean):", round(mean(si$n_screened)), "\n")
```

```{r si-plots, fig.height = 5.5}
cols <- c("RP_single", "RP_agg", "PCA", paste0("SI_q", QS))
lab  <- c("TARP\nsingle draw", "TARP\naggregated", "PCA", paste0("rSVD\nq=", QS))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(6, 4, 3, 1))
boxplot(si[, cols], names = lab, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.75, col = c("firebrick", "darkgreen", "steelblue", rep("grey70", length(QS))),
        ylab = "test MSPE", main = "Projection variants on the same screened SNPs")
abline(h = mean(si$baseline), lty = 3); text(1, mean(si$baseline), "mean-only predictor", pos = 3, cex = 0.7)
mu_q <- sapply(QS, function(q) mean(si[[paste0("SI_q", q)]])); se_q <- sapply(QS, function(q) sem(si[[paste0("SI_q", q)]]))
plot(QS, mu_q, type = "b", pch = 19, ylim = range(c(mu_q - 2 * se_q, mu_q + 2 * se_q, mean(si$PCA), mean(si$RP_agg))),
     xlab = "power iterations q", ylab = "mean test MSPE (+-2 SE)", main = "Randomized SVD between random projection and PCA")
arrows(QS, mu_q - 2 * se_q, QS, mu_q + 2 * se_q, angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.04)
abline(h = mean(si$PCA), col = "blue", lty = 2); abline(h = mean(si$RP_agg), col = "darkgreen", lty = 3)
legend("topright", c("exact PCA", "TARP aggregated"), col = c("blue", "darkgreen"), lty = c(2, 3), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
d_pca <- sapply(c("RP_single", "RP_agg", paste0("SI_q", QS)), function(m) si[[m]] - si$PCA)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Method = colnames(d_pca), Mean_MSPE = sapply(colnames(d_pca), function(m) mean(si[[m]])),
                        Diff_vs_PCA = colMeans(d_pca), SE = apply(d_pca, 2, sem), Beats_PCA = colSums(d_pca < 0)),
             digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Paired differences against exact PCA (negative = better than PCA)")
```

```{r si-cost}
tab_cost <- data.frame(q = c(QS, Inf),
  Energy_vs_PCA = c(sapply(QS, function(q) mean(si[[paste0("E_q", q)]])), 1),
  Seconds = c(sapply(QS, function(q) mean(si[[paste0("t_q", q)]])), mean(si$t_PCA)))
knitr::kable(tab_cost, digits = 3, caption = "Share of exact-PCA captured energy and mean wall time (single-threaded BLAS)")
cat("Aggregated TARP: median wall time per split", round(median(si$t_RP_agg)), "seconds (the mean is distorted by any pause of the machine).\n")
```

**Scaling benchmark.** Wall time for exact SVD (`prcomp`), exact PCA through the n x n Gram matrix, randomized SVD
(q = 2) and the paper's 100-draw aggregation (extrapolated from 5 draws) as the number of screened SNPs grows. Unless
`RUN_SCALING <- TRUE`, the values recorded in the original run (single-threaded, same laptop) are shown.

```{r scaling}
scaling <- data.frame(p_screened = c(5000, 20000, 50000, 100000),
  exact_svd = c(8.953, 35.725, 91.573, 189.92), exact_gram = c(2.822, 11.013, 23.434, 47.048),
  rsvd_q2 = c(2.23, 9.163, 24.314, 47.25), tarp_agg100_extrap = c(86.96, 366.92, 908.38, 1796.46),
  rsvd_energy_vs_exact = c(0.9975744, 0.9951787, 0.9925784, 0.9891172))
if (RUN_SCALING) {
  sp1 <- make_split(1); gw <- big_univLinReg(G2, y.train = y_all[sp1$tr], ind.train = sp1$tr, ncores = N_CORES)
  ord <- order(abs(gw$estim / gw$std.err), decreasing = TRUE); ord[is.na(ord)] <- length(ord)
  scaling <- do.call(rbind, lapply(scaling$p_screened, function(K) {
    X <- G2[sp1$tr, ord[1:K]]; cs <- apply(X, 2, sd); cs[cs == 0] <- 1; X <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = cs)
    t_svd <- system.time(prcomp(X, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE, rank. = K_DIM))[["elapsed"]]
    t_gram <- system.time(Vg <- gram_pca_basis(X, K_DIM))[["elapsed"]]
    t_rsvd <- system.time(Vr <- rsvd_basis(X, K_DIM, 2))[["elapsed"]]
    t_agg5 <- system.time(for (b in 1:5) { Zb <- X %*% tarp_omega(K, 315) })[["elapsed"]]
    data.frame(p_screened = K, exact_svd = t_svd, exact_gram = t_gram, rsvd_q2 = t_rsvd,
               tarp_agg100_extrap = t_agg5 * 20, rsvd_energy_vs_exact = energy(X, Vr) / energy(X, Vg))
  }))
}
knitr::kable(scaling, digits = 3, caption = "Seconds to obtain 100 projection directions (and rSVD energy relative to exact)")
matplot(scaling$p_screened, scaling[, c("exact_svd", "exact_gram", "rsvd_q2", "tarp_agg100_extrap")], type = "b", pch = 1:4,
        lty = 1, log = "xy", col = c("grey40", "blue", "steelblue", "darkgreen"), xlab = "screened SNPs (log scale)",
        ylab = "seconds (log scale)", main = "Cost of compressing the screened SNPs")
legend("topleft", c("exact SVD", "exact PCA via Gram matrix", "randomized SVD (q = 2)", "TARP, 100 draws (extrapolated)"),
       col = c("grey40", "blue", "steelblue", "darkgreen"), pch = 1:4, lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

```{r si-findings, results='asis'}
d_agg <- si$RP_agg - si$PCA
cat(sprintf("- **A single random projection is unreliable**: mean MSPE %.1f, against %.1f for the 100-draw aggregation and %.1f for exact PCA (mean-only predictor: %.1f).\n",
            mean(si$RP_single), mean(si$RP_agg), mean(si$PCA), mean(si$baseline)))
cat(sprintf("- **Aggregated TARP matches exact PCA** (difference %.1f, SE %.1f; aggregation wins in %d of %d splits), reproducing the paper's statement that RIS-RP and RIS-PCR are comparable.\n",
            mean(d_agg), sem(d_agg), sum(d_agg < 0), nrow(si)))
cat(sprintf("- **Randomized SVD closes the gap to PCA as q grows**: mean difference from PCA %.1f at q = 0 and %.1f at q = 2, recovering %.1f%% of the exact captured energy at q = 2.\n",
            mean(si$SI_q0 - si$PCA), mean(si$SI_q2 - si$PCA), 100 * mean(si$E_q2)))
cat(sprintf("- **Cost**: at 100,000 screened SNPs, randomized SVD (q = 2) takes %.0f s versus about %.0f s for the 100-draw aggregation (%.0fx cheaper) and %.0f s for exact SVD; exact PCA through the Gram matrix is just as fast as randomized SVD (%.0f s), so the saving is relative to the aggregation, not to PCA.\n",
            scaling$rsvd_q2[4], scaling$tarp_agg100_extrap[4], scaling$tarp_agg100_extrap[4] / scaling$rsvd_q2[4],
            scaling$exact_svd[4], scaling$exact_gram[4]))
```


# 5. Screening and variable selection: SIS, randomized SIS, iterated SIS and structure-adjusted SIS

**Terminology.** *Sure Independence Screening* (SIS; Fan and Lv, 2008) ranks predictors by the absolute marginal
correlation $|r_j|$ with the response and keeps the top $d$ (default $d=\lfloor n/\log n\rfloor$, here 120 for
n = 802 training accessions). TARP's first step is the *randomized* version, **randomized independence screening
(RIS)**: SNP $j$ survives with probability $q_j\propto|r_j|^{\delta}$, a soft threshold with no hard cutoff.
**"Random SIS projection" = RIS followed by a sparse random projection (RIS-RP)**, the method evaluated in
Section 4. This section studies the screening step itself, how it behaves when predictors are strongly correlated
(linkage disequilibrium, LD) and structured (ancestry), and how it compares with the alternatives:

| Screen | Rule |
|---|---|
| `SIS` (d = n/log n, 2000, or the RIS survivor count) | deterministic top-$d$ by absolute marginal correlation |
| `RIS` | Bernoulli($q_j$) with $q_j$ proportional to (absolute marginal correlation)$^{\delta}$ (TARP step 1) |
| `ISIS` | iterated SIS: select, fit a lasso, take residuals, re-screen (3 rounds) |
| `SISadj` | SIS on the response after removing the first five genomic (ancestry) axes |

After screening, the survivors are modeled with the lasso, ridge or elastic net (`glmnet`), the standard
"SIS + penalized regression" recipe, and compared with TARP's projections and with the dense GBLUP baseline.

```{r sis-helpers}
HAS_GLMNET <- requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE)
if (!HAS_GLMNET) message("glmnet is not installed: lasso/ridge-after-screening rows are skipped. ",
                         "Install once with: micromamba install -c conda-forge r-glmnet")
screen_scores <- function(tr_rows, y_vec) {              # signed t-statistic of every SNP against y_vec (training rows only)
  gw <- big_univLinReg(G2, y.train = y_vec, ind.train = tr_rows, ncores = N_CORES)
  tt <- gw$estim / gw$std.err; tt[is.na(tt)] <- 0; tt
}
sis_top <- function(score, d) order(abs(score), decreasing = TRUE)[1:d]
adjust_response <- function(tr_rows, y_vec) resid(lm(y_vec ~ pcs5[tr_rows, , drop = FALSE]))   # remove ancestry axes
isis_set <- function(tr_rows, y_vec, d_total, n_iter = 3) {
  d_step <- ceiling(d_total / n_iter); sel <- integer(0); y_c <- y_vec - mean(y_vec); y_res <- y_c
  for (it in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    tt <- screen_scores(tr_rows, y_res); tt[sel] <- 0
    sel <- c(sel, order(abs(tt), decreasing = TRUE)[1:d_step])
    if (it < n_iter) {
      Xs <- scale(G2[tr_rows, sel, drop = FALSE]); Xs[is.na(Xs)] <- 0
      fit <- if (HAS_GLMNET) {
        cv <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(Xs, y_c, alpha = 1, nfolds = 5); as.numeric(predict(cv, Xs, s = "lambda.min"))
      } else {
        as.numeric(Xs %*% solve(crossprod(Xs) + 0.1 * length(tr_rows) * diag(ncol(Xs)), crossprod(Xs, y_c)))
      }
      y_res <- y_c - fit
    }
  }
  sel
}
# penalized fit on a screened set; lambda by glmnet's internal 10-fold CV (in-sample, so subject to the screening
# bias discussed in Section 6, but the test MSPE below is untouched by it); optionally ancestry axes unpenalized
pen_fit <- function(sel, tr, te, y_tr, y_te, alpha, pcs_cov = FALSE) {
  if (!HAS_GLMNET) return(c(mspe = NA_real_, nz = NA_real_))
  X <- std_cols(G2[, sel, drop = FALSE], tr, te); keep <- apply(X$tr, 2, sd) > 1e-8
  x_tr <- X$tr[, keep, drop = FALSE]; x_te <- X$other[, keep, drop = FALSE]; pf <- rep(1, ncol(x_tr))
  if (pcs_cov) { x_tr <- cbind(pcs5[tr, ], x_tr); x_te <- cbind(pcs5[te, ], x_te); pf <- c(rep(0, ncol(pcs5)), pf) }
  cv <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(x_tr, y_tr, alpha = alpha, nfolds = 10, penalty.factor = pf)
  pr <- as.numeric(predict(cv, x_te, s = "lambda.min"))
  c(mspe = mean((y_te - pr)^2), nz = sum(as.numeric(coef(cv, s = "lambda.min"))[-1] != 0))
}
```

## 5.1 Prediction after screening: SIS, RIS, ISIS and structure-adjusted SIS with penalized regression

```{r sis-run}
run_rep_sis <- function(seed_i) {
  sp <- make_split(seed_i); tr <- sp$tr; te <- sp$te
  y_tr <- y_all[tr]; y_te <- y_all[te]; ym <- mean(y_tr)
  sc <- screen_set(tr, y_tr)                                 # RIS survivors
  tt <- screen_scores(tr, y_tr)
  d1 <- floor(length(tr) / log(length(tr))); d2 <- 2000; dR <- length(sc$inc)
  S <- list(SIS1 = sis_top(tt, d1), SIS2 = sis_top(tt, d2), SISR = sis_top(tt, dR), RIS = sc$inc,
            ADJ2 = sis_top(screen_scores(tr, adjust_response(tr, y_tr)), d2), ISIS2 = isis_set(tr, y_tr, d2))
  f <- function(sel, alpha, pc = FALSE) pen_fit(sel, tr, te, y_tr, y_te, alpha, pc)
  r1 <- f(S$SIS1, 1); r2 <- f(S$SIS2, 1); r3 <- f(S$SIS2, 0); r4 <- f(S$SISR, 0); r5 <- f(S$RIS, 0)
  r6 <- f(S$ISIS2, 1); r7 <- f(S$ADJ2, 1, TRUE); r8 <- f(S$ADJ2, 0, TRUE)
  data.frame(seed = seed_i, baseline = mean((y_te - ym)^2), d1 = d1, dR = dR,
    SIS_d1_lasso = unname(r1["mspe"]), SIS_2000_lasso = unname(r2["mspe"]), SIS_2000_ridge = unname(r3["mspe"]),
    SIS_RISsize_ridge = unname(r4["mspe"]), RIS_ridge = unname(r5["mspe"]), ISIS_2000_lasso = unname(r6["mspe"]),
    SISadj_2000_lasso_pc = unname(r7["mspe"]), SISadj_2000_ridge_pc = unname(r8["mspe"]),
    nz_SIS_d1_lasso = unname(r1["nz"]), nz_SIS_2000_lasso = unname(r2["nz"]), nz_ISIS_2000_lasso = unname(r6["nz"]),
    nz_SISadj_2000_lasso_pc = unname(r7["nz"]),
    GBLUP = mean((y_te - gblup_fit(tr, te, y_tr)$pred)^2))
}
sis_res <- run_seeds("sis", run_rep_sis)
```

```{r sis-plots, fig.height = 6}
mlab <- c("SIS d=120\n+ lasso", "SIS d=2000\n+ lasso", "SIS d=2000\n+ ridge", "SIS (RIS size)\n+ ridge", "RIS (Bernoulli)\n+ ridge",
          "ISIS d=2000\n+ lasso", "SIS-adj d=2000\n+ lasso + axes", "SIS-adj d=2000\n+ ridge + axes", "GBLUP\n(all SNPs)")
```
