## 5.2 What the screens select: genomic-structure tagging, marker redundancy and genomic concentration

Marginal screening ranks SNPs individually, but selected marker sets may differ substantially in the genomic information they represent. We examine four properties: (i) the mean absolute correlation of selected SNPs with the first genomic principal component (PC1), (ii) the average SNP-wise R-squared explained by the first ten genomic principal components (PC1–PC10), (iii) the mean pairwise absolute genotype correlation among selected SNPs, and (iv) the number of distinct 50-kb genomic regions represented by the selected markers. The PC-based diagnostics measure the association of selected markers with major axes of genomic variation. Pairwise genotype correlations provide a measure of marker redundancy, although they may reflect both local linkage disequilibrium and population structure. The positional grouping is a physical clustering heuristic: SNPs on the same chromosome separated by no more than 50 kb are grouped together. These regions are not formally identified LD blocks.

Each selected set is compared with five random marker references matched for the number of selected SNPs. The comparisons are descriptive: the random sets are not additionally matched for minor allele frequency or chromosome distribution.
Marginal screening ranks SNPs one at a time, so two issues can arise in genetic data:
(i) SNPs that tag ancestry may score highly when the phenotype tracks population structure,
and (ii) correlated SNPs may occupy multiple positions in the selected set, reducing its
effective genomic coverage. We summarize this using three diagnostics: the mean absolute
correlation of selected SNPs with the first ancestry axis, the mean pairwise correlation
among selected SNPs, and the number of distinct 50-kb genomic regions. The latter is a
positional clustering heuristic: SNPs on the same chromosome separated by no more than
50 kb are grouped together. It is not a formal LD-block definition.


```{r sel-diag, fig.height = 7}
# ================================================================
# SECTION 5.2: WHAT DO THE SELECTED SNP SETS ACTUALLY REPRESENT?
#
# Diagnostics:
# 1. Mean |cor(SNP, PC1)|
# 2. Mean SNP-wise R2 explained by PC1-PC10 jointly
# 3. Mean pairwise |SNP-SNP correlation| (LD redundancy diagnostic)
# 4. Number of 50-kb-gap genomic regions
#
# Each selected set is compared with size-matched random SNP sets.
# ================================================================

N_RANDOM_REF <- 5L
N_LD_SAMPLE <- 200L
REGION_GAP_BP <- 50000L

# ------------------------------------------------
# A. Recover the selected sets from the 10 splits
# ------------------------------------------------

sel_cache <- file.path("cache", "sel_sets.rds")

if (USE_CACHE && file.exists(sel_cache)) {

  sel_sets <- readRDS(sel_cache)

} else {

  sel_sets <- lapply(seq_len(N_REPS), function(s) {

    sp <- make_split(s)
    tr <- sp$tr
    y_tr <- y_all[tr]

    sc <- screen_set(tr, y_tr)
    tt <- screen_scores(tr, y_tr)

    list(
      SIS_d1 = sis_top(
        tt,
        floor(length(tr) / log(length(tr)))
      ),

      SIS_2000 = sis_top(tt, 2000),

      RIS = sc$inc,

      SISadj_2000 = sis_top(
        screen_scores(
          tr,
          adjust_response(tr, y_tr)
        ),
        2000
      )
    )
  })

  saveRDS(sel_sets, sel_cache)
}

# ------------------------------------------------
# B. Construct the first 10 genomic PC axes
# ------------------------------------------------

# Use the already-computed full genomic eigendecomposition.
# This is a genotype-only descriptive diagnostic.

N_STRUCT_PC <- 10L

pcs10 <- sweep(
  eK$vectors[, 1:N_STRUCT_PC, drop = FALSE],
  2,
  sqrt(eK$values[1:N_STRUCT_PC]),
  "*"
)

# Standardize PC scores so that correlations can be
# calculated directly using cross-products.

pcs10_z <- scale(pcs10)

n_obs <- nrow(G2)
p_obs <- ncol(G2)

stopifnot(nrow(pcs10_z) == n_obs)
stopifnot(nrow(map) == p_obs)

# Preserve these variables because the following LD and
# Manhattan chunks use chr_int and pos_bp.

chr_int <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(map$chromosome))
chr_label <- as.character(map$chromosome)
pos_bp <- as.numeric(map$physical.pos)

# ------------------------------------------------
# C. Function to calculate diagnostics for one SNP set
# ------------------------------------------------

sel_metrics <- function(sel) {

  sel <- unique(as.integer(sel))

  sel <- sel[
    !is.na(sel) &
      sel >= 1 &
      sel <= p_obs
  ]

  if (length(sel) == 0) {
    return(c(
      anc_cor = NA_real_,
      structure_r2_10 = NA_real_,
      pairwise_cor = NA_real_,
      loci = NA_real_,
      size = 0,
      variable_size = 0
    ))
  }

  # Extract selected genotypes.
  X_raw <- as.matrix(
    G2[, sel, drop = FALSE]
  )

  # Remove SNPs with zero or undefined variance.
  snp_sd <- apply(X_raw, 2, sd)

  keep <- is.finite(snp_sd) & snp_sd > 0

  if (!any(keep)) {
    return(c(
      anc_cor = NA_real_,
      structure_r2_10 = NA_real_,
      pairwise_cor = NA_real_,
      loci = NA_real_,
      size = length(sel),
      variable_size = 0
    ))
  }

  # Standardize each selected SNP across accessions.
  Xs <- scale(
    X_raw[, keep, drop = FALSE]
  )

  rm(X_raw)

  # ------------------------------------------------
  # Diagnostic 1 and 2:
  # Association with the first 10 genomic PCs
  # ------------------------------------------------

  # Because both matrices have centred, unit-SD columns,
  # these cross-products are sample correlations.

  cor_pc <- crossprod(
    pcs10_z,
    Xs
  ) / (n_obs - 1)

  # Diagnostic 1:
  # Mean absolute correlation with PC1.
  anc_cor <- mean(
    abs(cor_pc[1, ]),
    na.rm = TRUE
  )

  # Diagnostic 2:
  # For SNP j, its R2 from regression on PC1-PC10 is
  # the sum of squared correlations with those axes,
  # since the PC scores are mutually orthogonal.
  
  snp_r2_10 <- pmin(
    1,
    colSums(cor_pc^2)
  )

  structure_r2_10 <- mean(
    snp_r2_10,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )

  # ------------------------------------------------
  # Diagnostic 3:
  # Mean pairwise absolute correlation among selected SNPs
  # ------------------------------------------------

  m_ld <- min(
    ncol(Xs),
    N_LD_SAMPLE
  )

  if (m_ld >= 2) {

    # Use a fixed maximum sample size to keep computation feasible.
    ld_idx <- sample.int(
      ncol(Xs),
      m_ld
    )

    C_ld <- cor(
      Xs[, ld_idx, drop = FALSE]
    )

    pairwise_cor <- mean(
      abs(C_ld[upper.tri(C_ld)]),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )

  } else {

    pairwise_cor <- NA_real_
  }

  # ------------------------------------------------
  # Diagnostic 4:
  # Number of 50-kb-gap genomic regions
  # ------------------------------------------------

  chr_sel <- chr_label[sel]
  pos_sel <- pos_bp[sel]

  map_ok <- !is.na(chr_sel) &
    is.finite(pos_sel)

  chr_sel <- chr_sel[map_ok]
  pos_sel <- pos_sel[map_ok]

  if (length(pos_sel) == 0) {

    loci <- NA_real_

  } else {

    ord <- order(chr_sel, pos_sel)

    ch <- chr_sel[ord]
    ps <- pos_sel[ord]

    if (length(ps) == 1) {

      loci <- 1L

    } else {

      # A new region starts when:
      # (i) the chromosome changes, or
      # (ii) the gap from the previous selected SNP exceeds 50 kb.

      starts_region <- c(
        TRUE,
        ch[-1] != ch[-length(ch)] |
          diff(ps) > REGION_GAP_BP
      )

      loci <- sum(starts_region)
    }
  }

  c(
    anc_cor = anc_cor,
    structure_r2_10 = structure_r2_10,
    pairwise_cor = pairwise_cor,
    loci = loci,
    size = length(sel),
    variable_size = ncol(Xs)
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------
# D. Calculate diagnostics for selected and random sets
# ------------------------------------------------

set.seed(20261102)

selected_rows <- list()
random_rows <- list()

i_selected <- 0L
i_random <- 0L

for (s in seq_along(sel_sets)) {

  for (m in names(sel_sets[[s]])) {

    sel <- unique(sel_sets[[s]][[m]])

    # Diagnostics for the actual selected set.
    i_selected <- i_selected + 1L

    selected_rows[[i_selected]] <- data.frame(
      seed = s,
      set = m,
      t(sel_metrics(sel))
    )

    # Generate five random SNP sets of exactly the
    # same nominal size as the corresponding selected set.

    for (b in seq_len(N_RANDOM_REF)) {

      rand_sel <- sample.int(
        p_obs,
        size = length(sel),
        replace = FALSE
      )

      i_random <- i_random + 1L

      random_rows[[i_random]] <- data.frame(
        seed = s,
        set = m,
        reference = b,
        t(sel_metrics(rand_sel))
      )
    }
  }
}

diag_selected <- do.call(
  rbind,
  selected_rows
)

diag_random <- do.call(
  rbind,
  random_rows
)


# ------------------------------------------------
# E. Average the random references within each split
# ------------------------------------------------

random_by_split <- aggregate(
  cbind(
    anc_cor,
    structure_r2_10,
    pairwise_cor,
    loci,
    size,
    variable_size
  ) ~ seed + set,

  data = diag_random,

  FUN = function(z) mean(z, na.rm = TRUE)
)


# ------------------------------------------------
# F. Match every selected set with its random reference
# ------------------------------------------------

diag_compare <- merge(
  diag_selected,
  random_by_split,
  by = c("seed", "set"),
  suffixes = c("_selected", "_random")
)


# ------------------------------------------------
# G. Summarize selected-versus-random differences
# ------------------------------------------------

mean_diff <- function(a, b) {
  mean(a - b, na.rm = TRUE)
}

se_diff <- function(a, b) {

  z <- a - b

  sd(z, na.rm = TRUE) /
    sqrt(sum(is.finite(z)))
}

summarise_method <- function(method_name) {

  d <- diag_compare[
    diag_compare$set == method_name,
  ]

  region_density_selected <-
    1000 * d$loci_selected / d$size_selected

  region_density_random <-
    1000 * d$loci_random / d$size_random

  data.frame(

    set = method_name,

    mean_selected_size =
      mean(d$size_selected),

    PC1_mean_abs_r_selected =
      mean(d$anc_cor_selected),

    PC1_mean_abs_r_random =
      mean(d$anc_cor_random),

    PC1_mean_abs_r_diff =
      mean_diff(d$anc_cor_selected, d$anc_cor_random),

    PC1_mean_abs_r_diff_SE =
      se_diff(d$anc_cor_selected, d$anc_cor_random),

    PC1_10_mean_R2_selected =
      mean(d$structure_r2_10_selected),

    PC1_10_mean_R2_random =
      mean(d$structure_r2_10_random),

    PC1_10_mean_R2_diff =
      mean_diff(
        d$structure_r2_10_selected,
        d$structure_r2_10_random
      ),

    PC1_10_mean_R2_diff_SE =
      se_diff(
        d$structure_r2_10_selected,
        d$structure_r2_10_random
      ),

    pairwise_abs_r_selected =
      mean(d$pairwise_cor_selected),

    pairwise_abs_r_random =
      mean(d$pairwise_cor_random),

    pairwise_abs_r_diff =
      mean_diff(
        d$pairwise_cor_selected,
        d$pairwise_cor_random
      ),

    pairwise_abs_r_diff_SE =
      se_diff(
        d$pairwise_cor_selected,
        d$pairwise_cor_random
      ),

    regions_per_1000_selected =
      mean(region_density_selected, na.rm = TRUE),

    regions_per_1000_random =
      mean(region_density_random, na.rm = TRUE),

    regions_per_1000_diff =
      mean_diff(
        region_density_selected,
        region_density_random
      ),

    regions_per_1000_diff_SE =
      se_diff(
        region_density_selected,
        region_density_random
      )
  )
}

diag_summary <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(
    unique(diag_compare$set),
    summarise_method
  )
)


# ------------------------------------------------
# H. Preserve agg_diag for downstream report compatibility
# ------------------------------------------------

agg_diag <- aggregate(
  cbind(
    anc_cor,
    structure_r2_10,
    pairwise_cor,
    loci,
    size
  ) ~ set,

  data = diag_selected,

  FUN = mean
)

# Matched random reference for SIS with d = 2000.
rand_anc <- diag_summary$PC1_mean_abs_r_random[
  diag_summary$set == "SIS_2000"
]


# ------------------------------------------------
# I. Display the comparison table
# ------------------------------------------------

knitr::kable(
  diag_summary,
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste(
    "Selected SNP sets versus five size-matched random references;",
    "means over 10 splits."
  )
)


# ------------------------------------------------
# J. Plot selected sets versus matched random references
# ------------------------------------------------

screen_labels <- c(
  SIS_d1 = "SIS d~n/log n",

cat(
  "\nSection 5.2 diagnostics completed:",
  nrow(diag_selected), "selected sets;",
  nrow(diag_random), "random reference sets.\n"
)
```
The PC1-only comparison does not indicate elevated PC1 association among the selected markers: the mean absolute SNP–PC1 correlation for SIS with 2,000 markers is 0.105, compared with 0.108 for its random reference. In contrast, the average SNP-wise R-squared explained by PC1–PC10 is substantially higher for SIS (0.513) than for random markers (0.155). The corresponding value for SIS with d = n/log(n) is also 0.513, while RIS gives 0.334 and structure-adjusted SIS gives 0.217. Thus, examining PC1 alone would miss much of the association between SIS-selected markers and broader genomic structure.

The selected SIS markers also exhibit substantially higher pairwise genotype correlation than random markers: 0.436 versus 0.044 for SIS with 2,000 markers, and 0.583 versus 0.043 for SIS with d = n/log(n). This is consistent with considerable marker redundancy.

Physical concentration is also pronounced. SIS with 2,000 markers represents approximately 47.8 distinct 50-kb regions per 1,000 selected SNPs, compared with 401.0 for random markers. For SIS with d = n/log(n), the corresponding values are 96.6 and 943.7. In contrast, RIS represents 70.2 regions per 1,000 markers, compared with 42.4 for its random reference. These results indicate substantial differences in the genomic distribution of markers selected by the different procedures.

The main findings from Section 5.2
Finding 1
Ordinary SIS selects highly redundant markers.

Its mean pairwise absolute correlation is 0.436, compared with 0.044 for random markers. Its selected SNPs also have substantially higher PC1–PC10 \(R^2\).


Finding 2
Structure adjustment changes the selected marker set.

PC1–PC10 mean \(R^2\) decreases from 0.513 to 0.217, and mean pairwise correlation decreases from 0.436 to 0.190.


Finding 3
RIS selects a different genomic profile from ordinary SIS.

Its pairwise correlation is 0.185, substantially lower than ordinary SIS's 0.436. Its selected SNPs are also less physically concentrated than its size-matched random reference according to the 50-kb diagnostic.

```{r sel-stability}
jacc <- function(a, b) length(intersect(a, b)) / length(union(a, b))
stab <- sapply(names(sel_sets[[1]]), function(m)
  mean(combn(length(sel_sets), 2, function(ij) jacc(sel_sets[[ij[1]]][[m]], sel_sets[[ij[2]]][[m]]))))
barplot(stab, col = "steelblue", border = NA, las = 2, cex.names = 0.8, ylab = "mean Jaccard overlap between splits",
        main = "Stability of the selected set across the 10 splits")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Screen = names(stab), Mean_Jaccard = round(stab, 3)), row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "1 = identical sets on every split; each pair of splits shares about 64% of its training accessions")
```
SIS with 2,000 markers has the highest split-to-split Jaccard overlap (0.641), followed by SIS with d = n/log(n) (0.576) and structure-adjusted SIS (0.491). RIS has substantially lower overlap (0.056), consistent with its randomized selection mechanism. These values describe stability across the ten experimental splits, not independent-sample reproducibility: the training sets overlap substantially, sharing approximately 64% of their accessions on average.

```{r ld-structure, fig.height = 5}
# LD decay: mean r^2 against physical distance, from windows on random chromosomes at three SNP strides
set.seed(77)
ld_pairs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 10, 50), function(stride) do.call(rbind, lapply(1:15, function(i) {
  ch <- sample(1:5, 1); idx_ch <- which(chr_int == ch)
  st <- sample(seq_len(length(idx_ch) - 400 * stride), 1); idx <- idx_ch[st + stride * (0:399)]
  r2 <- suppressWarnings(cor(G2[, idx]))^2; dd <- abs(outer(pos_bp[idx], pos_bp[idx], "-"))
  ut <- upper.tri(r2); keep <- ut & !is.na(r2)
  data.frame(dist = dd[keep], r2 = r2[keep])
}))))
brk <- c(0, 500, 1e3, 2e3, 5e3, 1e4, 2e4, 5e4, 1e5, 2e5, 5e5)
ld_pairs$bin <- cut(ld_pairs$dist, brk, include.lowest = TRUE)
ld_curve <- aggregate(r2 ~ bin, data = ld_pairs, FUN = mean)
mids <- sqrt(brk[-length(brk)] * pmax(brk[-1], 1)); mids[1] <- 250; names(mids) <- levels(ld_pairs$bin)
ld_curve$mid <- mids[as.character(ld_curve$bin)]
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(ld_curve$mid / 1000, ld_curve$r2, type = "b", pch = 19, log = "x", xlab = "distance between SNPs (kb, log scale)",
     ylab = "mean r^2", main = "Linkage disequilibrium decay")
sel_h <- sort(sel_sets[[1]]$SIS_2000[1:80]); o <- order(chr_int[sel_h], pos_bp[sel_h]); sel_h <- sel_h[o]
cm <- abs(suppressWarnings(cor(G2[, sel_h]))); cm[is.na(cm)] <- 0
image(1:80, 1:80, cm[, 80:1], col = hcl.colors(30, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE), xlab = "top-80 SIS SNPs, in genome order", ylab = "",
      axes = FALSE, main = "|correlation| among the 80 top SIS SNPs")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The LD-decay curve summarizes mean pairwise r-squared across sampled chromosome windows as a function of physical distance. The correlation heatmap displays pairwise absolute genotype correlations among the 80 SIS markers shown from the first split, ordered by genomic position. These plots provide exploratory descriptions of local and genome-wide correlation patterns. The 50-kb positional regions reported above are a separate heuristic and should not be interpreted as inferred LD blocks.

## 5.3 Semi-synthetic simulation: does screening recover the truth, and what do LD and ancestry do to it?

On real data the causal SNPs are unknown. This simulation keeps the **real genotypes** (so the real LD and ancestry
structure are present) and plants a known signal:

$$y = \underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{j\in S}\beta_j \tilde x_j}_{\text{genetic, variance }h^2_g} + \underbrace{\gamma\,\tilde u_1}_{\text{ancestry, variance }h^2_a} + \varepsilon ,\qquad |S|=s,$$

with $\tilde x_j$ standardized causal SNPs and $\tilde u_1$ the first ancestry axis. Scenarios: **A** sparse (s = 20,
$h^2_g=0.5$, no ancestry effect); **B** sparse with ancestry confounding (s = 20, $h^2_g=0.3$, $h^2_a=0.4$);
**C** polygenic (s = 2000, $h^2_g=0.5$). Each screen is run on a training split and scored by
**exact recovery** (fraction of causal SNPs selected), **locus recovery** (fraction of causal SNPs having a selected SNP
with $|r|\ge 0.7$, i.e. tagged through LD) and **ancestry tagging** (mean $|r|$ of selected SNPs with axis 1).

```{r sim-run}
SIM_B <- 12
sim_scenarios <- list(A_sparse = list(s = 20, h2g = 0.5, h2a = 0), B_sparse_ancestry = list(s = 20, h2g = 0.3, h2a = 0.4),
                      C_polygenic = list(s = 2000, h2g = 0.5, h2a = 0))
sim_one <- function(scn_name, b) {
  scn <- sim_scenarios[[scn_name]]
  set.seed(5000 + b + 100 * match(scn_name, names(sim_scenarios)))
  causal <- sample(which(maf >= 0.1), scn$s)
  Xc <- scale(G2[, causal]); Xc[is.na(Xc)] <- 0
  g <- as.numeric(Xc %*% rnorm(scn$s)); g <- (g - mean(g)) / sd(g) * sqrt(scn$h2g)
  a <- anc_axis * sqrt(scn$h2a); e <- rnorm(n) * sqrt(max(1 - scn$h2g - scn$h2a, 0.01))
  y <- g + a + e
  sp <- make_split(9000 + b); tr <- sp$tr
  tt <- screen_scores(tr, y[tr]); r <- sign(tt) * sqrt(tt^2 / (tt^2 + length(tr) - 2))
  q_in <- abs(r)^max(0, (1 + log(p / length(tr))) / 2); q_in <- q_in / max(q_in)
  ris <- which(rbinom(p, 1, q_in) == 1)
  tt_adj <- screen_scores(tr, adjust_response(tr, y[tr]))
  d1 <- floor(length(tr) / log(length(tr)))
  sets <- list(SIS_d120 = sis_top(tt, d1), SIS_d2000 = sis_top(tt, 2000), RIS = ris,
               SISadj_d2000 = sis_top(tt_adj, 2000), Random_d2000 = sample(p, 2000))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sets), function(m) {
    sel <- sets[[m]]; Xs <- scale(G2[, sel]); Xs[is.na(Xs)] <- 0
    cc <- abs(crossprod(Xc, Xs)) / (n - 1)
    data.frame(scenario = scn_name, rep = b, method = m, exact = mean(causal %in% sel),
               locus = mean(apply(cc, 1, max) >= 0.7),
               anc_cor = mean(abs(crossprod(anc_axis, Xs)) / (n - 1)), size = length(sel))
  }))
}
sim_file <- file.path("cache", "sim_results.rds")
if (USE_CACHE && file.exists(sim_file)) {
  sim_res <- readRDS(sim_file)
} else {
  sim_res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sim_scenarios), function(sn) do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(SIM_B), function(b) {
    cat(sprintf("[simulation] %s replicate %d\n", sn, b)); sim_one(sn, b)}))))
  saveRDS(sim_res, sim_file)
}
```

```{r sim-plots, fig.height = 8}
sim_res$method <- factor(sim_res$method, levels = c("SIS_d120", "SIS_d2000", "RIS", "SISadj_d2000", "Random_d2000"))
par(mfrow = c(3, 3), mar = c(6, 4, 3, 1))
for (sn in names(sim_scenarios)) {
  d <- sim_res[sim_res$scenario == sn, ]
  boxplot(exact ~ method, data = d, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.7, ylim = c(0, 1), main = paste(sn, ": exact recovery"), xlab = "", ylab = "fraction of causal SNPs", col = "steelblue")
  boxplot(locus ~ method, data = d, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.7, ylim = c(0, 1), main = paste(sn, ": locus recovery"), xlab = "", ylab = "fraction tagged (|r| >= 0.7)", col = "darkorange")
  boxplot(anc_cor ~ method, data = d, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.7, main = paste(sn, ": ancestry tagging"), xlab = "", ylab = "mean |cor| with axis 1", col = "darkgreen")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))
sim_tab <- aggregate(cbind(exact, locus, anc_cor, size) ~ scenario + method, data = sim_res, FUN = mean)
knitr::kable(sim_tab, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE, caption = sprintf("Semi-synthetic simulation, mean over %d replicates", SIM_B))
```

```{r sim-findings, results='asis'}
            g("A_sparse", "SIS_d2000", "exact"), g("A_sparse", "SIS_d2000", "locus")))

Locus recovery in B: SIS %.2f versus adjusted SIS %.2f.\n",
            g("A_sparse", "SIS_d2000", "anc_cor"), g("B_sparse_ancestry", "SIS_d2000", "anc_cor"),
```

## 5.4 Overall conclusions from screening experiments

The experiments in this section investigate SNP screening from three
complementary perspectives: predictive performance, the genomic
characteristics of selected marker sets, and the ability to recover
known genetic signals under controlled semi-synthetic scenarios.

The main findings are summarized below.

**1. Screening performance depends on the selection strategy and the
number of retained markers.**

A very restrictive screening budget can discard useful predictive
information. For ordinary SIS followed by Lasso, increasing the
number of retained SNPs from approximately 119 to 2,000 reduced
the mean test MSPE from 168.977 to 137.479.

Among the screened prediction approaches, RIS followed by Ridge
achieved the lowest mean test MSPE (113.035), followed by ISIS
with Lasso (119.624) and structure-adjusted SIS with Ridge
(121.505). These results suggest that the choice of screening
procedure can substantially influence predictive performance.

However, full-SNP GBLUP remained the stronger average prediction
benchmark, with an approximate mean test MSPE of 107.243.
Thus, the best screened approach did not outperform dense
genomic prediction on average.

**2. Different screening methods select marker sets with different
genomic characteristics.**

The genomic diagnostics reveal substantial differences between
the selected SNP sets.

Ordinary SIS-selected markers exhibit considerably higher
average pairwise absolute genotype correlation than random
size-matched markers (0.436 versus 0.044 for the 2,000-marker
sets). They also show substantially higher average SNP-wise
R-squared explained by the first ten genomic PCs (0.513 versus
0.155).

These findings suggest that ordinary marginal screening tends
to select markers with overlapping genotype information and
stronger associations with broad genomic variation.

Structure-adjusted SIS reduces these patterns: its corresponding
PC1--PC10 mean R-squared is 0.217 and its mean pairwise
absolute correlation is 0.190. RIS also exhibits lower pairwise
correlation (0.185) than ordinary SIS.

The LD-decay analysis provides additional context: average
pairwise squared genotype correlation decreases with increasing
physical distance between SNPs. The correlation heatmap of the
top 80 SIS markers further illustrates the correlation structure
among selected markers.

The 50-kb positional grouping and the correlation diagnostics
should be interpreted as descriptive measures, not as formal
identification of LD blocks or causal genomic regions.

**3. Population structure can strongly influence marginal screening.**

The semi-synthetic experiment demonstrates the potential
consequences of ancestry confounding.

When the phenotype contains a substantial ancestry-related
component (Scenario B), ordinary SIS with 2,000 markers has
zero exact causal-SNP recovery and zero locus recovery, while
its mean absolute correlation with PC1 is 0.766.

Structure-adjusted SIS substantially changes this result:
exact recovery increases to 0.346, locus recovery to 0.400,
and ancestry tagging decreases to 0.068.

This controlled experiment illustrates how marginal screening
can prioritize ancestry-associated markers when population
structure is related to the phenotype, and how adjusting for
genomic PCs can improve recovery under the simulated
confounding mechanism.

**4. Exact causal-SNP recovery and recovery of correlated markers
are different objectives.**

Even in the sparse scenario without ancestry confounding
(Scenario A), exact recovery is incomplete. For example,
ordinary SIS with 2,000 markers recovers 0.288 of the causal
SNPs exactly, while its locus recovery is 0.312.

This distinction is important because linkage disequilibrium
can cause a selected marker to be strongly correlated with
a causal SNP without being the causal SNP itself.

Consequently, screening performance should not be evaluated
only through exact SNP recovery. The ability to identify
correlated markers that tag causal loci can also be informative.

**5. Marginal screening struggles when the genetic signal is
highly polygenic.**

In Scenario C, the phenotype-generating genetic component
involves 2,000 causal SNPs.

All screening procedures show limited recovery. RIS achieves
the highest locus recovery among the considered screening
methods (0.110), but this still represents only a small
fraction of the causal loci.

This suggests that screening based on individual marginal
associations can struggle when the genetic signal is distributed
across many predictors, motivating the use of approaches that
retain and model information across a broader collection of
markers.

**6. SNP-level selection can be less stable than regional selection.**

The supplementary SIS subsampling analysis gives a mean
Jaccard overlap of 0.597 at the individual-SNP level and
0.687 when selected SNPs are represented by 250-kb genomic
windows.

Thus, different subsamples can select different individual
markers while more consistently prioritizing the same broader
genomic windows.

This is compatible with nearby or correlated SNPs acting as
alternative markers for overlapping genetic information.
It does not establish that the recurrent windows contain
causal genes.

**7. The top SIS candidates contain substantial correlation
redundancy.**

The correlation-pruning analysis reduces the initial set of
2,000 SIS candidates to 535 markers under the implemented
absolute-correlation threshold of 0.9.

This indicates that many of the top marginally associated
candidates have highly correlated genotype profiles.
Correlation-based pruning therefore offers a possible way
to construct a smaller, less redundant candidate set.

The resulting markers should not, however, be interpreted
as a set of confirmed causal variants.

### Overall interpretation

Taken together, these results show that SNP screening is
not simply a matter of ranking markers by their marginal
association with the phenotype.

Its performance and selected marker composition depend on
the genetic architecture, population structure, linkage
disequilibrium and the selection rule itself.

Randomized screening followed by Ridge provides the strongest
prediction performance among the screened approaches in the
observed FT10 experiment. Structure-adjusted screening is
particularly useful in the semi-synthetic scenario with
ancestry confounding, while the polygenic scenario highlights
the limitations of marginal screening when genetic effects
are distributed across many loci.

The genomic diagnostics and stability analyses further show
that selected SNPs may be correlated, ancestry-associated,
physically concentrated, or variable in their exact identities
across samples.

An important distinction is therefore between identifying
markers that are useful for prediction, identifying markers
that tag broader genomic regions, and recovering the actual
causal variants. These are related but different objectives,
and success at one does not guarantee success at the others.


# 6. Theoretical foundations: Genomic Best Linear Unbiased Prediction (GBLUP)

## 6.1 Motivation: from individual SNP effects to genomic relationships

The preceding sections considered approaches that screen SNPs and construct lower-dimensional representations before performing regression.

An alternative is to avoid explicit variable selection and retain information from the entire genome.

Genomic Best Linear Unbiased Prediction (GBLUP) is a standard approach to genomic prediction that models the genetic effects of individuals through a genomic relationship matrix.

The central idea is that genetically similar accessions are expected to have more similar genetic values than genetically dissimilar accessions.

Let

\[
X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}
\]

denote the genotype matrix, where rows correspond to accessions and columns correspond to SNPs.

Rather than estimating a separate unrestricted fixed coefficient for every SNP, GBLUP introduces an individual-level genetic effect

\[
g=(g_1,\ldots,g_n)^\top.
\]

The phenotype model is

\[
\boxed{
y=\mathbf 1\mu+g+\varepsilon,
}
\]

where

- \(\mu\) is the overall population mean;
- \(g\) represents the additive genomic values of the accessions;
- \(\varepsilon\) represents residual environmental and unexplained variation.

The genomic effects are assigned the covariance structure

\[
\boxed{
g\sim N(0,\sigma_g^2K),
}
\]

where \(K\) is the genomic relationship matrix.

The residual errors satisfy

\[
\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma_e^2I_n),
\]

with \(g\) and \(\varepsilon\) assumed independent.

Consequently,

\[
\boxed{
y\sim N\left(
\mathbf 1\mu,
\sigma_g^2K+\sigma_e^2I_n
\right).
}
\]

The covariance between the phenotypes of accessions \(i\) and \(j\) is therefore

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(y_i,y_j)
=
\sigma_g^2K_{ij}
+
\sigma_e^2\mathbb I(i=j).
\]

This is the fundamental modelling assumption behind GBLUP: genomic similarity determines the covariance structure of genetic effects.

## 6.2 Constructing the genomic relationship matrix

The genomic relationship matrix is constructed from standardized SNP genotypes.

For SNP \(j\), let

\[
\bar x_j=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{ij}
\]

and let \(s_j\) denote its sample standard deviation.

The standardized genotype is

\[
Z_{ij}=
\frac{x_{ij}-\bar x_j}{s_j}.
\]

Writing the standardized genotype matrix as

\[
Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_*},
\]

where \(p_*\) denotes the number of nonconstant SNPs, the relationship matrix is defined as

\[
\boxed{
K=\frac{1}{p_*}ZZ^\top.
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
K_{ik}
=
\frac{1}{p_*}
\sum_{j=1}^{p_*}Z_{ij}Z_{kj}.
\]

Thus, \(K_{ik}\) measures the average standardized genotype similarity between accessions \(i\) and \(k\).

The diagonal elements measure each accession's standardized genomic similarity with itself, while the off-diagonal elements describe pairwise genomic similarity.

The matrix has dimension

\[
K\in\mathbb R^{n\times n},
\]

not \(p_*\times p_*\).

This distinction is crucial. The genomic relationship matrix describes relationships between accessions, whereas the SNP correlation matrix describes relationships between genetic markers.

Because

\[
K=\frac{1}{p_*}ZZ^\top,
\]

it is symmetric and positive semidefinite:

\[
a^\top Ka
=
\frac{1}{p_*}\|Z^\top a\|_2^2
\geq 0
\]

for every \(a\in\mathbb R^n\).

It can therefore be used as a valid covariance kernel.

### Construction in our study

Our implementation constructs \(K\) using blocks of 20,000 SNPs to avoid loading the entire standardized genotype matrix into memory at once.

For each block, SNP columns are centered and scaled, and their contribution to the relationship matrix is accumulated:

\[
ZZ^\top
=
\sum_{j=1}^{p_*}z_jz_j^\top.
\]

The final matrix is divided by the number of nonconstant SNPs:

\[
K_{\mathrm{full}}
=
\frac{1}{p_*}
\sum_{j=1}^{p_*}z_jz_j^\top.
\]

The blockwise calculation is mathematically identical to constructing the complete standardized genotype matrix and computing \(ZZ^\top/p_*\), but it is more memory-efficient.

The implementation uses all nonconstant SNPs, rather than selecting markers according to their association with FT10.

## 6.3 GBLUP as a linear mixed model

The model can be written as

\[
y=\mathbf 1\mu+g+\varepsilon,
\]

with

\[
g\sim N(0,\sigma_g^2K),
\qquad
\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma_e^2I).
\]

This is a linear mixed model because the overall mean is treated as a fixed effect, whereas the genomic effects are random effects.

The covariance matrix of the phenotype is

\[
V=\sigma_g^2K+\sigma_e^2I.
\]

For known variance components, the generalized least-squares estimator of the overall mean is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\mu=
\frac{\mathbf 1^\top V^{-1}y}
{\mathbf 1^\top V^{-1}\mathbf 1}.
}
\]

The BLUP of the genomic effects is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat g
=
\sigma_g^2K V^{-1}
(y-\mathbf 1\widehat\mu).
}
\]

This is the best linear unbiased predictor under the specified Gaussian mixed model and known covariance parameters.

For a test accession, let \(K_{\mathrm{te,tr}}\) denote its genomic relationships with the training accessions.

The predicted genomic value is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat g_{\mathrm{te}}
=
\sigma_g^2K_{\mathrm{te,tr}}
V_{\mathrm{tr}}^{-1}
(y_{\mathrm{tr}}-\mathbf 1\widehat\mu).
}
\]

The corresponding phenotype prediction is

\[
\widehat y_{\mathrm{te}}
=
\widehat\mu\mathbf 1+
\widehat g_{\mathrm{te}}.
\]

The prediction therefore uses the genetic relationships between test and training accessions.

An important consequence is that a test accession can receive a prediction even though its phenotype is completely unobserved, provided its genomic relationships with the training accessions can be calculated.

## 6.4 Connection between GBLUP and kernel ridge regression

The mixed-model formulation has a particularly useful computational interpretation.

Define

\[
\lambda=\frac{\sigma_e^2}{\sigma_g^2}.
\]

After dividing the covariance matrix by \(\sigma_g^2\),

\[
V=\sigma_g^2(K+\lambda I).
\]

For a centered response vector

\[
y_c=y_{\mathrm{tr}}-\bar y_{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf 1,
\]

the genomic prediction can be written in the kernel form

\[
\boxed{
\widehat g_{\mathrm{te}}
=
K_{\mathrm{te,tr}}
(K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}+\lambda I)^{-1}y_c.
}
\]

This is precisely the prediction equation for kernel ridge regression using the genomic relationship matrix as its kernel.

The parameter \(\lambda\) controls the amount of regularization.

- Small \(\lambda\) allows the model to follow the training phenotypes more closely.
- Large \(\lambda\) produces stronger shrinkage towards the population mean.
- Intermediate values balance the fit to the observed data against regularization.

Thus, GBLUP can be understood both as a Gaussian linear mixed model and as kernel ridge regression.

The two formulations produce the same prediction equation when the kernel and variance ratio are defined consistently.

## 6.5 Dual representation and why GBLUP is computationally attractive

A conventional SNP-effect model can be written as

\[
y_c=Z\beta+\varepsilon.
\]

Suppose the marker effects have prior distribution

\[
\beta\sim N(0,\tau^2I).
\]

Then the induced covariance of the genetic values is

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(Z\beta)
=
\tau^2ZZ^\top.
\]

This shows why the genomic relationship matrix appears naturally: it is the covariance induced among individuals by random SNP effects.

The marker-space and individual-space formulations are related through the identity

\[
Z(Z^\top Z+\lambda I_p)^{-1}Z^\top
=
ZZ^\top(ZZ^\top+\lambda I_n)^{-1}.
\]

This is an instance of the primal-dual equivalence used in ridge regression and kernel methods.

The important computational consequence is that, when \(p\gg n\), it is often preferable to work with an \(n\times n\) relationship matrix rather than solve a system involving all \(p\) SNP effects.

In our study, there are approximately 1,003 accessions and 1.7 million SNPs. The relationship matrix is therefore only about \(1,003\times1,003\), despite being constructed using the entire genome.

## 6.6 Fitting GBLUP in our implementation

We construct the full genomic relationship matrix once and extract the appropriate training and test blocks:

\[
K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}
\]

and

\[
K_{\mathrm{te,tr}}.
\]

For a given value of \(\lambda\), the training prediction coefficients are

\[
\alpha_\lambda
=
(K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}+\lambda I)^{-1}y_c.
\]

The test predictions are

\[
\boxed{
\widehat y_{\mathrm{te}}(\lambda)
=
\bar y_{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf 1+
K_{\mathrm{te,tr}}\alpha_\lambda.
}
\]

In our implementation, we do not explicitly invert the matrix for every candidate value of \(\lambda\).

Instead, we use the eigendecomposition

\[
K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}=U\Lambda U^\top,
\]

where

\[
\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_{n_{\mathrm{tr}}})
\]

and \(U\) is orthogonal.

Then

\[
(K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}+\lambda I)^{-1}
=
U(\Lambda+\lambda I)^{-1}U^\top.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\widehat y_{\mathrm{te}}(\lambda)
=
\bar y_{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf 1+
K_{\mathrm{te,tr}}
U
(\Lambda+\lambda I)^{-1}
U^\top y_c.
}
\]

One eigendecomposition can consequently be reused for every candidate regularization parameter.

### Selection of the regularization parameter

We consider a grid of candidate values,

\[
\lambda\in
\left\{10^{-3},10^{-3+0.1},\ldots,10^3\right\}.
\]

The regularization parameter is selected using leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) within the training data.

For a fixed \(\lambda\), define the kernel smoother

\[
H_\lambda
=
K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}
(K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}+\lambda I)^{-1}.
\]

The fitted training response is

\[
\widehat y=H_\lambda y_c.
\]

The leave-one-out residual for observation \(i\) can be calculated without refitting the model \(n_{\mathrm{tr}}\) times:

\[
\boxed{
e_{i,-i}(\lambda)
=
\frac{y_{c,i}-\widehat y_i}
{1-(H_\lambda)_{ii}}.
}
\]

Hence,

\[
\operatorname{CV}(\lambda)
=
\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{tr}}}
\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{tr}}}
\left[
\frac{y_{c,i}-\widehat y_i}
{1-(H_\lambda)_{ii}}
\right]^2.
\]

We choose

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\lambda
=
\arg\min_{\lambda\in\mathcal L}
\operatorname{CV}(\lambda),
}
\]

where \(\mathcal L\) denotes the candidate grid.

The final test prediction is then calculated using the selected value of \(\widehat\lambda\).

In our R implementation, `kernel_all()` performs the eigendecomposition-based calculations and evaluates LOOCV for the candidate values of \(\lambda\). The function `gblup_fit()` selects the minimum-LOOCV value and returns the resulting test predictions.

This implementation uses a fixed grid and LOOCV selection of the regularization parameter; it does not estimate variance components by REML.

## 6.7 Targeted GBLUP: incorporating screened information

Although GBLUP uses the entire genome, a potential limitation is that a small number of strongly associated SNPs may receive relatively little individual emphasis when their information is distributed across a very large number of markers.

To investigate whether screening can improve the dense genomic predictor, we construct a second kernel using the RIS-selected SNPs.

Let \(Z_{\mathcal S}\) denote the standardized genotype matrix containing the selected SNPs. The screened relationship kernel is

\[
\boxed{
K_{\mathrm{screened}}
=
\frac{1}{p_\gamma}
Z_{\mathcal S}Z_{\mathcal S}^\top.
}
\]

We then define a combined kernel:

\[
\boxed{
K_w
=
K_{\mathrm{full}}+
wK_{\mathrm{screened}},
}
\]

where \(w\geq0\) controls the additional contribution of the screened SNP set.

This construction has several useful properties.

When

\[
w=0,
\]

we recover ordinary full-genome GBLUP:

\[
K_w=K_{\mathrm{full}}.
\]

For positive \(w\), the screened SNPs contribute an additional covariance component.

The combined model is

\[
y=\mathbf 1\mu+g_{\mathrm{full}}+
g_{\mathrm{screened}}+\varepsilon,
\]

where

\[
g_{\mathrm{full}}\sim
N(0,\sigma_g^2K_{\mathrm{full}})
\]

and

\[
g_{\mathrm{screened}}\sim
N(0,\sigma_g^2wK_{\mathrm{screened}}).
\]

Assuming independence between the two random components,

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(g_{\mathrm{full}}+
g_{\mathrm{screened}})
=
\sigma_g^2
(K_{\mathrm{full}}+
wK_{\mathrm{screened}}).
\]

Thus, targeted GBLUP does not discard the genome-wide relationship structure. It adds an extra covariance component based on the screened markers.

### Interpretation of the screening weight

Because the full kernel averages over approximately \(p_*\) standardized SNPs, whereas the screened kernel averages over only \(p_\gamma\) SNPs, the additional contribution can be substantial even for moderate values of \(w\).

For a selected SNP, its coefficient in the combined covariance is approximately

\[
\frac{1}{p_*}+\frac{w}{p_\gamma},
\]

compared with

\[
\frac{1}{p_*}
\]

for a SNP that is not in the screened set.

The relative increase in the coefficient of a selected SNP is therefore

\[
\boxed{
1+w\frac{p_*}{p_\gamma}.
}
\]

This illustrates why \(w\) should be tuned rather than chosen arbitrarily.

### Nested cross-validation for targeted GBLUP

The combined model has two tuning parameters:

\[
(w,\lambda).
\]

The parameter \(w\) controls the contribution of the screened kernel, while \(\lambda\) controls regularization.

We select these parameters using inner cross-validation within each outer training set.

For each inner fold:

1. Divide the outer training observations into inner training and validation sets.
2. Recalculate RIS screening using only the inner training observations.
3. Construct the screened kernel from that newly selected SNP set.
4. Combine it with the corresponding full genomic kernel.
5. Evaluate predictions across candidate values of \(w\) and \(\lambda\).
6. Select the parameter combination with the lowest average inner-validation MSPE.

The selected parameters are then used to evaluate the untouched outer test set.

This re-screening step is essential because RIS uses the phenotype. Using a screened SNP set calculated from the complete outer training data inside the inner validation folds would allow the inner validation phenotypes to influence feature selection.

The outer test observations remain completely separate from screening and tuning.

### Computational interpretation

The full genomic kernel is constructed using all nonconstant SNPs. The main computational operations are:

- Constructing the genomic relationship matrix.
- Extracting training and test kernel blocks.
- Performing an eigendecomposition of the training kernel.
- Evaluating the regularization grid.
- Computing test predictions.

The eigendecomposition is performed in individual space, with dimension determined by the number of training accessions rather than the number of SNPs.

For targeted GBLUP, the screened kernel must additionally be constructed and the screening procedure repeated within the inner folds.

The method therefore combines the computational advantages of kernel-based prediction with the possibility of giving additional emphasis to a phenotype-informed SNP set.

### Summary of the modelling distinction

The central difference between ordinary GBLUP and targeted GBLUP is the covariance structure assigned to the genomic effects.

Ordinary GBLUP uses

\[
\boxed{
K=K_{\mathrm{full}}.
}
\]

Targeted GBLUP uses

\[
\boxed{
K=K_{\mathrm{full}}+wK_{\mathrm{screened}}.
}
\]

The former distributes genetic information across the complete genome, whereas the latter retains the complete genome-wide relationship structure while adding a second component based on RIS-selected SNPs.

The empirical comparison in the following section therefore addresses a specific question:

**Does emphasizing SNPs selected for their marginal association with FT10 improve prediction beyond the information already captured by the full genomic relationship matrix?**

This is evaluated using paired outer train-test splits and nested tuning of the targeted model.


## 6.8 Does screening add anything to a dense kernel in our situation? Targeted GBLUP

Screening is good at finding large-effect SNPs, which a dense ridge dilutes. **Targeted GBLUP** keeps the dense kernel
and adds TARP's own screened set as a second kernel, $K = K_{full} + w\,K_{screened}$: screened SNPs receive a
prior-variance boost of about $1 + w\,p/p_{screened}$. $w=0$ is GBLUP; large $w$ approaches the screened-only ridge.
$(w,\lambda)$ are chosen by nested CV with re-screening inside each fold.

```{r e3-run}
run_rep_e3 <- function(seed_i) {
  sp <- make_split(seed_i); tr <- sp$tr; te <- sp$te
  y_tr <- y_all[tr]; y_te <- y_all[te]; y_mean <- mean(y_tr)
  sc <- screen_set(tr, y_tr); Ks_all <- screened_gram(sc$inc)
  set.seed(seed_i * 1000 + 7)
  fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(K_IN), length.out = length(tr)))
  cv <- array(0, c(K_IN, length(W_GRID), length(LAM_GRID)))
  for (f in seq_len(K_IN)) {
    in_tr <- tr[fold != f]; in_va <- tr[fold == f]; y_in <- y_all[in_tr]; ym <- mean(y_in)
    Ks_f <- screened_gram(screen_set(in_tr, y_in)$inc)                           # re-screen inside the fold
    for (iw in seq_along(W_GRID)) {
      w <- W_GRID[iw]
      cv[f, iw, ] <- mse_curve(kernel_curve(Kfull[in_tr, in_tr] + w * Ks_f[in_tr, in_tr],
                                             Kfull[in_va, in_tr] + w * Ks_f[in_va, in_tr], y_in - ym, LAM_GRID),
                               y_all[in_va] - ym)
    }
  }
  cvm <- apply(cv, c(2, 3), mean); jl_w <- apply(cvm, 1, which.min)
  best <- arrayInd(which.min(cvm), dim(cvm)); iw_star <- best[1, 1]; il_star <- best[1, 2]
  te_m <- t(vapply(seq_along(W_GRID), function(iw) {
    w <- W_GRID[iw]
    mse_curve(kernel_curve(Kfull[tr, tr] + w * Ks_all[tr, tr], Kfull[te, tr] + w * Ks_all[te, tr], y_tr - y_mean, LAM_GRID),
              y_te - y_mean)
  }, numeric(length(LAM_GRID))))
  out <- data.frame(seed = seed_i, n_screened = length(sc$inc), TwoK_honest = te_m[iw_star, il_star],
                    GBLUP_nested = te_m[1, jl_w[1]], TwoK_oracle = min(te_m), w_sel = W_GRID[iw_star],
                    lam_sel = LAM_GRID[il_star], cv_min = min(cvm))
  for (iw in seq_along(W_GRID)) out[[paste0("T_w", W_GRID[iw])]] <- te_m[iw, jl_w[iw]]
  out
}
e3 <- run_seeds("e3", run_rep_e3, legacy = "exp3_results.rds")
```

```{r e3-plots, fig.height = 5}
mu_w <- sapply(wcols, function(cn) mean(e3[[cn]])); dmat <- sapply(wcols, function(cn) e3[[cn]] - e3$T_w0)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(seq_along(W_GRID), mu_w, type = "b", pch = 19, xaxt = "n", xlab = "w (weight on the screened kernel)", ylab = "mean test MSPE",
     main = "Targeted GBLUP: error against w")
```

```{r e3-sis-pruned, fig.height=5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ============================================================
# SECTION 6 (ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENT):
# SIS + CORRELATION PRUNING + TARGETED GBLUP
#
# Compare:
#   1. Full-SNP GBLUP
#   2. RIS-targeted GBLUP (existing e3)
#   3. SIS-pruned targeted GBLUP (this experiment)
#
# SIS procedure:
#   - Rank SNPs by absolute marginal t-statistic.
#   - Retain the top 2,000 candidates.
#   - Greedily remove SNPs with |r| >= 0.90 with an
#     already-retained, higher-ranked SNP.
#
# IMPORTANT:
# Screening and pruning are repeated inside every
# inner CV training fold to avoid validation leakage.
# ============================================================


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. SIS SCREENING FOLLOWED BY CORRELATION PRUNING
# ------------------------------------------------------------

sis_prune_select <- function(train_rows, y_train,
                             d = 2000L,
                             cor_cut = 0.90) {

  # Marginal association scores, calculated using
  # only the supplied training observations.
  tt <- screen_scores(train_rows, y_train)

  # Rank SNPs by absolute t-statistic.
  ord <- order(abs(tt), decreasing = TRUE, na.last = NA)
  ord <- ord[is.finite(tt[ord])]

  # Retain the top d candidates.
  d_use <- min(d, length(ord))
  candidates <- ord[seq_len(d_use)]

  # Extract candidate genotypes from training accessions only.
  Xc <- as.matrix(
    G2[train_rows, candidates, drop = FALSE]
  )

  # Remove zero-variance or invalid SNPs.
  snp_sd <- apply(Xc, 2, sd)
  valid <- is.finite(snp_sd) & snp_sd > 1e-8

  candidates <- candidates[valid]
  Xc <- Xc[, valid, drop = FALSE]

  if (length(candidates) == 0) {
    stop("No variable SNPs remain after SIS screening.")
  }

  # Calculate pairwise genotype correlations among
  # the candidate SNPs using training genotypes only.
  C <- suppressWarnings(cor(Xc))

  C[!is.finite(C)] <- 0
  C <- abs(C)

  # A SNP is not considered correlated with itself
  # during the pruning comparisons.
  diag(C) <- 0

  # Greedy pruning:
  # Retain the strongest remaining SNP and discard
  # candidates correlated with it above the threshold.
  blocked <- rep(FALSE, length(candidates))
  keep_idx <- integer(0)

  for (j in seq_along(candidates)) {

    if (!blocked[j]) {

      keep_idx <- c(keep_idx, j)

      blocked <- blocked | (C[j, ] >= cor_cut)

      blocked[j] <- TRUE
    }
  }

  selected <- candidates[keep_idx]

  list(
    selected = selected,
    n_candidates = length(candidates),
    n_retained = length(selected),
    n_removed = length(candidates) - length(selected)
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. CONSTRUCT TRAINING AND VALIDATION/TEST KERNELS
# ------------------------------------------------------------

sis_pruned_kernel_pair <- function(train_rows,
                                   new_rows,
                                   selected) {

  if (length(selected) == 0) {
    stop("The pruned SNP set is empty.")
  }

  # Extract genotypes.
  X_tr <- as.matrix(
    G2[train_rows, selected, drop = FALSE]
  )

  X_new <- as.matrix(
    G2[new_rows, selected, drop = FALSE]
  )

  # Standardization parameters are estimated ONLY
  # from the training accessions.
  cm <- colMeans(X_tr)
  cs <- apply(X_tr, 2, sd)

  keep <- is.finite(cs) & cs > 1e-8

  X_tr <- X_tr[, keep, drop = FALSE]
  X_new <- X_new[, keep, drop = FALSE]

  cm <- cm[keep]
  cs <- cs[keep]

  if (ncol(X_tr) == 0) {
    stop("No variable SNPs remain for kernel construction.")
  }

  # Apply training means and standard deviations
  # to both training and new observations.
  Z_tr <- scale(
    X_tr,
    center = cm,
    scale = cs
  )

  Z_new <- scale(
    X_new,
    center = cm,
    scale = cs
  )

  m_used <- ncol(Z_tr)

  # Training-training kernel.
  K_tr <- tcrossprod(Z_tr) / m_used

  # New-training kernel.
  K_new <- Z_new %*% t(Z_tr) / m_used

  list(
    K_train = K_tr,
    K_new = K_new,
    m_used = m_used
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. ONE OUTER TRAIN-TEST SPLIT
# ------------------------------------------------------------

run_rep_e3_sis_pruned <- function(seed_i) {

  sp <- make_split(seed_i)

  tr <- sp$tr
  te <- sp$te

  y_tr <- y_all[tr]
  y_te <- y_all[te]

  y_mean <- mean(y_tr)

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # A. Outer-training SIS + pruning
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  selected_outer <- sis_prune_select(
    train_rows = tr,
    y_train = y_tr,
    d = 2000,
    cor_cut = 0.90
  )

  # Build the screened kernel using the selected SNPs.
  K_outer <- sis_pruned_kernel_pair(
    train_rows = tr,
    new_rows = te,
    selected = selected_outer$selected
  )

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # B. Inner cross-validation
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  set.seed(seed_i * 1000 + 7)

  fold <- sample(
    rep(seq_len(K_IN), length.out = length(tr))
  )

  cv <- array(
    NA_real_,
    dim = c(K_IN, length(W_GRID), length(LAM_GRID))
  )

  for (f in seq_len(K_IN)) {

    in_tr <- tr[fold != f]
    in_va <- tr[fold == f]

    y_in <- y_all[in_tr]
    ym <- mean(y_in)

    # IMPORTANT:
    # Re-screen and re-prune inside every inner training fold.
    selected_f <- sis_prune_select(
      train_rows = in_tr,
      y_train = y_in,
      d = 2000,
      cor_cut = 0.90
    )

    # Construct inner training-validation kernels.
    K_f <- sis_pruned_kernel_pair(
      train_rows = in_tr,
      new_rows = in_va,
      selected = selected_f$selected
    )

    for (iw in seq_along(W_GRID)) {

      w <- W_GRID[iw]

      K_train_combined <-
        Kfull[in_tr, in_tr] +
        w * K_f$K_train

      K_valid_combined <-
        Kfull[in_va, in_tr] +
        w * K_f$K_new

      cv[f, iw, ] <- mse_curve(
        kernel_curve(
          K_train_combined,
          K_valid_combined,
          y_in - ym,
          LAM_GRID
        ),
        y_all[in_va] - ym
      )
    }
  }

  # Average validation MSPE over inner folds.
  cvm <- apply(cv, c(2, 3), mean)

  # Best lambda for each fixed w.
  jl_w <- apply(cvm, 1, which.min)

  # Jointly optimal w and lambda.
  best <- arrayInd(
    which.min(cvm),
    dim(cvm)
  )

  iw_star <- best[1, 1]
  il_star <- best[1, 2]


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # C. Outer test-set evaluation
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  te_m <- t(
    vapply(
      seq_along(W_GRID),
      function(iw) {

        w <- W_GRID[iw]

        K_train_combined <-
          Kfull[tr, tr] +
          w * K_outer$K_train

        K_test_combined <-
          Kfull[te, tr] +
          w * K_outer$K_new

        mse_curve(
          kernel_curve(
            K_train_combined,
            K_test_combined,
            y_tr - y_mean,
            LAM_GRID
          ),
          y_te - y_mean
        )

      },
      numeric(length(LAM_GRID))
    )
  )


  # Nested-CV-selected targeted GBLUP.
  honest_mspe <- te_m[iw_star, il_star]

  # Nested-CV-selected ordinary GBLUP (w = 0).
  gblup_mspe <- te_m[1, jl_w[1]]

  # Optimistic oracle: minimum test error across all w/lambda.
  # This is a diagnostic only and is NOT a valid tuned estimate.
  oracle_mspe <- min(te_m)


  out <- data.frame(
    seed = seed_i,

    n_candidates = selected_outer$n_candidates,

    n_pruned = selected_outer$n_retained,

    n_removed = selected_outer$n_removed,

    TwoK_honest = honest_mspe,

    GBLUP_nested = gblup_mspe,

    TwoK_oracle = oracle_mspe,

    w_sel = W_GRID[iw_star],

    lam_sel = LAM_GRID[il_star],

    cv_min = min(cvm)
  )

  # Store test MSPE at each w, using its CV-selected lambda.
  for (iw in seq_along(W_GRID)) {

    out[[paste0("T_w", W_GRID[iw])]] <-
      te_m[iw, jl_w[iw]]
  }

  out
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. RUN THE TEN OUTER SPLITS
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Separate cache name so this experiment cannot accidentally
# reuse the RIS-targeted GBLUP results.

e3_sis_pruned <- run_seeds(
  name = "e3_sis_pruned",
  fun = run_rep_e3_sis_pruned,
  legacy = NULL
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. REPORT THE PRUNING RESULTS
# ------------------------------------------------------------

pruning_summary <- data.frame(
  Seed = e3_sis_pruned$seed,
  SIS_candidates = e3_sis_pruned$n_candidates,
  SNPs_retained = e3_sis_pruned$n_pruned,
```

# 7 Other clustering methods specific to categorical data:

## 7.1 Latent class analysis (LCA) of the genotypes, fitted by EM

A latent class model for binary genotypes (a Bernoulli mixture) is fitted by the EM algorithm on a thinned, evenly
spaced panel of 800 SNPs with minor allele frequency at least 0.1: each accession gets soft class memberships
$R$ ($n\times K$), with class-specific allele probabilities $\theta_{kj}$ and mixing weights $\pi_k$. No response is used.
Neighbouring SNPs are not independent given the class, so BIC favors many classes; the classes are flexible ancestry
features, not a taxonomy.

```{r lca}
lca_em <- function(B, K, n_init = 10, iters = 300, tol = 1e-7) {
  n_ <- nrow(B); best <- NULL
  for (s in seq_len(n_init)) {
    R <- matrix(runif(n_ * K), n_, K); R <- R / rowSums(R); ll_old <- -Inf
    for (it in seq_len(iters)) {
      pi_k <- pmax(colMeans(R), 1e-8)                                              # M-step
      theta <- sweep(t(R) %*% B + 0.5, 1, colSums(R) + 1, "/")
      logp <- B %*% t(log(theta)) + (1 - B) %*% t(log(1 - theta))                  # E-step
      logp <- sweep(logp, 2, log(pi_k), "+")
      m <- apply(logp, 1, max); lse <- m + log(rowSums(exp(logp - m)))
      R <- exp(logp - lse); ll <- sum(lse)
      if (abs(ll - ll_old) < tol * abs(ll)) break
      ll_old <- ll
    }
    if (is.null(best) || ll > best$ll) best <- list(R = R, ll = ll)
  }
  best
}
set.seed(2025)
Xp <- G2[, round(seq(1, p, length.out = 30000))]; f_l <- colMeans(Xp) / 2
Xp <- Xp[, f_l > 0.1 & f_l < 0.9]
B_lca <- (Xp[, round(seq(1, ncol(Xp), length.out = min(800, ncol(Xp))))] >= 1) * 1; rm(Xp)
K_LCA_SET <- c(2:8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 24)
lca_file <- file.path("cache", "lca_fits.rds")
if (USE_CACHE && file.exists(lca_file)) {
  fits <- readRDS(lca_file)
} else {
  fits <- lapply(K_LCA_SET, function(k) lca_em(B_lca, k)); names(fits) <- K_LCA_SET; saveRDS(fits, lca_file)
}
bic <- sapply(names(fits), function(k) { k <- as.integer(k); -2 * fits[[as.character(k)]]$ll + ((k - 1) + k * ncol(B_lca)) * log(n) })
Rmem8 <- fits[["8"]]$R; hard8 <- max.col(Rmem8)
cat("Class sizes at K = 8:", paste(table(hard8), collapse = " / "), "\nMean FT10 by class:", paste(round(tapply(y_all, hard8, mean), 1), collapse = " / "), "\n")
```

```{r interactive-class-sizes, fig.width=13, fig.height=9}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)

K_values <- 3:8

# --------------------------------------------------
# 1. Calculate class assignments and class summaries
# --------------------------------------------------

class_sizes <- bind_rows(lapply(K_values, function(k) {

  R <- fits[[as.character(k)]]$R

  # Modal posterior class assignment
  assignment <- max.col(R, ties.method = "first")

  stopifnot(length(assignment) == length(y_all))

  df <- data.frame(
    Class = assignment,
    FT10 = y_all
  )

  df %>%
    group_by(Class) %>%
    summarise(
      N = n(),
      Mean_FT10 = mean(FT10, na.rm = TRUE),
      SD_FT10 = sd(FT10, na.rm = TRUE),
      N_FT10 = sum(!is.na(FT10)),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      K = paste0("K = ", k),
      Percentage = 100 * N / sum(N),
      Class = factor(
        paste0("Class ", Class),
        levels = paste0("Class ", 1:k)
      ),
      Hover = paste0(
        "<b>", K, " | ", Class, "</b>",
        "<br>Number of accessions: ", N,
        "<br>Percentage: ", round(Percentage, 2), "%",
        "<br>Mean FT10: ", round(Mean_FT10, 3),
        "<br>SD FT10: ", round(SD_FT10, 3),
        "<br>Non-missing FT10: ", N_FT10
      ),
      Bar_Label = paste0(
        "N = ", N,
        "<br>Mean = ", round(Mean_FT10, 1)
      )
    )
}))

# --------------------------------------------------
# 2. Interactive bar plot
# --------------------------------------------------

p_class <- ggplot(
  class_sizes,
  aes(
    x = Class,
    y = N,
    fill = Class,
    text = Hover
  )
) +

  geom_col(width = 0.72, show.legend = FALSE) +

  geom_text(
    aes(label = Bar_Label),
    vjust = -0.35,
    size = 3,
    lineheight = 1.1
  ) +

  facet_wrap(~K, ncol = 3, scales = "free_x") +

  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +

  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.22))
  ) +

  labs(
    title = "Latent Class Sizes and Phenotypic Profiles",
    subtitle = "Modal posterior assignment across LCA solutions",
    x = "Latent class",
    y = "Number of accessions"
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +

  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

ggplotly(p_class, tooltip = "text") %>%
  layout(
    hoverlabel = list(align = "left"),
    margin = list(t = 90)
  )
```

```{r lca-genomic-heatmap, fig.width=11, fig.height=11, dpi=220, out.width="100%"}

# ============================================================
# GENOMIC RELATIONSHIP HEATMAP ORDERED BY LCA CLASS (K = 8)
# ============================================================

# 1. Validate input data
Kfull <- as.matrix(Kfull)

stopifnot(
  nrow(Kfull) == 1003L,
  ncol(Kfull) == 1003L,
  length(hard8) == nrow(Kfull),
  length(y_all) == nrow(Kfull),
  all(hard8 %in% 1:8)
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Order accessions within each LCA class using hierarchical
#    clustering based on genomic relationship distances
# ------------------------------------------------------------

within_class_order <- lapply(seq_len(8), function(k) {

  idx <- which(hard8 == k)

  if (length(idx) <= 2) {
    return(idx)
  }

  d2 <- outer(
    diag(Kfull)[idx],
    diag(Kfull)[idx],
    "+"
  ) - 2 * Kfull[idx, idx, drop = FALSE]

  d2 <- pmax(d2, 0)

  d <- stats::as.dist(sqrt(d2))

  hc <- stats::hclust(d, method = "average")

  idx[hc$order]
})

# Combine class-wise ordering
ord <- unlist(within_class_order, use.names = FALSE)

# Validate ordering
stopifnot(
  length(ord) == nrow(Kfull),
  !anyNA(ord),
  !anyDuplicated(ord),
  setequal(ord, seq_len(nrow(Kfull)))
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Reorder genomic relationship matrix and annotations
# ------------------------------------------------------------

K_ord <- Kfull[ord, ord, drop = FALSE]

class_ord <- factor(
  paste0("Class ", hard8[ord]),
  levels = paste0("Class ", seq_len(8))
)

ft10_ord <- y_all[ord]

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Colour palettes
# ------------------------------------------------------------

class_cols <- setNames(
  grDevices::hcl.colors(8, palette = "Dark 3"),
  levels(class_ord)
)

# FT10: low = red, middle = orange, high = yellow
ft_range <- range(y_all, na.rm = TRUE)

if (diff(ft_range) == 0) {
  ft_range <- ft_range + c(-0.5, 0.5)
}

ft10_col_fun <- circlize::colorRamp2(
  c(
    ft_range[1],
    mean(ft_range),
    ft_range[2]
  ),
  c("#B2182B", "#F46D43", "#FFFF00")
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Clip extreme relationship values for visual contrast
# ------------------------------------------------------------

offdiag <- K_ord[upper.tri(K_ord)]

lim <- as.numeric(
  stats::quantile(
    abs(offdiag),
    0.995,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
)

lim <- max(lim, 1e-8)

# IMPORTANT: Preserve matrix dimensions while clipping
K_ord_plot <- K_ord

K_ord_plot[K_ord_plot > lim] <- lim
K_ord_plot[K_ord_plot < -lim] <- -lim

# Relationship colours:
# Negative = blue, zero = white, positive = red
K_col_fun <- circlize::colorRamp2(
  c(-lim, 0, lim),
  c("#2166AC", "#F7F7F7", "#B2182B")
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Verify dimensions and alignment
# ------------------------------------------------------------

cat("\n========== DIMENSION CHECK ==========\n")

cat("K_ord dimensions:      ", dim(K_ord), "\n")
cat("K_ord_plot dimensions: ", dim(K_ord_plot), "\n")
cat("class_ord length:      ", length(class_ord), "\n")
cat("ft10_ord length:       ", length(ft10_ord), "\n")
cat("Clip limit:            ", round(lim, 4), "\n")

cat("\nClass distribution:\n")
print(table(class_ord))

cat("=====================================\n")

stopifnot(
  is.matrix(K_ord_plot),
  identical(dim(K_ord_plot), c(1003L, 1003L)),
  length(class_ord) == nrow(K_ord_plot),
  length(class_ord) == ncol(K_ord_plot),
  length(ft10_ord) == nrow(K_ord_plot)
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Top annotation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ha_top <- ComplexHeatmap::HeatmapAnnotation(

  LCA_Class = class_ord,
  FT10 = ft10_ord,

  col = list(
    LCA_Class = class_cols,
    FT10 = ft10_col_fun
  ),

  annotation_name_side = "left",

  annotation_legend_param = list(
    LCA_Class = list(title = "LCA class"),
    FT10 = list(title = "FT10 (days)")
  )
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Left annotation
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ha_left <- ComplexHeatmap::rowAnnotation(

  LCA_Class = class_ord,
  FT10 = ft10_ord,

  col = list(
    LCA_Class = class_cols,
    FT10 = ft10_col_fun
  ),

  show_legend = FALSE,
  annotation_name_side = "top"
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 9. Construct heatmap
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ht <- ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(

  K_ord_plot,

  name = "Genomic\nrelationship",

  col = K_col_fun,

  top_annotation = ha_top,
  left_annotation = ha_left,

  cluster_rows = FALSE,
  cluster_columns = FALSE,

  # Separate the matrix into eight LCA class blocks
  row_split = class_ord,
  column_split = class_ord,

  cluster_row_slices = FALSE,
  cluster_column_slices = FALSE,

  row_gap = grid::unit(0.8, "mm"),
  column_gap = grid::unit(0.8, "mm"),

  show_row_names = FALSE,
  show_column_names = FALSE,

  row_title = NULL,

  column_title =
    "Genome-wide relationship matrix ordered by LCA class (K = 8)",

  column_title_gp = grid::gpar(
    fontsize = 13,
    fontface = "bold"
  ),

  use_raster = TRUE,
  raster_quality = 3,

  border = FALSE,

  heatmap_legend_param = list(
    title = "Relationship",
    at = round(c(-lim, 0, lim), 3)
  )
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 10. Draw heatmap
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ComplexHeatmap::draw(
  ht,
  heatmap_legend_side = "right",
  annotation_legend_side = "right"
)
```

```{r lca-20k-ft10, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE, fig.width=11, fig.height=7}

# ============================================================
# 20,000 SNPs MOST ASSOCIATED WITH FT10
# SIX-CLASS BERNOULLI LATENT CLASS ANALYSIS USING EM
# ============================================================

library(bigstatsr)
library(ggplot2)

dir.create("cache", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create("output/lca_20k", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

set.seed(2025)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. BASIC CHECKS
# ------------------------------------------------------------

stopifnot(exists("G2"))
stopifnot(exists("y_all"))

y <- as.numeric(y_all)

n <- length(y)
p <- ncol(G2)

stopifnot(nrow(G2) == n)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(y)))

cat("Number of accessions:", n, "\n")
cat("Number of genomic markers:", p, "\n")


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. MARGINAL SNP-FT10 ASSOCIATION SCREENING
# ------------------------------------------------------------

cat("\nCalculating marginal SNP-FT10 associations...\n")

ncores_use <- if (exists("N_CORES")) {
  N_CORES
} else {
  max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 1L)
}

gw20 <- big_univLinReg(
  G2,
  y.train = y,
  ind.train = seq_len(n),
  ncores = ncores_use
)

# Absolute t-statistics measure strength of marginal association
t_score <- as.numeric(gw20$estim) /
  as.numeric(gw20$std.err)

stopifnot(length(t_score) == p)

valid_idx <- which(
  is.finite(t_score) &
    is.finite(gw20$std.err) &
    gw20$std.err > 0
)

N_SELECT <- min(20000L, length(valid_idx))

selected_snps <- valid_idx[
  order(
    abs(t_score[valid_idx]),
    decreasing = TRUE
  )[seq_len(N_SELECT)]
]

selected_t <- t_score[selected_snps]

cat("Selected SNPs:", length(selected_snps), "\n")
cat("Maximum absolute t-statistic:",
    max(abs(selected_t)), "\n")


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. CONSTRUCT THE BINARY GENOTYPE MATRIX
# ------------------------------------------------------------

cat("\nConstructing binary genotype matrix...\n")

X20 <- as.matrix(G2[, selected_snps])

stopifnot(nrow(X20) == n)

# Same binary threshold used in the earlier LCA analysis:
# dosage >= 1 -> 1
# dosage <  1 -> 0

B20 <- 1L * (X20 >= 1)

rm(X20)
gc()

# Remove constant indicators
keep <- colSums(B20) > 0 &
  colSums(B20) < nrow(B20)

B20 <- B20[, keep, drop = FALSE]
selected_snps <- selected_snps[keep]
selected_t <- selected_t[keep]

J <- ncol(B20)
K <- 6L

colnames(B20) <- paste0("SNP_", selected_snps)

cat("Final binary matrix dimensions:",
    nrow(B20), "x", ncol(B20), "\n")


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. STABLE BERNOULLI LCA EM ALGORITHM
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Model:
#
# P(B_i) = sum_k pi_k P(B_i | class k)
#
# Conditional independence:
#
# P(B_i | class k) =
#   product_j theta[j,k]^B[i,j] *
#   (1-theta[j,k])^(1-B[i,j])
#
# pi_k     = class proportions
# theta    = class-specific SNP probabilities
#
# Additive pseudocount alpha stabilizes estimates of theta.
#
# Likelihood is evaluated using log-sum-exp.


fit_lca_bernoulli <- function(
    B,
    K = 6,
    n_init = 3,
    max_iter = 200,
    tol = 1e-6,
    alpha = 0.5,
    seed = 2025,
    verbose = TRUE
) {

  B <- as.matrix(B)

  n <- nrow(B)
  J <- ncol(B)

  if (anyNA(B) || !all(B %in% c(0, 1))) {
    stop("B must contain only 0 and 1, without missing values.")
  }

  # Convert to double precision for matrix multiplication
  storage.mode(B) <- "double"

  # E-step: stable posterior probability calculation
  estep <- function(B, pi_k, theta) {

    logit_theta <- log(theta) - log1p(-theta)

    # Sum_j log(1-theta_jk), separately for each class
    offset <- rowSums(log1p(-theta)) + log(pi_k)

    # Log joint probability, excluding the constant terms
    logp <- B %*% t(logit_theta)

    logp <- sweep(
      logp,
      2,
      offset,
      "+"
    )

    # Log-sum-exp for each accession
    row_max <- apply(logp, 1, max)

    log_norm <- row_max +
      log(
        rowSums(
          exp(
            sweep(logp, 1, row_max, "-")
          )
        )
      )

    R <- exp(
      sweep(logp, 1, log_norm, "-")
    )

    list(
      R = R,
      ll = sum(log_norm)
    )
  }


  best <- NULL
  run_loglik <- numeric(n_init)

  for (s in seq_len(n_init)) {

    set.seed(seed + s)

    if (verbose) {
      cat("\nStarting EM initialization", s, "\n")
    }

    # Random initial posterior probabilities
    R <- matrix(
      rexp(n * K),
      nrow = n,
      ncol = K
    )

    R <- R / rowSums(R)

    ll_old <- -Inf
    converged <- FALSE
    ll_trace <- numeric(max_iter)

    for (it in seq_len(max_iter)) {

      # ---------------- M-step ----------------

      nk <- colSums(R)

      pi_k <- pmax(nk / n, 1e-12)
      pi_k <- pi_k / sum(pi_k)

      weighted_counts <- t(R) %*% B

      theta <- sweep(
        weighted_counts + alpha,
        1,
        nk + 2 * alpha,
        "/"
      )

      theta <- pmin(
        pmax(theta, 1e-8),
        1 - 1e-8
      )

      # ---------------- E-step ----------------

      est <- estep(B, pi_k, theta)

      R_new <- est$R
      ll <- est$ll

      ll_trace[it] <- ll

      # Convergence check
      if (
        is.finite(ll_old) &&
        abs(ll - ll_old) <= tol * (1 + abs(ll_old))
      ) {

        converged <- TRUE
        R <- R_new

        break
      }

      R <- R_new
      ll_old <- ll

      if (
        verbose &&
        (it == 1 || it %% 25 == 0)
      ) {
        cat(
          "Initialization", s,
          "| Iteration", it,
          "| Log-likelihood:", round(ll, 4),
          "\n"
        )
      }
    }

    # Re-estimate parameters using the final responsibilities
    nk <- colSums(R)

    pi_k <- pmax(nk / n, 1e-12)
    pi_k <- pi_k / sum(pi_k)

    theta <- sweep(
      t(R) %*% B + alpha,
      1,
      nk + 2 * alpha,
      "/"
    )

    theta <- pmin(
      pmax(theta, 1e-8),
      1 - 1e-8
    )

    # Final E-step
    est <- estep(B, pi_k, theta)

    R <- est$R
    ll <- est$ll

    run_loglik[s] <- ll

    if (verbose) {
      cat(
        "Completed initialization", s,
        "| Log-likelihood:", round(ll, 4),
        "| Iterations:", it,
        "| Converged:", converged,
        "\n"
      )
    }

    current <- list(
      R = R,
      theta = theta,
      pi = pi_k,
      ll = ll,
      n_iter = it,
      converged = converged,
      ll_trace = ll_trace[seq_len(it)],
      initialization = s
    )

    if (is.null(best) || ll > best$ll) {
      best <- current
    }
  }

  best$run_loglik <- run_loglik
  best$K <- K
  best$J <- J
  best$n <- n
  best$alpha <- alpha

  best
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. FIT SIX-CLASS MODEL
# ------------------------------------------------------------

cat("\nFitting six-class LCA using", J, "SNPs...\n")
```
