```{r lca-alluvial-ft10, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=14, fig.height=9 , eval=FALSE}

# ============================================================
# INTERACTIVE LCA ALLUVIAL PLOT COLOURED BY MEAN FT10
# K = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
# ============================================================

library(plotly)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. SETTINGS AND INPUT VALIDATION
# ------------------------------------------------------------

K_values <- 2:8

stopifnot(
  is.list(fits),
  length(y_all) > 0,
  is.numeric(y_all)
)

n_accessions <- length(y_all)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. EXTRACT MODAL CLASS ASSIGNMENTS
# ------------------------------------------------------------

hard_k <- lapply(K_values, function(k) {

  model <- fits[[as.character(k)]]

  if (is.null(model)) {
    stop(paste("Missing LCA model for K =", k))
  }

  R <- model$R

  if (is.null(R)) {
    stop(paste("Posterior membership matrix R missing for K =", k))
  }

  if (nrow(R) != n_accessions) {
    stop(paste(
      "Number of accessions does not match y_all for K =", k
    ))
  }

  if (ncol(R) != k) {
    stop(paste(
      "Unexpected number of classes for K =", k
    ))
  }

  # Assign each accession to its most likely latent class
  max.col(R, ties.method = "first")

})

names(hard_k) <- as.character(K_values)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. CREATE NODES AND CALCULATE MEAN FT10
# ------------------------------------------------------------

nodes <- do.call(rbind, lapply(K_values, function(k) {

  assignment <- hard_k[[as.character(k)]]

  counts <- tabulate(assignment, nbins = k)

  # Mean FT10 within each modal class
  mean_ft10 <- vapply(seq_len(k), function(j) {

    values <- y_all[assignment == j]

    if (all(is.na(values))) {
      return(NA_real_)
    }

    mean(values, na.rm = TRUE)

  }, numeric(1))

  data.frame(
    K = k,
    class = seq_len(k),
    n = counts,
    proportion = counts / n_accessions,
    mean_FT10 = mean_ft10
  )

}))

# Unique node identifiers
nodes$key <- paste(
  nodes$K,
  nodes$class,
  sep = "_"
)

# Informative hover labels
nodes$label <- sprintf(
  "K = %d | Class %d<br>Accessions: %d (%.1f%%)<br>Mean FT10: %.2f days",
  nodes$K,
  nodes$class,
  nodes$n,
  100 * nodes$proportion,
  nodes$mean_FT10
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. COLOUR NODES BY MEAN FT10
# 
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. COLOUR NODES BY MEAN FT10: RED -> YELLOW
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Common colour scale across all K solutions
ft_range <- range(
  nodes$mean_FT10,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

if (length(ft_range) != 2 || any(!is.finite(ft_range))) {
  stop("Unable to calculate a valid FT10 colour scale.")
}

# Red -> Orange -> Yellow
ft_palette <- grDevices::colorRampPalette(
  c(
    "#B2182B",  # Deep red: low FT10
    "#EF6548",  # Orange-red
    "#FDBB3D",  # Orange-yellow
    "#FFFF00"   # Bright yellow: high FT10
  )
)(100)

if (diff(ft_range) < 1e-10) {

  colour_index <- rep(50L, nrow(nodes))

} else {

  colour_index <- round(
    1 + 99 * (
      nodes$mean_FT10 - ft_range[1]
    ) / diff(ft_range)
  )

}

colour_index <- pmax(1, pmin(100, colour_index))

nodes$color <- ft_palette[colour_index]

# Missing values shown in grey
nodes$color[is.na(nodes$mean_FT10)] <- "#999999"


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. POSITION NODES
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Each K solution gets its own vertical column
nodes$x <- (
  nodes$K - min(K_values)
) / (
  max(K_values) - min(K_values)
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. CONSTRUCT FLOWS BETWEEN CONSECUTIVE SOLUTIONS
# ------------------------------------------------------------

flows <- list()

for (k in 2:7) {

  assignment_from <- hard_k[[as.character(k)]]
  assignment_to <- hard_k[[as.character(k + 1)]]

  # Transition table
  transition <- table(
    factor(assignment_from, levels = seq_len(k)),
    factor(assignment_to, levels = seq_len(k + 1))
  )

  transition <- as.matrix(transition)

  # Identify non-zero transitions
  ij <- which(
    transition > 0,
    arr.ind = TRUE
  )

  if (nrow(ij) == 0) next

  source_class <- ij[, 1]
  target_class <- ij[, 2]

  flow_n <- transition[ij]

  # Identify source and target nodes
  source_key <- paste(
    k,
    source_class,
    sep = "_"
  )

  target_key <- paste(
    k + 1,
    target_class,
    sep = "_"
  )

  source_id <- match(
    source_key,
    nodes$key
  ) - 1L

  target_id <- match(
    target_key,
    nodes$key
  ) - 1L

  # Percentage of each source class moving to a destination
  source_sizes <- rowSums(transition)

  source_percent <- 100 * flow_n /
    source_sizes[source_class]

  flows[[as.character(k)]] <- data.frame(
    source = source_id,
    target = target_id,
    value = as.numeric(flow_n),
    source_percent = source_percent
  )

}

links <- do.call(
  rbind,
  flows
)

# Neutral grey ribbons
links$color <- rep(
  "rgba(110,110,110,0.25)",
  nrow(links)
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. CREATE INTERACTIVE SANKEY PLOT
# ------------------------------------------------------------

p_alluvial <- plotly::plot_ly(
  type = "sankey",
  arrangement = "snap",
  orientation = "h",

  node = list(
    label = nodes$label,
    x = nodes$x,
    color = nodes$color,
    pad = 18,
    thickness = 22,
    line = list(
      color = "rgba(50,50,50,0.45)",
      width = 0.6
    ),
    hovertemplate = "%{label}<extra></extra>"
  ),

  link = list(
    source = links$source,
    target = links$target,
    value = links$value,
    color = links$color,
    customdata = links$source_percent,
    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "From: %{source.label}",
      "<br>To: %{target.label}",
      "<br>Accessions: %{value}",
      "<br>Source class percentage: %{customdata:.1f}%",
      "<extra></extra>"
    )
  )
)

# Simple layout without custom annotation lists
p_alluvial <- plotly::layout(
  p_alluvial,

  title = list(
    text = paste0(
      "Evolution of LCA Class Assignments",
      "<br><sup>Classes coloured by mean FT10</sup>"
    ),
    x = 0.5
  ),

  font = list(
    family = "Arial",
    size = 12
  ),

  margin = list(
    l = 30,
    r = 30,
    t = 90,
    b = 40
  )
)

# Render
p_alluvial

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. DISPLAY PLOT
# ------------------------------------------------------------

p_alluvial

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 9. CLASS-WISE FT10 SUMMARY TABLE
# ------------------------------------------------------------

cat("\n========================================\n")
cat("CLASS-WISE FLOWERING TIME SUMMARY\n")
cat("========================================\n")

print(
  nodes[, c(
    "K",
    "class",
    "n",
    "proportion",
    "mean_FT10"
  )],
  row.names = FALSE
)

cat("\n========================================\n")

# ============================================================
```

```{r lca-motivation-conclusions, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

cat("
### Motivation for Latent Class Analysis

The preceding PCA and K-means analyses provided an initial characterization of genomic variation and population structure among the accessions. However, these approaches primarily describe variation through continuous genomic axes and geometric partitions of the resulting low-dimensional representation. This motivated us to investigate whether the observed genotype profiles could also be represented through a probabilistic grouping of accessions.

We therefore employed Latent Class Analysis (LCA), a finite mixture model that assumes the presence of an unobserved categorical variable representing the latent genetic group to which each accession belongs. Unlike K-means, which assigns accessions according to distances in a selected PC space, LCA models the joint distribution of categorical genotype indicators through class-specific response probabilities. Each latent class is consequently characterized by a distinct profile of SNP indicator probabilities, while each accession receives posterior probabilities of membership in the different classes.

Our main motivation was to determine whether this alternative representation of genomic heterogeneity would reveal groups of accessions with noticeably different flowering-time characteristics. In particular, we were interested in exploring whether the genomic marker profiles could distinguish groups exhibiting relatively earlier or later flowering.

### LCA Results and Findings

We fitted a six-class Bernoulli latent class model using 20,000 SNPs selected according to the magnitude of their marginal association with FT10. The resulting binary genotype matrix contained 1,003 accessions and 20,000 marker indicators. The model was estimated using an EM algorithm with three random initializations, retaining the solution with the highest observed-data log-likelihood.

The fitted model converged to a solution with log-likelihood approximately -4,900,303. The resulting classification was noticeably unbalanced: 521 accessions (51.9%) belonged to Class 1, while the remaining accessions were distributed across five smaller classes.

An interesting pattern emerged when the estimated classes were examined against FT10. The mean FT10 values differed considerably across the six groups. Class 5 exhibited the highest mean flowering-time value (110.82), followed by Class 2 (101.76) and Class 4 (94.38). In contrast, Classes 1, 3 and 6 had lower mean values of 75.78, 77.64 and 80.65, respectively. The difference between the highest and lowest class means was approximately 35 FT10 units.

Thus, the fitted latent groups displayed considerable heterogeneity in their flowering-time distributions. In particular, the model distinguished groups with comparatively high and low mean FT10 values, suggesting that the selected genomic marker profiles contain information that can separate accessions exhibiting different flowering-time characteristics.

The result is interesting because the objective of this exercise was not to directly classify accessions using their observed FT10 values. Instead, the LCA constructed groups from multivariate genotype patterns, and we subsequently examined how flowering time varied across those groups. However, because the SNPs were selected using their marginal association with FT10, the resulting phenotype differences are exploratory and should not be treated as independent validation of a genotype-based classification.

### Computational and Statistical Limitations

Despite the interesting descriptive results, this analysis comes with important computational and statistical limitations.

First, the analysis is computationally demanding. Even after reducing the original genomic marker set to 20,000 SNPs, the resulting data matrix contains more than 20 million binary genotype observations. For a six-class model, the Bernoulli response probabilities alone involve approximately 120,000 class-specific marker parameters, in addition to the class mixing proportions. At every EM iteration, the algorithm must repeatedly evaluate the contribution of all selected markers across all accessions and latent classes. Consequently, computational and memory requirements increase substantially with both the number of markers and the number of latent classes. Repeated random initializations add further computational cost.

Second, the local independence assumption underlying standard LCA is particularly restrictive in this genomic setting. The model assumes that, conditional on latent class membership, the selected SNP indicators are mutually independent. However, genetic markers are not generally independent because linkage disequilibrium induces correlations between SNPs in nearby genomic regions. Since the selected markers were not LD-pruned, this assumption is unlikely to hold exactly. Correlated markers may therefore contribute redundant information, potentially influencing the estimated class profiles and producing an overly strong impression of separation.

Third, the marker-selection procedure was phenotype-guided: SNPs were selected using their marginal association with FT10 before fitting the latent class model. Although FT10 itself was not included in the EM likelihood, it influenced the composition of the marker panel. The observed differences in class-wise flowering time must therefore be interpreted with this selection step in mind.

Finally, convergence of the EM algorithm does not guarantee that the global maximum of the likelihood has been attained or that the selected number of classes is optimal. The three initializations reached different likelihood values, indicating some sensitivity to initialization. Additional random starts, comparisons across alternative values of the number of classes, and assessments of classification stability would be required for a stronger evaluation.

### Overall Conclusion

The LCA provides an interesting complementary view of genomic heterogeneity among the accessions. The six-class solution produced groups with substantially different mean FT10 values, indicating that the estimated genomic profiles can be used to organize accessions into groups exhibiting contrasting flowering-time characteristics. The separation is particularly notable between the groups with the highest and lowest mean FT10 values.

At the same time, the analysis highlights the difficulty of applying conventional latent class models to very high-dimensional genomic data. The considerable computational burden, the likely violation of local independence due to linkage disequilibrium, and the phenotype-guided marker-selection procedure limit the strength of the conclusions that can currently be drawn.

We therefore regard this analysis as an exploratory investigation of latent genomic groupings rather than a definitive reconstruction of genetic populations. Nevertheless, it provides a useful starting point for further work involving LD-pruned marker panels, phenotype-independent marker selection, and more extensive assessments of latent class stability.
")

```


## 7.2 Relatedness-only predictors, ancestry-explicit GBLUP and within-lineage correlation

Predictors that use **only relatedness** (no SNP effects): the mean FT10 of the k genetically closest training
accessions (kNN on the genomic distance), a Nadaraya-Watson kernel smoother on the same distances, and LCA class
memberships. They are compared with GBLUP, and with ancestry-explicit GBLUP ("Q+K": the dense kernel plus a linear
kernel on the LCA memberships or the top-5 axes, weight chosen by LOOCV). Finally, the **within-class correlation**:
test accessions and their predictions are centered within their latent class, and the pooled correlation is computed.
A predictor that only knows lineage scores about zero.

```{r struct-run}
K_NN_GRID <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20, 30, 50, 80); H_GRID <- c(0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1)
WQ_GRID <- c(0, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100); K_WITHIN <- c(4, 6, 8, 12)
knn_predict <- function(D_tt, D_te, y_tr, k_grid) {
  n_tr <- length(y_tr); kmax <- max(k_grid); Dt <- D_tt; diag(Dt) <- Inf
  loo <- matrix(0, n_tr, length(k_grid))
  for (i in seq_len(n_tr)) { nn <- order(Dt[i, ])[1:kmax]; loo[i, ] <- (cumsum(y_tr[nn]) / seq_len(kmax))[k_grid] }
  kbest <- k_grid[which.min(colMeans((y_tr - loo)^2))]
  list(pred = vapply(seq_len(nrow(D_te)), function(i) mean(y_tr[order(D_te[i, ])[1:kbest]]), numeric(1)), k = kbest)
}
nw_apply <- function(D, y_tr, h, th, drop_self = FALSE) {
  W <- exp(-pmax(D, 0) / (2 * h * th)); if (drop_self) diag(W) <- 0
  den <- rowSums(W); num <- as.numeric(W %*% y_tr); ifelse(den < 1e-8, mean(y_tr), num / pmax(den, 1e-300))
}
nw_predict <- function(D_tt, D_te, y_tr, h_grid) {
  th <- median(D_tt[upper.tri(D_tt)])
  mse <- sapply(h_grid, function(h) mean((y_tr - nw_apply(D_tt, y_tr, h, th, TRUE))^2)); hb <- h_grid[which.min(mse)]
  list(pred = nw_apply(D_te, y_tr, hb, th), h = hb)
}
within_cor <- function(y, pr, g, min_n = 5) {
  tb <- table(g); keep <- as.integer(names(tb)[tb >= min_n]); ix <- g %in% keep
  yc <- y[ix] - ave(y[ix], g[ix]); pc <- pr[ix] - ave(pr[ix], g[ix])
  c(r = cor(yc, pc), slope = sum(yc * pc) / sum(pc^2), n = sum(ix), frac = sum(yc^2) / sum((y - mean(y))^2))
}
lin_kernel <- function(M) { Kq <- tcrossprod(scale(M, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)); Kq / mean(diag(Kq)) }
qk_fit <- function(Kq, tr, te, y_c, y_new_c) {
  res <- lapply(WQ_GRID, function(w) kernel_all(Kfull[tr, tr] + w * Kq[tr, tr], Kfull[te, tr] + w * Kq[te, tr], y_c, y_new_c, LAM_GRID))
  loo <- sapply(res, function(r) r$loo); ib <- arrayInd(which.min(loo), dim(loo))
  list(mspe = res[[ib[1, 2]]]$test[ib[1, 1]], w = WQ_GRID[ib[1, 2]])
}
K_lca_kernel <- lin_kernel(Rmem8[, -ncol(Rmem8), drop = FALSE]); K_pc_kernel <- lin_kernel(pcs5)
hard_k <- lapply(K_WITHIN, function(k) max.col(fits[[as.character(k)]]$R)); names(hard_k) <- K_WITHIN

run_rep_struct <- function(seed_i) {
  sp <- make_split(seed_i); tr <- sp$tr; te <- sp$te
  y_tr <- y_all[tr]; y_te <- y_all[te]; ym <- mean(y_tr); y_c <- y_tr - ym; y_new_c <- y_te - ym
  X1 <- cbind(1, Rmem8[, -ncol(Rmem8), drop = FALSE])                       # class-membership-only predictor
  beta <- solve(crossprod(X1[tr, ]) + 1e-6 * diag(ncol(X1)), crossprod(X1[tr, ], y_tr))
  qk_l <- qk_fit(K_lca_kernel, tr, te, y_c, y_new_c); qk_p <- qk_fit(K_pc_kernel, tr, te, y_c, y_new_c)
  D_tt <- gdist(tr, tr); D_te <- gdist(te, tr)
  kn <- knn_predict(D_tt, D_te, y_tr, K_NN_GRID); nw <- nw_predict(D_tt, D_te, y_tr, H_GRID); gb <- gblup_fit(tr, te, y_tr)
  out <- data.frame(seed = seed_i, baseline = mean((y_te - ym)^2), class_only = mean((y_te - X1[te, ] %*% beta)^2),
                    GBLUP = mean((y_te - gb$pred)^2), QK_LCA = qk_l$mspe, w_LCA = qk_l$w, QK_PC = qk_p$mspe, w_PC = qk_p$w,
                    kNN = mean((y_te - kn$pred)^2), k_sel = kn$k, NW = mean((y_te - nw$pred)^2), h_sel = nw$h)
  for (k in K_WITHIN) {
    g_te <- hard_k[[as.character(k)]][te]; wg <- within_cor(y_te, gb$pred, g_te); wk <- within_cor(y_te, kn$pred, g_te)
    out[[paste0("wcG_", k)]] <- unname(wg["r"]); out[[paste0("wcK_", k)]] <- unname(wk["r"]); out[[paste0("wfrac_", k)]] <- unname(wg["frac"])
  }
  out
}
struct <- run_seeds("struct", run_rep_struct)
```

```{r struct-plots, fig.height = 5.5}

class_only_sweep <- function(Rk) {                       # class-only predictor for any LCA fit, over the same splits
  mean(sapply(seq_len(N_REPS), function(s) {
    sp <- make_split(s); X <- cbind(1, Rk[, -ncol(Rk), drop = FALSE])
    b <- solve(crossprod(X[sp$tr, ]) + 1e-6 * diag(ncol(X)), crossprod(X[sp$tr, ], y_all[sp$tr]))
    mean((y_all[sp$te] - X[sp$te, ] %*% b)^2)
  }))
}
sweep_k <- data.frame(K = as.integer(names(fits)), class_only = sapply(fits, function(f) class_only_sweep(f$R)))
```


Relatedness and ancestry explain a large share of the predictable signal, but GBLUP predicts *within* lineages too, so
comparisons between SNP-level methods are comparisons on genuine genome-wide signal. Part of that within-lineage
signal is fine-scale relatedness (the nearest-relatives predictor also has within-class skill); since GBLUP is itself a
kernel smoother, fine-scale relatedness and additive SNP effects cannot be separated further with these data.
Two further structure-based ideas (a fixed-gating mixture of experts and a shared-plus-class-interaction kernel) were
tried during development and gave no gain (the mixture of experts was clearly worse and unstable); they are not
reproduced here.

# 8. A second trait (FT16)

```{r trait-fn}
run_rep_trait <- function(seed_i, y_full, pool, run_tarp = TRUE) {
  sp <- make_split(seed_i, pool); tr <- sp$tr; te <- sp$te
  y_tr <- y_full[tr]; y_te <- y_full[te]; ym <- mean(y_tr); y_c <- y_tr - ym; y_new_c <- y_te - ym
  base <- mean((y_te - ym)^2)
  sc <- screen_set(tr, y_tr); Ks_all <- screened_gram(sc$inc)
  g <- kernel_all(Kfull[tr, tr], Kfull[te, tr], y_c, y_new_c, LAM_GRID); GBLUP <- g$test[which.min(g$loo)]
  set.seed(seed_i * 1000 + 7)
  fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(K_IN), length.out = length(tr)))
  cvw <- array(0, c(K_IN, length(W_GRID), length(LAM_GRID))); cvs <- matrix(0, K_IN, length(LAM_GRID))
  for (f in seq_len(K_IN)) {
    in_tr <- tr[fold != f]; in_va <- tr[fold == f]; y_in <- y_full[in_tr]; ymf <- mean(y_in); yv <- y_full[in_va] - ymf
    Ks_f <- screened_gram(screen_set(in_tr, y_in)$inc)
    for (iw in seq_along(W_GRID)) {
      wv <- W_GRID[iw]
      cvw[f, iw, ] <- mse_curve(kernel_curve(Kfull[in_tr, in_tr] + wv * Ks_f[in_tr, in_tr], Kfull[in_va, in_tr] + wv * Ks_f[in_va, in_tr],
                                              y_in - ymf, LAM_GRID), yv)
    }
    cvs[f, ] <- mse_curve(kernel_curve(Ks_f[in_tr, in_tr], Ks_f[in_va, in_tr], y_in - ymf, LAM_GRID), yv)
  }
  cvm <- apply(cvw, c(2, 3), mean); ib <- arrayInd(which.min(cvm), dim(cvm)); iw_s <- ib[1, 1]; il_s <- ib[1, 2]
  ils <- which.min(colMeans(cvs)); w_s <- W_GRID[iw_s]
  TGB <- mse_curve(kernel_curve(Kfull[tr, tr] + w_s * Ks_all[tr, tr], Kfull[te, tr] + w_s * Ks_all[te, tr], y_c, LAM_GRID), y_new_c)[il_s]
  SCR <- mse_curve(kernel_curve(Ks_all[tr, tr], Ks_all[te, tr], y_c, LAM_GRID), y_new_c)[ils]
  AGG <- NA_real_
  if (run_tarp) {
    X <- std_cols(G2[, sc$inc], tr, te); set.seed(seed_i * 1000 + 17)
    AGG <- mean((y_te - agg_tarp_pred(X$tr, X$other, y_c, ym, p))^2)
  }
  data.frame(seed = seed_i, n_pool = length(pool), baseline = base, GBLUP = GBLUP, TGB = TGB, SCR = SCR, AGG = AGG, w_sel = w_s)
}
pool16 <- which(!is.na(y16)); cat("FT16: accessions with genotype and phenotype:", length(pool16), "\n")
t16 <- run_seeds("trait_FT16", function(s) run_rep_trait(s, y16, pool16), legacy = "trait_FT16_results.rds")
traits <- list(FT10 = NULL, FT16 = t16)
if (!is.null(THIRD_TRAIT$file)) {                        # optional third trait: set THIRD_TRAIT in the parameters chunk
  d3 <- read.csv(THIRD_TRAIT$file)
  y3 <- as.numeric(d3[[THIRD_TRAIT$y_col]][match(as.character(fam$sample.ID), as.character(d3[[THIRD_TRAIT$id_col]]))])
  pool3 <- which(!is.na(y3)); cat(THIRD_TRAIT$name, ": accessions with genotype and phenotype:", length(pool3), "\n")
  stopifnot(length(pool3) >= 200)
  traits[[THIRD_TRAIT$name]] <- run_seeds(paste0("trait_", gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]", "_", THIRD_TRAIT$name)),
                                          function(s) run_rep_trait(s, y3, pool3))
}
ii <- match(e3$seed,si$seed)
traits$FT10 <- data.frame(
  seed=e3$seed,baseline=si$baseline[ii],
  GBLUP=e3$GBLUP_nested,TGB=e3$TwoK_honest,
  AGG=si$RP_agg[ii]
)
```

```{r trait-plots, fig.height = 5}
tr_rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(traits), function(nm) {
  df <- traits[[nm]]; ms <- c("GBLUP","TGB","AGG")
  data.frame(Trait = nm, Method = ms, Mean_MSPE = sapply(ms, function(m) mean(df[[m]], na.rm = TRUE)),
             R2 = sapply(ms, function(m) mean(1 - df[[m]] / df$baseline, na.rm = TRUE)),
             Diff_vs_GBLUP = sapply(ms, function(m) mean(df[[m]] - df$GBLUP, na.rm = TRUE)),
             SE = sapply(ms, function(m) sem((df[[m]] - df$GBLUP)[!is.na(df[[m]])])),
             Beats_GBLUP = sapply(ms, function(m) sum(df[[m]] < df$GBLUP, na.rm = TRUE)),
             Pct_of_GBLUP_MSPE = sapply(ms, function(m) 100 * mean(df[[m]] - df$GBLUP, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(df$GBLUP)))
}))
rownames(tr_rows) <- NULL
knitr::kable(tr_rows, digits=3, caption="GBLUP = full-SNP GBLUP; TGB = targeted GBLUP; AGG = aggregated TARP. Last column: percentage difference from GBLUP MSPE.")
par(mfrow = c(1, length(traits)))
for (nm in names(traits)) {
  df <- traits[[nm]]; d <- sapply(c("TGB","AGG"), function(m) 100 * (df[[m]]-df$GBLUP)/df$GBLUP)
  boxplot(d, col = "steelblue", ylab = "% difference in MSPE vs GBLUP", main = nm); abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

FT16 is the same accessions at another temperature and is strongly correlated with FT10, so agreement between the two
shows the result is not an artifact of the 10 degree measurement, not that it holds for traits with a different
genetic architecture. The key test of **when screening helps** is a trait dominated by a few large-effect loci
(for example a DOG1-related germination trait, available from the Dryad repository of Martinez-Berdeja et al. 2020 and
AraPheno): download it, convert to CSV, set `THIRD_TRAIT <- list(file = "...csv", id_col = "...", y_col = "...", name = "DOG1 germination")`
in the parameters chunk and re-render. The chunk above then runs the same four methods on it and adds it to the table.
If screening is going to beat a dense kernel anywhere, it should be there.


# 9. Prediction power:

## 9.1 Every method on one scale (FT10)


```{r synthesis-data, fig.height=7.5}
named <- function(df, col) {
  if (is.null(df) || !col %in% names(df)) return(NULL)
  setNames(as.numeric(df[[col]]), as.character(df$seed))
}

cands <- list(
  "Nearest-relatives smoother (kNN)" = named(struct, "kNN"),
  "Nadaraya-Watson smoother" = named(struct, "NW"),
  "LCA class memberships (K=8)" = named(struct, "class_only"),
  "TARP, single random projection" = named(si, "RP_single"),
  "SIS d=120 + Lasso" = named(sis_res, "SIS_d1_lasso"),
  "SIS d=2000 + Lasso" = named(sis_res, "SIS_2000_lasso"),
  "SIS d=2000 + Ridge" = named(sis_res, "SIS_2000_ridge"),
  "ISIS d=2000 + Lasso" = named(sis_res, "ISIS_2000_lasso"),
  "Structure-adjusted SIS + Lasso" = named(sis_res, "SISadj_2000_lasso_pc"),
  "PCA on RIS-screened SNPs" = named(si, "PCA"),
  "TARP, aggregated (100 draws)" = named(si, "RP_agg"),
  "Randomized SVD (q=2)" = named(si, "SI_q2"),

  "GBLUP (all SNPs)" = named(e3, "GBLUP_nested")
)

if (length(missing_methods))
  warning("Unavailable synthesis results: ", paste(missing_methods, collapse=", "))

cands <- lapply(cands, function(v) v[is.finite(v)])
cands <- cands[lengths(cands) > 0]

gb_name <- "GBLUP (all SNPs)"
stopifnot(gb_name %in% names(cands))

base_s <- named(si, "baseline")
if (is.null(base_s)) stop("si$baseline is unavailable.")
common <- Reduce(intersect, c(list(names(base_s)), lapply(cands, names)))

  warning("Only ", length(common), " common splits are available.")

gbn <- cands[[gb_name]]

r2s <- lapply(cands, function(v) 1-v/base_s)

o <- order(mu)

method_names <- names(mu)[o]
bar_cols <- ifelse(method_names == gb_name, "steelblue",
  ifelse(method_names == "Targeted GBLUP", "mediumpurple",
  ifelse(grepl("SIS|ISIS", method_names), "darkorange",
  ifelse(grepl("TARP|PCA|Randomized SVD", method_names), "darkgreen", "grey70"))))

par(mar=c(4,19,3,1))
bp <- barplot(mu[o], horiz=TRUE, las=1, cex.names=0.75,
  col=bar_cols, border=NA,
  xlim=range(c(0,mu-2*se,mu+2*se)),
  xlab="Test R-squared (mean over matched splits; bars = +/- 2 SE)",
  main="Predictive performance by method: FT10")
arrows(mu[o]-2*se[o], bp, mu[o]+2*se[o], bp,
       angle=90, code=3, length=0.03)
abline(v=0, lty=2)
legend("bottomright",
  c("GBLUP","Targeted GBLUP","SIS family","TARP and projections","Relatedness only"),
  fill=c("steelblue","mediumpurple","darkorange","darkgreen","grey70"),
  bty="n", cex=0.75)

names(dd) <- ms

tab_all <- data.frame(
  Method=names(mu),
  R2=unname(mu),
  R2_SE=unname(se),
  Mean_MSPE=vapply(cands, mean, numeric(1)),
  Diff_vs_GBLUP=vapply(names(mu), function(m)
    if (m == gb_name) 0 else mean(dd[[m]]), numeric(1)),

knitr::kable(tab_all, digits=3, row.names=FALSE,
```

The ten splits reuse the same accessions, so these standard errors describe split-to-split variation only and are
optimistic; read the ordering and the size of the gaps, not the nominal significance.

## 9.2 Key findings (computed from the results above)


```{r key-findings, results='asis'}
R2 <- function(v) mean(1-v/base_s[names(v)])
rp <- named(si,"RP_single")[common]
agg <- named(si,"RP_agg")[common]
pca <- named(si,"PCA")[common]
dga <- agg-gbn
sis_r2 <- r2s[grepl("SIS",names(r2s))]
best_sis <- names(sis_r2)[which.max(vapply(sis_r2,mean,numeric(1)))]
cat(sprintf("1. **TARP.** Single projection MSPE %.2f; aggregated TARP %.2f; PCA %.2f. Aggregated TARP minus PCA: %.2f (SE %.2f).\n",
            mean(rp),mean(agg),mean(pca),mean(agg-pca),sem(agg-pca)))
cat(sprintf("2. **GBLUP.** Full-SNP GBLUP R-squared %.3f versus %.3f for aggregated TARP; GBLUP has lower MSPE in %d of %d splits.\n",
            R2(gbn),R2(agg),sum(dga>0),length(dga)))
cat(sprintf("3. **SIS methods.** Best screened method: %s (R-squared %.3f); SIS with d=120 gives %.3f; structure-adjusted SIS gives %.3f.\n",
            best_sis,mean(sis_r2[[best_sis]]),R2(named(sis_res,"SIS_d1_lasso")[common]),
            R2(named(sis_res,"SISadj_2000_lasso_pc")[common])))
cat(sprintf("4. **Population structure.** Test R-squared: nearest-relatives smoother %.3f; LCA class memberships %.3f; GBLUP %.3f. GBLUP within-class correlation at K=8 is %.3f.\n",
            R2(named(struct,"kNN")[common]),R2(named(struct,"class_only")[common]),
            R2(gbn),wtab$GBLUP_r[wtab$K==8]))
dt <- cands[["Targeted GBLUP"]]-gbn
cat(sprintf("5. **Targeted GBLUP.** Mean MSPE difference from ordinary GBLUP: %.2f (SE %.2f); better in %d of %d splits.\n",
            mean(dt),sem(dt),sum(dt<0),length(dt)))
f16 <- tr_rows[tr_rows$Trait=="FT16",]
cat(sprintf("6. **FT16 replication.** Targeted GBLUP differs from GBLUP by %+.1f%% MSPE; aggregated TARP differs by %+.1f%%.\n",
            f16$Pct_of_GBLUP_MSPE[f16$Method=="TGB"],
            f16$Pct_of_GBLUP_MSPE[f16$Method=="AGG"]))
```
#### Key Findings and Overall Conclusions

The comparative evaluation highlights several interesting differences in the predictive performance of the considered methods.

Full-SNP GBLUP emerged as a strong predictive benchmark, achieving a mean test MSPE of approximately 107.2. Among the screening-based approaches, RIS followed by Ridge regression performed best, with a mean MSPE of approximately 113.0. Although screening followed by penalized regression provided competitive predictions, the results suggest that reducing the genomic marker set can lead to some loss of predictive information. In particular, increasing the screening budget substantially improved the performance of SIS followed by Lasso, illustrating the importance of retaining a sufficiently large candidate marker set.

For dimensionality reduction, aggregated TARP achieved a mean MSPE of 117.5, closely matching the performance of PCA (118.3). The paired difference was small relative to its standard error, suggesting comparable predictive performance across the evaluated splits. In contrast, using a single random projection resulted in substantially poorer predictions, highlighting the importance of aggregation when employing randomized projections.

Targeted GBLUP provided a small average improvement over ordinary GBLUP, with a reduction in MSPE of approximately 0.57 and better performance in seven out of ten splits. However, the improvement was modest relative to its split-to-split variability, and therefore does not establish a clear predictive advantage.

Overall, the results indicate that different computational strategies can provide competitive alternatives to conventional genomic prediction, but their effectiveness depends on how genomic information is screened, compressed and incorporated into the prediction model. Aggregated random projections offer an interesting computational alternative to PCA, while screening-based methods can reduce dimensionality at the cost of some predictive accuracy. Full-SNP GBLUP remains a particularly strong benchmark for FT10 prediction in the present analysis.



# 6. Theoretical foundations: Genomic Best Linear Unbiased Prediction (GBLUP)

## 6.1 Motivation: from individual SNP effects to genomic relationships

The preceding sections considered approaches that screen SNPs and construct lower-dimensional representations before performing regression.

An alternative is to avoid explicit variable selection and retain information from the entire genome.

Genomic Best Linear Unbiased Prediction (GBLUP) is a standard approach to genomic prediction that models the genetic effects of individuals through a genomic relationship matrix.

The central idea is that genetically similar accessions are expected to have more similar genetic values than genetically dissimilar accessions.

Let

\[
X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}
\]

denote the genotype matrix, where rows correspond to accessions and columns correspond to SNPs.

Rather than estimating a separate unrestricted fixed coefficient for every SNP, GBLUP introduces an individual-level genetic effect

\[
g=(g_1,\ldots,g_n)^\top.
\]

The phenotype model is

\[
\boxed{
y=\mathbf 1\mu+g+\varepsilon,
}
\]

where

- \(\mu\) is the overall population mean;
- \(g\) represents the additive genomic values of the accessions;
- \(\varepsilon\) represents residual environmental and unexplained variation.

The genomic effects are assigned the covariance structure

\[
\boxed{
g\sim N(0,\sigma_g^2K),
}
\]

where \(K\) is the genomic relationship matrix.

The residual errors satisfy

\[
\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma_e^2I_n),
\]

with \(g\) and \(\varepsilon\) assumed independent.

Consequently,

\[
\boxed{
y\sim N\left(
\mathbf 1\mu,
\sigma_g^2K+\sigma_e^2I_n
\right).
}
\]

The covariance between the phenotypes of accessions \(i\) and \(j\) is therefore

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(y_i,y_j)
=
\sigma_g^2K_{ij}
+
\sigma_e^2\mathbb I(i=j).
\]

This is the fundamental modelling assumption behind GBLUP: genomic similarity determines the covariance structure of genetic effects.

## 6.2 Constructing the genomic relationship matrix

The genomic relationship matrix is constructed from standardized SNP genotypes.

For SNP \(j\), let

\[
\bar x_j=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{ij}
\]

and let \(s_j\) denote its sample standard deviation.

The standardized genotype is

\[
Z_{ij}=
\frac{x_{ij}-\bar x_j}{s_j}.
\]

Writing the standardized genotype matrix as

\[
Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_*},
\]

where \(p_*\) denotes the number of nonconstant SNPs, the relationship matrix is defined as

\[
\boxed{
K=\frac{1}{p_*}ZZ^\top.
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
K_{ik}
=
\frac{1}{p_*}
\sum_{j=1}^{p_*}Z_{ij}Z_{kj}.
\]

Thus, \(K_{ik}\) measures the average standardized genotype similarity between accessions \(i\) and \(k\).

The diagonal elements measure each accession's standardized genomic similarity with itself, while the off-diagonal elements describe pairwise genomic similarity.

The matrix has dimension

\[
K\in\mathbb R^{n\times n},
\]

not \(p_*\times p_*\).

This distinction is crucial. The genomic relationship matrix describes relationships between accessions, whereas the SNP correlation matrix describes relationships between genetic markers.

Because

\[
K=\frac{1}{p_*}ZZ^\top,
\]

it is symmetric and positive semidefinite:

\[
a^\top Ka
=
\frac{1}{p_*}\|Z^\top a\|_2^2
\geq 0
\]

for every \(a\in\mathbb R^n\).

It can therefore be used as a valid covariance kernel.

### Construction in our study

Our implementation constructs \(K\) using blocks of 20,000 SNPs to avoid loading the entire standardized genotype matrix into memory at once.

For each block, SNP columns are centered and scaled, and their contribution to the relationship matrix is accumulated:

\[
ZZ^\top
=
\sum_{j=1}^{p_*}z_jz_j^\top.
\]

The final matrix is divided by the number of nonconstant SNPs:

\[
K_{\mathrm{full}}
=
\frac{1}{p_*}
\sum_{j=1}^{p_*}z_jz_j^\top.
\]

The blockwise calculation is mathematically identical to constructing the complete standardized genotype matrix and computing \(ZZ^\top/p_*\), but it is more memory-efficient.

The implementation uses all nonconstant SNPs, rather than selecting markers according to their association with FT10.

## 6.3 GBLUP as a linear mixed model

The model can be written as

\[
y=\mathbf 1\mu+g+\varepsilon,
\]

with

\[
g\sim N(0,\sigma_g^2K),
\qquad
\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma_e^2I).
\]

This is a linear mixed model because the overall mean is treated as a fixed effect, whereas the genomic effects are random effects.

The covariance matrix of the phenotype is

\[
V=\sigma_g^2K+\sigma_e^2I.
\]

For known variance components, the generalized least-squares estimator of the overall mean is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\mu=
\frac{\mathbf 1^\top V^{-1}y}
{\mathbf 1^\top V^{-1}\mathbf 1}.
}
\]

The BLUP of the genomic effects is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat g
=
\sigma_g^2K V^{-1}
(y-\mathbf 1\widehat\mu).
}
\]

This is the best linear unbiased predictor under the specified Gaussian mixed model and known covariance parameters.

For a test accession, let \(K_{\mathrm{te,tr}}\) denote its genomic relationships with the training accessions.

The predicted genomic value is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat g_{\mathrm{te}}
=
\sigma_g^2K_{\mathrm{te,tr}}
V_{\mathrm{tr}}^{-1}
(y_{\mathrm{tr}}-\mathbf 1\widehat\mu).
}
\]

The corresponding phenotype prediction is

\[
\widehat y_{\mathrm{te}}
=
\widehat\mu\mathbf 1+
\widehat g_{\mathrm{te}}.
\]

The prediction therefore uses the genetic relationships between test and training accessions.

An important consequence is that a test accession can receive a prediction even though its phenotype is completely unobserved, provided its genomic relationships with the training accessions can be calculated.

## 6.4 Connection between GBLUP and kernel ridge regression

The mixed-model formulation has a particularly useful computational interpretation.

Define

\[
\lambda=\frac{\sigma_e^2}{\sigma_g^2}.
\]

After dividing the covariance matrix by \(\sigma_g^2\),

\[
V=\sigma_g^2(K+\lambda I).
\]

For a centered response vector

\[
y_c=y_{\mathrm{tr}}-\bar y_{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf 1,
\]

the genomic prediction can be written in the kernel form

\[
\boxed{
\widehat g_{\mathrm{te}}
=
K_{\mathrm{te,tr}}
(K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}+\lambda I)^{-1}y_c.
}
\]

This is precisely the prediction equation for kernel ridge regression using the genomic relationship matrix as its kernel.

The parameter \(\lambda\) controls the amount of regularization.

- Small \(\lambda\) allows the model to follow the training phenotypes more closely.
- Large \(\lambda\) produces stronger shrinkage towards the population mean.
- Intermediate values balance the fit to the observed data against regularization.

Thus, GBLUP can be understood both as a Gaussian linear mixed model and as kernel ridge regression.

The two formulations produce the same prediction equation when the kernel and variance ratio are defined consistently.

## 6.5 Dual representation and why GBLUP is computationally attractive

A conventional SNP-effect model can be written as

\[
y_c=Z\beta+\varepsilon.
\]

Suppose the marker effects have prior distribution

\[
\beta\sim N(0,\tau^2I).
\]

Then the induced covariance of the genetic values is

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(Z\beta)
=
\tau^2ZZ^\top.
\]

This shows why the genomic relationship matrix appears naturally: it is the covariance induced among individuals by random SNP effects.

The marker-space and individual-space formulations are related through the identity

\[
Z(Z^\top Z+\lambda I_p)^{-1}Z^\top
=
ZZ^\top(ZZ^\top+\lambda I_n)^{-1}.
\]

This is an instance of the primal-dual equivalence used in ridge regression and kernel methods.

The important computational consequence is that, when \(p\gg n\), it is often preferable to work with an \(n\times n\) relationship matrix rather than solve a system involving all \(p\) SNP effects.

In our study, there are approximately 1,003 accessions and 1.7 million SNPs. The relationship matrix is therefore only about \(1,003\times1,003\), despite being constructed using the entire genome.

## 6.6 Fitting GBLUP in our implementation

We construct the full genomic relationship matrix once and extract the appropriate training and test blocks:

\[
K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}
\]

and

\[
K_{\mathrm{te,tr}}.
\]

For a given value of \(\lambda\), the training prediction coefficients are

\[
\alpha_\lambda
=
(K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}+\lambda I)^{-1}y_c.
\]

The test predictions are

\[
\boxed{
\widehat y_{\mathrm{te}}(\lambda)
=
\bar y_{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf 1+
K_{\mathrm{te,tr}}\alpha_\lambda.
}
\]

In our implementation, we do not explicitly invert the matrix for every candidate value of \(\lambda\).

Instead, we use the eigendecomposition

\[
K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}=U\Lambda U^\top,
\]

where

\[
\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_{n_{\mathrm{tr}}})
\]

and \(U\) is orthogonal.

Then

\[
(K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}+\lambda I)^{-1}
=
U(\Lambda+\lambda I)^{-1}U^\top.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\widehat y_{\mathrm{te}}(\lambda)
=
\bar y_{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf 1+
K_{\mathrm{te,tr}}
U
(\Lambda+\lambda I)^{-1}
U^\top y_c.
}
\]

One eigendecomposition can consequently be reused for every candidate regularization parameter.

### Selection of the regularization parameter

We consider a grid of candidate values,

\[
\lambda\in
\left\{10^{-3},10^{-3+0.1},\ldots,10^3\right\}.
\]

The regularization parameter is selected using leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) within the training data.

For a fixed \(\lambda\), define the kernel smoother

\[
H_\lambda
=
K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}
(K_{\mathrm{tr,tr}}+\lambda I)^{-1}.
\]

The fitted training response is

\[
\widehat y=H_\lambda y_c.
\]

The leave-one-out residual for observation \(i\) can be calculated without refitting the model \(n_{\mathrm{tr}}\) times:

\[
\boxed{
e_{i,-i}(\lambda)
=
\frac{y_{c,i}-\widehat y_i}
{1-(H_\lambda)_{ii}}.
}
\]

Hence,

\[
\operatorname{CV}(\lambda)
=
\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{tr}}}
\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{tr}}}
\left[
\frac{y_{c,i}-\widehat y_i}
{1-(H_\lambda)_{ii}}
\right]^2.
\]

We choose

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\lambda
=
\arg\min_{\lambda\in\mathcal L}
\operatorname{CV}(\lambda),
}
\]

where \(\mathcal L\) denotes the candidate grid.

The final test prediction is then calculated using the selected value of \(\widehat\lambda\).

In our R implementation, `kernel_all()` performs the eigendecomposition-based calculations and evaluates LOOCV for the candidate values of \(\lambda\). The function `gblup_fit()` selects the minimum-LOOCV value and returns the resulting test predictions.

This implementation uses a fixed grid and LOOCV selection of the regularization parameter; it does not estimate variance components by REML.

## 6.7 Targeted GBLUP: incorporating screened information

Although GBLUP uses the entire genome, a potential limitation is that a small number of strongly associated SNPs may receive relatively little individual emphasis when their information is distributed across a very large number of markers.

To investigate whether screening can improve the dense genomic predictor, we construct a second kernel using the RIS-selected SNPs.

Let \(Z_{\mathcal S}\) denote the standardized genotype matrix containing the selected SNPs. The screened relationship kernel is

\[
\boxed{
K_{\mathrm{screened}}
=
\frac{1}{p_\gamma}
Z_{\mathcal S}Z_{\mathcal S}^\top.
}
\]

We then define a combined kernel:

\[
\boxed{
K_w
=
K_{\mathrm{full}}+
wK_{\mathrm{screened}},
}
\]

where \(w\geq0\) controls the additional contribution of the screened SNP set.

This construction has several useful properties.

When

\[
w=0,
\]

we recover ordinary full-genome GBLUP:

\[
K_w=K_{\mathrm{full}}.
\]

For positive \(w\), the screened SNPs contribute an additional covariance component.

The combined model is

\[
y=\mathbf 1\mu+g_{\mathrm{full}}+
g_{\mathrm{screened}}+\varepsilon,
\]

where

\[
g_{\mathrm{full}}\sim
N(0,\sigma_g^2K_{\mathrm{full}})
\]

and

\[
g_{\mathrm{screened}}\sim
N(0,\sigma_g^2wK_{\mathrm{screened}}).
\]

Assuming independence between the two random components,

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(g_{\mathrm{full}}+
g_{\mathrm{screened}})
=
\sigma_g^2
(K_{\mathrm{full}}+
wK_{\mathrm{screened}}).
\]

Thus, targeted GBLUP does not discard the genome-wide relationship structure. It adds an extra covariance component based on the screened markers.

### Interpretation of the screening weight

Because the full kernel averages over approximately \(p_*\) standardized SNPs, whereas the screened kernel averages over only \(p_\gamma\) SNPs, the additional contribution can be substantial even for moderate values of \(w\).

For a selected SNP, its coefficient in the combined covariance is approximately

\[
\frac{1}{p_*}+\frac{w}{p_\gamma},
\]

compared with

\[
\frac{1}{p_*}
\]

for a SNP that is not in the screened set.

The relative increase in the coefficient of a selected SNP is therefore

\[
\boxed{
1+w\frac{p_*}{p_\gamma}.
}
\]

This illustrates why \(w\) should be tuned rather than chosen arbitrarily.

## 6.8 Nested cross-validation for targeted GBLUP

The combined model has two tuning parameters:

\[
(w,\lambda).
\]

The parameter \(w\) controls the contribution of the screened kernel, while \(\lambda\) controls regularization.

We select these parameters using inner cross-validation within each outer training set.

For each inner fold:

1. Divide the outer training observations into inner training and validation sets.
2. Recalculate RIS screening using only the inner training observations.
3. Construct the screened kernel from that newly selected SNP set.
4. Combine it with the corresponding full genomic kernel.
5. Evaluate predictions across candidate values of \(w\) and \(\lambda\).
6. Select the parameter combination with the lowest average inner-validation MSPE.

The selected parameters are then used to evaluate the untouched outer test set.

This re-screening step is essential because RIS uses the phenotype. Using a screened SNP set calculated from the complete outer training data inside the inner validation folds would allow the inner validation phenotypes to influence feature selection.

The outer test observations remain completely separate from screening and tuning.

## 6.9 Computational interpretation

The full genomic kernel is constructed using all nonconstant SNPs. The main computational operations are:

- Constructing the genomic relationship matrix.
- Extracting training and test kernel blocks.
- Performing an eigendecomposition of the training kernel.
- Evaluating the regularization grid.
- Computing test predictions.

The eigendecomposition is performed in individual space, with dimension determined by the number of training accessions rather than the number of SNPs.

For targeted GBLUP, the screened kernel must additionally be constructed and the screening procedure repeated within the inner folds.

The method therefore combines the computational advantages of kernel-based prediction with the possibility of giving additional emphasis to a phenotype-informed SNP set.

## 6.10 Summary of the modelling distinction

The central difference between ordinary GBLUP and targeted GBLUP is the covariance structure assigned to the genomic effects.

Ordinary GBLUP uses

\[
\boxed{
K=K_{\mathrm{full}}.
}
\]

Targeted GBLUP uses

\[
\boxed{
K=K_{\mathrm{full}}+wK_{\mathrm{screened}}.
}
\]

The former distributes genetic information across the complete genome, whereas the latter retains the complete genome-wide relationship structure while adding a second component based on RIS-selected SNPs.

The empirical comparison in the following section therefore addresses a specific question:

**Does emphasizing SNPs selected for their marginal association with FT10 improve prediction beyond the information already captured by the full genomic relationship matrix?**

This is evaluated using paired outer train-test splits and nested tuning of the targeted model.

```{r interactive-tradeoff, fig.width=14, fig.height=11}
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Prepare data
# -------------------------------------------------------

tradeoff_data <- sim_raw %>%
  filter(
    method != "Mean_only_baseline",
    is.finite(mspe),

    elapsed_seconds > 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    method_label = recode(
      method,
      "TARP_RIS_RP_aggregated" = "Aggregated TARP",
      "SIS_top_d_plus_NIG" = "SIS + NIG",
      "Exact_Gram_PCA_plus_NIG" = "Exact Gram PCA + NIG",
      "GBLUP_fixed_lambda" = "GBLUP (fixed lambda)"
    )
  )

methods <- c(
  "TARP_RIS_RP_aggregated",
  "SIS_top_d_plus_NIG",
  "Exact_Gram_PCA_plus_NIG",
  "GBLUP_fixed_lambda"
)

method_names <- c(
  "TARP_RIS_RP_aggregated" = "Aggregated TARP",
  "SIS_top_d_plus_NIG" = "SIS + NIG",
  "Exact_Gram_PCA_plus_NIG" = "Exact Gram PCA + NIG",
  "GBLUP_fixed_lambda" = "GBLUP (fixed lambda)"
)

method_colours <- c(
  "TARP_RIS_RP_aggregated" = "#0072B2",
  "SIS_top_d_plus_NIG" = "#D55E00",
  "Exact_Gram_PCA_plus_NIG" = "#009E73",
  "GBLUP_fixed_lambda" = "#CC79A7"
)

rho_values <- sort(unique(tradeoff_data$rho_latent))

rho_symbols <- c(
  "circle",
  "triangle-up",
  "square",
  "diamond"
)

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Define the 12 panels
# -------------------------------------------------------

panel_design <- expand.grid(
  p = sort(unique(tradeoff_data$p)),
  n = sort(unique(tradeoff_data$n)),
  signal_layout = c("distributed", "clustered"),
  KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Arrange as four rows x three columns
panel_design <- panel_design %>%
  arrange(
    factor(signal_layout,
           levels = c("distributed", "clustered")),
    n,
    p
  )

panel_plots <- vector("list", nrow(panel_design))

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Build each interactive panel
# -------------------------------------------------------

for (i in seq_len(nrow(panel_design))) {

  spec <- panel_design[i, ]

  d <- tradeoff_data %>%
    filter(
      signal_layout == spec$signal_layout,
      n == spec$n,
      p == spec$p
    )

  pp <- plotly::plot_ly()

  for (m in methods) {

    for (j in seq_along(rho_values)) {

      rho_j <- rho_values[j]

      z <- d %>%
        filter(
          method == m,
          rho_latent == rho_j
        )

      if (nrow(z) == 0) next

      # Detailed hover text
      z$hover_text <- paste0(
        "<b>", method_names[[m]], "</b>",
        "<br>Runtime: ", signif(z$elapsed_seconds, 4), " seconds",
        "<br>Test MSPE: ", round(z$mspe, 4),
        "<br>Latent correlation: ", sprintf("%.2f", rho_j),
        "<br>Architecture: ", z$signal_layout,
        "<br>Sample size: ", z$n,
        "<br>SNP dimension: ", z$p,
        "<br>Replicate: ", z$replicate
      )

      # One trace for every method x dependence combination
      legend_name <- paste0(
        method_names[[m]],
        " | rho = ",
        sprintf("%.2f", rho_j)
      )

      group_name <- paste(m, rho_j, sep = "_")

      pp <- plotly::add_trace(
        pp,
        data = z,
        x = ~elapsed_seconds,
        y = ~mspe,
        type = "scatter",
        mode = "markers",
        name = legend_name,
        legendgroup = group_name,

        # Legend entries displayed only once, in panel 1
        showlegend = (i == 1),

        marker = list(
          color = unname(method_colours[m]),
          symbol = rho_symbols[j],
          size = 9,
          opacity = 0.85,
          line = list(
            color = "white",
            width = 0.5
          )
        ),

        text = ~hover_text,
        hoverinfo = "text"
      )
    }
  }

  panel_plots[[i]] <- pp
}

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Combine all panels into one interactive figure
# -------------------------------------------------------

p_tradeoff_plotly <- do.call(
  plotly::subplot,
  c(
    panel_plots,
    list(
      nrows = 4,
      shareX = TRUE,
      shareY = TRUE,
      titleX = TRUE,
      titleY = TRUE,
      margin = 0.035
    )
  )
)

# Panel titles

      ),

      xanchor = "center",
      yanchor = "top"
    )
  }
)

# Global layout and legend
p_tradeoff_plotly <- p_tradeoff_plotly %>%
  plotly::layout(
    title = list(
      text = paste0(

  )
```

## 10.2 Computational complexity: theoretical and empirical comparison

### Objective

This section examines whether the observed computational behaviour of the implemented prediction methods is consistent with their dominant theoretical operations. The benchmark varies the sample size, the number of SNPs, the within-block dependence parameter, and the arrangement of causal SNPs. Runtime is treated as an empirical measure of implementation cost; it is not itself a proof of an asymptotic rate.

The comparison focuses on five rows recorded by the simulation: aggregated TARP, SIS followed by NIG regression, exact Gram-matrix PCA followed by NIG regression, fixed-lambda GBLUP, and a mean-only prediction baseline. The mean-only baseline is retained for prediction-error context but excluded from method-runtime comparisons.

### Simulation design

#### Genotype generation

For each simulation case, an $n\times p$ biallelic genotype matrix is generated. SNPs are coded as 0 or 2, and each SNP has a minor-allele frequency drawn independently from $\operatorname{Uniform}(0.05,0.50)$. Markers are placed in consecutive blocks of 50 SNPs.

For individual $i$ and marker $j$ in block $b(j)$, a latent Gaussian variable is generated as

$$
Z_{ij}=\sqrt{\rho}\,U_{i,b(j)}+\sqrt{1-\rho}\,\varepsilon_{ij},
$$

where the block factor and marker-specific errors are independent standard normal variables. Genotypes are obtained by thresholding,

$$
X_{ij}=2\,I\{Z_{ij}>\Phi^{-1}(1-f_j)\},
$$

where $f_j$ is the marker-specific allele frequency. At $\rho=0$, markers are independent in the latent construction. Positive $\rho$ induces within-block latent dependence. Because thresholding produces binary genotypes, the observed Pearson correlation between genotype columns is not generally equal to the specified latent correlation.

#### Causal architectures and response

Twelve causal SNPs are selected. Under the **distributed** architecture, one causal SNP is selected from each of 12 different blocks. Under the **clustered** architecture, all 12 causal SNPs are selected from one block. The selected causal genotype columns are standardized, and their coefficients are assigned random signs with magnitude $1/\sqrt{12}$. The resulting genetic score is standardized to unit variance and independent $N(0,1)$ noise is added:

$$
Y_i=g_i+\varepsilon_i,\qquad \varepsilon_i\sim N(0,1).
$$

Thus the signal and noise variances are each one by construction, giving a target signal-to-total-variance ratio of $1/(1+1)=0.5$ (up to finite-sample variation in the generated noise).

#### Factors and replication

| Factor | Values |
|:--|:--|
| Sample size, $n$ | 200, 400 |
| SNP dimension, $p$ | 2,000; 10,000; 50,000 |
| Latent within-block correlation, $\rho$ | 0, 0.30, 0.60, 0.85 |
| Causal architecture | Distributed, clustered |
| Block size | 50 SNPs |
| Number of causal SNPs | 12 |
| Replicates per design point | 3 |
| Training/test split | 80% / 20% |
| TARP projections, $B$ | 100 |
| TARP sparsity parameter, $\psi$ | 0.25 |
| TARP PCA comparison dimension, $k$ | Up to 100 |
| SIS maximum selection parameter | 2,000, additionally capped at $\lfloor 3n_{\mathrm{train}}/4\rfloor$ |

The design contains $2\times3\times4\times2\times3=144$ cases. Each case produces five method-level rows, for 720 rows in the raw results file. For each case, the training rows are sampled once and shared across all methods. Marginal screening, standardization, projection construction and model fitting use training data; the test response is used only to calculate prediction error.

### Methods benchmarked

**Aggregated TARP.** The implementation first computes training-set marginal correlations. Its RIS exponent is

$$
\delta=\max\left\{0,\frac{1+\log(p/n_{\mathrm{train}})}{2}\right\},
$$

and the inclusion probability for marker $j$ is proportional to $|r_j|^\delta$, normalized by the largest such score. The selected predictors are standardized using training-set means and standard deviations. Each projection matrix has independent entries with probabilities $\psi$, $\psi$, and $1-2\psi$ at $+1/\sqrt{2\psi}$, $-1/\sqrt{2\psi}$, and zero, respectively. The implementation uses $\psi=0.25$ and averages predictions from $B=100$ projections. For projection $b$, its dimension is sampled from the interval $[2\log(p),3n_{\mathrm{train}}/4]$.

For a projected training matrix $Z$, the implemented NIG posterior mean is

$$
\widehat\theta=(I+Z^\top Z)^{-1}Z^\top(Y_{\mathrm{train}}-\bar Y_{\mathrm{train}}).
$$

Predictions from the 100 projection-specific fits are averaged.

**SIS + NIG.** Markers are ranked by absolute training marginal correlation. The retained dimension is

$$
d=\min\left\{2000,\left\lfloor\frac{3n_{\mathrm{train}}}{4}\right\rfloor,p\right\}.
$$

With the present 80/20 split, this gives $d=120$ for $n=200$ and $d=240$ for $n=400$. The same NIG posterior-mean regression is fitted to the selected and standardized markers.

**Exact Gram PCA + NIG.** PCA is obtained from the training Gram matrix $G=X_{\mathrm{train}}X_{\mathrm{train}}^\top$, an $n_{\mathrm{train}}\times n_{\mathrm{train}}$ matrix. Up to 100 positive components are retained, subject to the available rank. The corresponding training and test scores are then used in the NIG regression.

**GBLUP (fixed $\lambda$).** The training relationship matrix is $K_{\mathrm{train}}=X_{\mathrm{train}}X_{\mathrm{train}}^\top/p$, with the analogous train-test kernel. Kernel ridge predictions are calculated using the fixed value $\lambda=1$. This is a computational reference, not a tuned GBLUP comparison.

**Mean-only baseline.** The training-response mean is used for every test prediction. Its recorded elapsed time is zero by construction, so it is not included in logarithmic runtime plots or pooled runtime summaries.

### Theoretical operation counts

Let $n_{\mathrm{tr}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{te}}$ be the training and test sample sizes, $p$ the full number of markers, $p_\gamma$ the number retained by RIS, $m_b$ the dimension of projection $b$, $B$ the number of projections, $d$ the number retained by SIS, and $k$ the number of retained PCs. The expressions below describe dominant dense linear-algebra operations; constants, memory movement, sparse-matrix effects and implementation overhead are omitted.

#### RIS and aggregated TARP

Computing marginal correlations over all $p$ markers costs $O(n_{\mathrm{tr}}p)$. For projection $b$, multiplying the selected train and test matrices by the projection matrix costs

$$
O\{(n_{\mathrm{tr}}+n_{\mathrm{te}})p_\gamma m_b\}.
$$

The posterior-mean calculation involves forming $Z^\top Z$ and solving an $m_b\times m_b$ linear system, costing $O(n_{\mathrm{tr}}m_b^2+m_b^3)$. Prediction in the compressed space costs $O(n_{\mathrm{te}}m_b)$. Therefore a useful implementation-level expression is

$$
O\left[n_{\mathrm{tr}}p+\sum_{b=1}^{B}\left\{(n_{\mathrm{tr}}+n_{\mathrm{te}})p_\gamma m_b+n_{\mathrm{tr}}m_b^2+m_b^3+n_{\mathrm{te}}m_b\right\}\right].
$$

When $n_{\mathrm{te}}\leq n_{\mathrm{tr}}$ and $m_b<n_{\mathrm{tr}}$, the dominant terms can be summarized approximately as

$$
O\left(n_{\mathrm{tr}}p+B n_{\mathrm{tr}}p_\gamma\bar m+B n_{\mathrm{tr}}\bar m^2\right),
$$

where $\bar m$ is a representative projection dimension. This has the same structure as the RIS-RP complexity given by Mukhopadhyay and Dunson (2019): the screening step is done once, while projection and Bayesian fitting are repeated across the aggregate.

#### SIS + NIG

Computing marginal scores costs $O(n_{\mathrm{tr}}p)$ and sorting the $p$ scores costs $O(p\log p)$. Standardizing the selected matrix costs $O(n_{\mathrm{tr}}d)$; the NIG fit costs $O(n_{\mathrm{tr}}d^2+d^3)$; and test prediction costs $O(n_{\mathrm{te}}d)$. Thus,

$$
O\left(n_{\mathrm{tr}}p+p\log p+n_{\mathrm{tr}}d^2+d^3+n_{\mathrm{te}}d\right).
$$

#### Exact Gram PCA + NIG

Forming the training Gram matrix costs $O(n_{\mathrm{tr}}^2p)$, and its full eigendecomposition costs $O(n_{\mathrm{tr}}^3)$. Recovering $k$ right singular directions and projecting test observations cost approximately $O\{p(n_{\mathrm{tr}}+n_{\mathrm{te}})k\}$. The NIG fit adds $O(n_{\mathrm{tr}}k^2+k^3)$, giving

$$
O\left(n_{\mathrm{tr}}^2p+n_{\mathrm{tr}}^3+p(n_{\mathrm{tr}}+n_{\mathrm{te}})k+n_{\mathrm{tr}}k^2+k^3\right).
$$

#### GBLUP

Constructing the training and test kernels costs $O(n_{\mathrm{tr}}^2p+n_{\mathrm{te}}n_{\mathrm{tr}}p)$. Solving the regularized training system costs $O(n_{\mathrm{tr}}^3)$, followed by a test-kernel multiplication. The dominant terms are

$$
O\left((n_{\mathrm{tr}}^2+n_{\mathrm{te}}n_{\mathrm{tr}})p+n_{\mathrm{tr}}^3\right).
$$

### Theoretical versus empirical comparison

The table below is deliberately qualitative. It asks whether the observed runtime pattern is in the direction expected from the dominant operations; it does not claim that the finite grid establishes an asymptotic exponent.

| Method / operation | Dominant theoretical dependence | Empirical pattern in this benchmark | Assessment |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| RIS screening | $n_{\mathrm{train}}p$ | Screening-based methods become more costly as the SNP dimension increases. | Qualitatively consistent |
| Aggregated TARP | $n_{\mathrm{train}}p+B n_{\mathrm{train}}p_\gamma\bar m+B n_{\mathrm{train}}\bar m^2$ | Runtime includes one screening stage and repeated projection/fitting stages; it is slower than SIS in the pooled summaries. | Qualitatively consistent |
| SIS + NIG | $n_{\mathrm{train}}p+p\log p+n_{\mathrm{train}}d^2+d^3$ | Lowest pooled median runtime; selected dimension is capped at 120 or 240 in this design. | Qualitatively consistent |
| Exact Gram PCA + NIG | $n_{\mathrm{train}}^2p+n_{\mathrm{train}}^3$ (plus score construction and fit) | Runtime rises with SNP dimension and is relatively costly at larger sample size. | Qualitatively consistent |
| GBLUP, fixed $\lambda$ | $n_{\mathrm{train}}^2p+n_{\mathrm{train}}^3$ | Runtime rises with SNP dimension and sample size because full train and train-test kernels are constructed. | Qualitatively consistent |
| NIG fit within TARP | $n_{\mathrm{train}}m^2+m^3$ per projection | Included in end-to-end TARP time, but not timed as a separate scaling experiment. | Not independently assessed |
| Aggregation over $B$ | Approximately linear in $B$ for fixed dimensions and projection sizes | $B=100$ is fixed in the full benchmark. | Not tested directly |

**Overall assessment.** The observed runtime trends are broadly consistent with the leading-order computational operations of the implemented algorithms. Screening followed by a capped low-dimensional regression has the lowest observed runtime. Exact Gram PCA and GBLUP incur costs associated with forming and decomposing or solving systems based on the full genotype matrix. Aggregated TARP incurs additional work because the projection and Bayesian fit are repeated. The practical TARP cost also depends on $p_\gamma$ and the sampled projection dimensions, not only on the original $p$.

### Dependence, architecture and screening dimension

The leading-order expressions do not contain $\rho$ or the causal architecture explicitly. Nevertheless, both can affect the realised number of RIS-selected markers, $p_\gamma$, which enters the projection cost. Thus dependence can affect runtime indirectly through the screening result.

The observed genotype-correlation diagnostic increases with the latent Gaussian correlation parameter. This verifies that the dependence manipulation is reflected in the generated binary genotype matrix. The observed Pearson correlation should not be interpreted as equal to the latent $\rho$, because genotype thresholding and allele frequencies affect its magnitude.

The number-of-selected-markers plot should be read alongside the runtime plot: it helps determine whether changes in TARP runtime accompany changes in the size of the selected set. SIS has a prescribed cap, whereas the RIS set size is random and depends on the marginal correlation scores.

### Empirical runtime summary

The following chunk computes a pooled descriptive summary from the saved replicate-level results. These pooled values combine different $n$, $p$, $\rho$ and causal architectures; matched-condition comparisons are more appropriate for attributing runtime differences to a particular design factor.

```{r empirical-runtime-summary, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

method_names <- c(
  "TARP_RIS_RP_aggregated" = "Aggregated TARP",
  "SIS_top_d_plus_NIG" = "SIS + NIG",
  "Exact_Gram_PCA_plus_NIG" = "Exact Gram PCA + NIG",
  "GBLUP_fixed_lambda" = "GBLUP (fixed lambda)"
)

runtime_table <- sim_raw %>%
  filter(method != "Mean_only_baseline") %>%
  group_by(method) %>%
  summarise(
    Replicate_runs = n(),
    Median_seconds = median(elapsed_seconds, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean_seconds = mean(elapsed_seconds, na.rm = TRUE),
    Minimum_seconds = min(elapsed_seconds, na.rm = TRUE),
    Maximum_seconds = max(elapsed_seconds, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Method = unname(method_names[method])
  ) %>%
  select(
    Method, Replicate_runs, Median_seconds, Mean_seconds,
    Minimum_seconds, Maximum_seconds
  )

knitr::kable(
  runtime_table,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Pooled empirical runtime across all simulation conditions (seconds)."
)
```

### Limitations and conclusion

The benchmark includes three SNP dimensions, two sample sizes and three replicates per design point. This grid is useful for checking qualitative runtime trends, but is too small to estimate asymptotic exponents reliably. Furthermore, the number of TARP projections is fixed at 100, so the predicted linear increase in runtime with $B$ is not directly tested. The individual costs of screening, sparse projection multiplication, NIG fitting and prediction are not all varied independently. Recorded elapsed times also depend on hardware, memory behaviour, BLAS implementation and operating-system load.

The GBLUP comparator uses a fixed regularization parameter, $\lambda=1$, and is therefore a computational reference rather than a tuned predictive benchmark. The mean-only baseline has zero recorded runtime by construction and is excluded from log-runtime comparisons.

In conclusion, the simulation provides qualitative empirical support for the dominant-operation complexity of the implementations. SIS + NIG is the fastest method in the pooled runtime summary because its downstream regression is restricted to a small selected set. Exact Gram PCA and GBLUP incur full-matrix costs, while aggregated TARP trades additional repeated projection and fitting work for a randomized, screened low-dimensional representation. These findings support qualitative agreement with theoretical complexity, but do not constitute a formal verification of asymptotic rates.

```{r overall-conclusions, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat("\n### 10.6 Overall conclusion\n\n")

cat(
  "This study investigated genomic structure and flowering-time ",
  "prediction in an Arabidopsis panel comprising 1,003 accessions ",
  "and approximately 1.71 million quality-controlled SNPs. ",
  "The genomic relationship matrix and PCA revealed substantial ",
  "genome-wide heterogeneity, although the leading principal ",
  "components individually captured only a modest fraction of total ",
  "genomic variation. In particular, PC3 and PC7 exhibited notable ",
  "associations with FT10, with a joint in-sample R-squared of ",
  "approximately 0.332. K-means clustering and latent class models ",
  "provided complementary representations of this heterogeneity, ",
  "and the resulting groups displayed appreciable differences in ",
  "their mean flowering times. The six-class LCA based on 20,000 ",
  "FT10-associated SNPs, for example, produced class means ranging ",
  "from approximately 75.8 to 110.8. These findings suggest that ",
  "genomic structure is relevant to flowering-time variation, ",
  "although the phenotype-guided marker selection in this particular ",
  "LCA makes its class-wise phenotype differences exploratory.\n\n",
  sep = ""
)

cat(
  "The prediction experiments demonstrated meaningful differences ",
  "between modelling strategies. Full-SNP GBLUP provided a strong ",
  "benchmark, with a mean FT10 test MSPE of approximately 107.2. ",
  "Targeted GBLUP achieved a small average reduction in MSPE of ",
  "approximately 0.57, performing better in seven of ten splits; ",
  "however, this improvement was modest relative to its split-to-split ",
  "standard error. Aggregated TARP achieved predictive performance ",
  "close to PCA, with mean MSPE values of approximately 117.5 and ",
  "118.3, respectively, whereas a single random projection performed ",
  "considerably worse. Among the screening-based approaches, RIS ",
  "followed by Ridge regression was the strongest reported method, ",
  "while the results also showed that very restrictive screening ",
  "budgets could lead to substantial losses in predictive accuracy. ",
  "Randomized SVD with two power iterations recovered approximately ",
  "99% of the energy captured by exact PCA, illustrating the potential ",
  "of randomized dimensionality reduction as a computationally ",
  "attractive alternative.\n\n",
  sep = ""
)

cat(
  "The separate computational simulation study reinforced the ",
  "trade-off between runtime and predictive performance. Screening ",
  "followed by NIG was particularly fast, while aggregated TARP, ",
  "Gram-matrix PCA and GBLUP required more computation. The results ",
  "therefore suggest that computationally efficient approximations ",
  "can be useful, but their predictive performance must be evaluated ",
  "against the information retained by the full genomic relationship ",
  "structure.\n\n",
  sep = ""
)

cat(
  "Several limitations qualify these findings. The number of ",
  "accessions is small relative to the number of genomic markers; ",
  "linkage disequilibrium challenges the conditional-independence ",
  "assumption of standard LCA; and phenotype-guided SNP or PC ",
  "selection can produce optimistic in-sample associations. In ",
  "particular, the high in-sample fit obtained using large numbers ",
  "of phenotype-selected genomic PCs should not be interpreted as ",
  "evidence of predictive performance. The ten repeated train-test ",
  "splits also reuse the same accession panel, so the reported ",
  "split-to-split standard errors do not represent uncertainty across ",
  "independent populations. Finally, FT16 is available for only ",
  "970 accessions, and its predictive replication should be ",
  "interpreted on that observed subset.\n\n",
  sep = ""
)

cat(
  "Overall, the study shows that genome-wide relatedness and ",
  "population structure contain useful information for explaining ",
  "and predicting flowering-time variation. GBLUP remains a strong ",
  "predictive benchmark in this dataset, while aggregated TARP, ",
  "randomized dimensionality reduction and screening-based methods ",
  "offer different accuracy-computation trade-offs. Future work ",
  "should prioritize independent validation, LD-pruned and ",
  "phenotype-independent marker panels, more extensive assessment ",
  "of latent-class stability, and nested evaluation of all ",
  "phenotype-dependent selection and tuning steps."
)
```
